questions.q: A 17-year-old holding a learner's permit is practicing driving. Other than a licensed driving instructor, who is the only person who may ride along as a passenger?
options: A licensed friend who is 18 years old and has held a driver's license for one full year
One person at least 20 years old who has held a license, unsuspended, for four or more consecutive years
Any licensed adult at least 18 years old who has a clean driving record for the past year
One person who is at least 21 years old and has held a license for two consecutive years
questions.ref: Pp. 5-6, Learner's Permit Passenger Restrictions: only a licensed instructor, or one person providing instruction who is at least 20, licensed 4+ consecutive years, no suspension in the prior four years.
questions.why: A 16- or 17-year-old permit holder may carry only a licensed driving instructor, or one person giving instruction who is at least 20 years old and has held a license for four or more years in a row with no suspension in the last four years. (Driver's Manual, page 6)
wrong: The person must be at least 20 years old with four or more years of licensed driving, not 18 with one year.
Being 18 with a clean record for one year is not enough; the rule is at least 20 years old and licensed four or more years in a row.
The age is at least 20, but the license must have been held for four or more years in a row, not two.

questions.q: A 16-year-old gets a learner's permit and completes driver education at a licensed commercial driving school. How long after the permit is issued must the teen wait before taking the road test?
options: 90 days
180 days
60 days
120 days
questions.ref: P. 6: applicants who complete driver education through a commercial or secondary school wait 120 days after permit issuance; all others wait 180 days (90 days is for applicants 18+).
questions.why: Teens who complete driver education at a commercial driving school or a high school program must wait 120 days after the permit is issued before the road test. (Driver's Manual, page 6)
wrong: The 90 day wait is for applicants who are 18 or older.
180 days is the wait for teens who did not train through a commercial or high school program.
The manual has no 60 day wait; the wait after school training is 120 days.

questions.q: Which of the following is allowed for a 17-year-old who has held a driver's license for nine months?
options: Driving to a job that ends at 11:30 p.m.
Driving to a friend's house at 11:30 p.m. to socialize
Taking calls on a hands-free earpiece while driving to school
Driving a classmate who is not a family member home from school in daylight
questions.ref: P. 8: curfew (11 p.m.-5 a.m.) excepts employment; months 7-12 allow only immediate-family additional passengers; no cell phone use, even hands-free, for 16-17 year olds.
questions.why: The 11 at night to 5 in the morning curfew does not apply when a teen is traveling for a job. (Driver's Manual, page 8)
wrong: Visiting a friend is not one of the curfew exceptions, so driving at 11:30 at night for this is not allowed.
Drivers who are 16 or 17 may not use any cell phone, even a hands-free one. (page 8)
In months seven through twelve, the only extra passengers allowed are immediate family members.

questions.q: Maria is 18, has never held a license in any state, and has just received her learner's permit. Which statement is true for her?
options: She may take the road test as soon as she completes 30 hours of classroom instruction, with no required waiting period
She must wait 180 days after getting the permit and also complete two hours of parent training
She must hold the permit at least 90 days before the road test and show an 8-hour safe driving course certificate
She does not need any driver education course because she is an adult; only the knowledge test
questions.ref: Pp. 4, 7: applicants 18+ must hold the permit at least 90 days and, if never licensed, take an 8-hour safe driving practices course and present the certificate.
questions.why: A person 18 or older must hold the permit at least 90 days before the road test, and someone never licensed must take an 8-hour safe driving practices course and show the certificate. (Driver's Manual, pages 4 and 7)
wrong: Adults must still hold the permit for at least 90 days, and the 30 hour classroom course is a teen requirement.
The 180 day wait and parent training are rules for 16- and 17-year-olds, not for adults.
Anyone never licensed, at any age, must take the 8-hour safe driving practices course.

questions.q: You use the 'penny test' on a tire by placing Lincoln's head into a tread groove. Part of Lincoln's head is covered by the tread. What does this tell you?
options: The tire has a safe amount of tread remaining
The tire is worn out and must be replaced immediately
The tire pressure is too low and needs more air
The tire will hydroplane at any speed on a wet road
questions.ref: P. 11: if any part of Lincoln's head is covered by the tread, you are driving with a safe amount of tread.
questions.why: In the penny test, if any part of Lincoln's head is covered by the tread, you have a safe amount of tread. (Driver's Manual, page 11)
wrong: A covered head means the tread is still deep enough, so the tire is not worn out.
The penny test checks tread depth, not air pressure; pressure is checked with a tire gauge.
The penny test does not measure hydroplaning, and a covered head means the tread is safe.

questions.q: A child is 20 months old but weighs 35 pounds. Under Connecticut's child restraint requirements, which restraint must be used?
options: A forward-facing child restraint with a 5-point harness, because the child weighs more than 30 pounds
A booster seat used with the vehicle's lap and shoulder belt
A rear-facing car seat with a 5-point harness, because the more restrictive category applies
The vehicle's seat belt alone, because the child is over 30 pounds
questions.ref: P. 12: if age and weight fall in two categories (the manual's example is under age two but over 30 pounds), the more restrictive requirement (rear-facing seat) applies.
questions.why: When a child's age and weight fall into two categories, such as under two years old but over 30 pounds, the more restrictive rule applies, which is a rear-facing seat. (Driver's Manual, page 12)
wrong: Weight alone does not decide it; a child under two must still ride rear-facing because the stricter category wins.
Booster seats are for older and heavier children, not a child under two.
A seat belt alone is never right for a child under two; a rear-facing seat with a 5-point harness is required.

questions.q: You are 25 years old and stopped at a red light. Which of the following is legal in Connecticut?
options: Holding the phone to read a text message because your vehicle is not moving
Holding the phone to make a call, since the vehicle is temporarily stopped by a signal
Holding your phone to type a new destination into its navigation app
Talking on the phone through a hands-free accessory
questions.ref: P. 13: hand-held phones/mobile devices are prohibited, including when stopped for traffic or a signal; hands-free accessories are permitted.
questions.why: Drivers 18 and older may talk on the phone only with a hands-free accessory, and hand-held use is banned even when stopped at a light. (Driver's Manual, page 13)
wrong: Hand-held phone use is illegal even when you are temporarily stopped at a traffic signal.
Being stopped by a signal does not make hand-held calls legal.
Typing into a hand-held phone is not allowed while stopped for a signal either.

questions.q: On a highway, looking 12 seconds ahead of your vehicle is about how far?
options: About one city block, the same distance as in city traffic
A quarter of a mile, or about four city blocks
One-third of a mile, which is about 10 seconds ahead
About half a mile, or roughly 24 seconds ahead
questions.ref: P. 14: safer drivers look 12 seconds ahead; in the city that is about one block, on the highway about four city blocks (a quarter of a mile).
questions.why: On the highway, looking 12 seconds ahead is about four city blocks, or a quarter of a mile. (Driver's Manual, page 14)
wrong: One block is the 12 second distance in the city; on the highway it is about four blocks.
One-third of a mile is the distance you must see ahead at hills and curves, not the 12 second look-ahead.
Half a mile is too far; the manual says about a quarter of a mile.

questions.q: You find an opening in traffic and move into the middle of a four-second gap. What is the following distance between you and the vehicle behind you?
options: Four seconds
Three seconds
Two seconds
One second
questions.ref: P. 20: if you move into the middle of a four-second opening, both you and the vehicle behind have a two-second following distance.
questions.why: If you move into the middle of a four-second opening, both you and the vehicle behind you have a two-second following distance. (Driver's Manual, page 20)
wrong: Four seconds is the whole opening, and you split it in half by moving into the middle.
Splitting a four-second gap in half leaves two seconds, not three.
Half of a four-second gap is two seconds, not one.

questions.q: You are traveling on a highway and realize you just missed the exit you needed. What should you do?
options: Continue to a place where you can safely turn around; do not back up
Stop on the shoulder and back up slowly to the exit with your flashers on
Slow down in your travel lane and back up carefully to the exit
Pull onto the shoulder and drive along it until you reach the exit again
questions.ref: Pp. 20, 24: if you miss your turn or exit, do not back up but go on to where you can safely turn around; unless told to by officials, never drive on the shoulder (p. 20).
questions.why: If you miss your exit, do not back up; go on to a place where you can safely turn around. (Driver's Manual, page 24)
wrong: Backing up on a highway is illegal and unsafe, even on the shoulder with flashers on.
Never back up in a travel lane, because other drivers do not expect it.
Unless officials tell you to, never drive on the shoulder of the road. (page 20)

questions.q: You are on a two-lane road at 55 mph and want to pass. Allowing for an oncoming vehicle traveling at the same speed, about how much clear road do you need to pass safely?
options: About 400 feet, the distance needed to stop at 50 mph
About 800 feet, the distance you travel in ten seconds
About one mile, or roughly 5,280 feet
More than 1,600 feet (about one-third of a mile)
questions.ref: P. 23: at 55 mph you travel over 800 feet in the 10 seconds needed to pass, and so does an oncoming vehicle, so you need over 1,600 feet.
questions.why: At 55 miles per hour you travel over 800 feet in the 10 seconds a pass takes, and so does an oncoming car, so you need over 1,600 feet, about one-third of a mile. (Driver's Manual, page 23)
wrong: About 400 feet is the stopping distance at 50 miles per hour, far too short for passing.
800 feet covers only your own travel and ignores the oncoming car, which also covers 800 feet.
A full mile is much more than the manual's figure of just over 1,600 feet.

questions.q: You are approaching an ice cream truck in your lane. It is stopped with flashing lights and its stop signal arm and crossing arm extended. What must you do?
options: Stop at least 25 feet away and wait until the arms are retracted before passing
Stop at least 10 feet away, then pass at no more than 5 mph and yield to pedestrians
Slow to 15 mph and pass, tapping your horn lightly to warn the children
Stop at least 10 feet away, then pass at no more than 10 mph and yield to pedestrians
questions.ref: P. 18: stop at least 10 feet from the front or back of the truck, then proceed at a reasonable speed up to 5 mph and yield to pedestrians crossing to or from the truck.
questions.why: You must stop at least 10 feet from the front or back of the ice cream truck, then pass at up to 5 miles per hour while yielding to pedestrians. (Driver's Manual, page 18)
wrong: The stopping distance is at least 10 feet, and you may pass after stopping without waiting for the arms to retract.
You must stop first, and the manual never says to tap your horn here.
The stop distance is right, but the top speed for passing is 5 miles per hour, not 10.

questions.q: You have a green light, but a pedestrian carrying a white cane is still crossing the road in front of your vehicle. What should you do?
options: Remain stopped until the pedestrian is out of the road, and do not use your horn
Tap your horn lightly so the pedestrian knows that you are waiting for him or her
Proceed slowly behind the pedestrian since you have the green light
Edge forward to show the pedestrian where your vehicle is positioned
questions.ref: Pp. 16, 36: stop and stay stopped until the pedestrian is out of the road, even with a green light; do not use your horn near a blind pedestrian.
questions.why: For a pedestrian with a white cane, stop and stay stopped until the person is out of the road, even if you have a green light, and do not use your horn. (Driver's Manual, pages 16 and 36)
wrong: Do not use your horn around blind pedestrians, because it could confuse or frighten them.
A green light does not let you go; you must remain stopped until the pedestrian is out of the road.
You must stay stopped, not creep forward, while the pedestrian crosses.

questions.q: You have just passed a bicyclist, and you plan to turn right at the next intersection. What should you do?
options: Turn right right away, since you are already ahead of the bicyclist
Speed up and tap your horn to warn the bicyclist before you turn
Not turn right immediately; slow down and let the bicyclist clear the intersection first
Slow down or stop quickly in front of the bicyclist so that you can signal your turn
questions.ref: Pp. 17, 24: do not turn right immediately after passing a bicyclist; slow down and let the cyclist clear the intersection first. Do not slow or stop quickly.
questions.why: Never turn right right after passing a bicyclist; slow down and let the cyclist clear the intersection first. (Driver's Manual, pages 17 and 24)
wrong: Turning right just after passing a bicyclist can cut the rider off and cause a crash.
Speeding up and honking can startle the bicyclist into your path.
The manual says do not slow down or stop quickly in front of a bicyclist, because your brakes are stronger than theirs.

questions.q: A car is pulled over on the shoulder of the highway with its hazard lights flashing. You are in the right lane. According to Connecticut's Move Over Law, you must:
options: Hold the posted speed limit and stay in your lane, since it is not an emergency vehicle
Come to a complete stop until the vehicle returns to traffic
Move over one lane only if the vehicle is a police car or ambulance
Slow down below the posted speed limit and move over one lane when it is safe to do so
questions.ref: P. 16: when any vehicle is pulled over on any part of a highway, drivers must slow down (below the posted limit) and move over one lane when safe.
questions.why: Connecticut's Move Over Law says when any vehicle is pulled over on a highway, you must slow down below the posted speed limit and move over one lane when it is safe. (Driver's Manual, page 16)
wrong: The law covers any vehicle pulled over, not just emergency vehicles, and you must slow down.
The law asks you to slow down and move over, not to stop.
The law applies to any vehicle that is pulled over, not only police cars or ambulances.

questions.q: Which statement about sharing the road with large trucks is correct?
options: Trucks can accelerate faster than cars because of their powerful engines
If you cannot see the truck driver's face in his side mirror, he cannot see you
When a truck approaches an intersection, passing it on the right is safe
A truck's blind spots are limited to the area alongside the cab
questions.ref: Pp. 19-20: No-Zones exist on the sides, front and rear; trucks accelerate more slowly; resist passing on the right near an intersection; if you can't see the driver's face in his mirror he can't see you.
questions.why: Trucks have large blind spots on the sides, and if you cannot see the driver's face in his side mirror, he cannot see you. (Driver's Manual, page 19)
wrong: The manual says trucks accelerate more slowly than cars.
Do not pass on the right of a truck near an intersection, because a right-turning truck could trap you against the curb. (page 20)
No-Zones are on the sides, front, and rear of a truck, not only beside the cab.

questions.q: Snow has packed down on the road you are driving on. About how much should you reduce your speed?
options: Cut your speed in half
Reduce your speed by about 10 mph
Slow to a crawl
Reduce your speed by about one-quarter
questions.ref: P. 25: on a wet road reduce speed by about 10 mph; on packed snow cut your speed in half; on ice slow to a crawl.
questions.why: On packed snow, you should cut your speed in half. (Driver's Manual, page 25)
wrong: Slowing by about 10 miles per hour is the advice for a wet road, not packed snow.
Slowing to a crawl is the advice for ice.
The manual says to cut your speed in half on packed snow, not by one-quarter.

questions.q: On a long highway trip you notice you are yawning repeatedly and drifting toward the edge of your lane. What is the best response?
options: Turn up the radio and roll down the window until you arrive
Speed up so you shorten the time you must stay awake
Drink two cups of coffee and keep driving, since caffeine prevents fatigue-related crashes
Pull off at the next exit or rest area and take a 15 to 20 minute nap
questions.ref: P. 28: warning signs include turning up the radio/rolling down the window and drifting; stop driving, nap 15-20 minutes; do not rely on caffeine, which wears off.
questions.why: Yawning and drifting are warning signs of fatigue, so stop driving and take a 15 to 20 minute nap in a safe place. (Driver's Manual, page 28)
wrong: Turning up the radio and opening the window are warning signs of fatigue, not a cure.
Speeding while tired raises your crash risk, and the manual says to stop driving.
Caffeine wears off, and the manual says not to rely on it to prevent fatigue.

questions.q: Which of the following contains the same amount of alcohol as a 12-ounce regular beer?
options: An 8-ounce glass of wine
Three ounces of 80-proof liquor
A 5-ounce glass of wine
A 16-ounce mug of beer
questions.ref: P. 33: one alcohol drink is 1.5 oz of 80-proof liquor, 12 oz of beer, or a 5 oz glass of wine.
questions.why: One alcohol drink is 12 ounces of beer, a 5 ounce glass of wine, or 1.5 ounces of 80-proof liquor. (Driver's Manual, page 33)
wrong: A drink of wine is 5 ounces, so 8 ounces is more than one drink.
A drink of liquor is 1.5 ounces, so 3 ounces is two drinks.
A drink of beer is 12 ounces, so 16 ounces is more than one drink.

questions.q: A 19-year-old driver arrested for DUI tests at .02 percent BAC. What does Connecticut's zero tolerance law require?
options: No penalty, because .02 percent is too low to be considered impaired
A suspension of at least 45 days and an ignition interlock device for at least one year
A suspension of at least 30 days with no ignition interlock requirement
A suspension of at least 45 days and an ignition interlock device for only six months
questions.ref: P. 33: under 21, a test result of .02 percent or higher means a suspension of at least 45 days and an IID for at least one year (six months applies to adults who fail a test).
questions.why: Under zero tolerance, a driver under 21 who tests at 0.02 percent or higher faces a suspension of at least 45 days and an ignition interlock device for at least one year. (Driver's Manual, page 33)
wrong: For drivers under 21, 0.02 percent or higher does bring a penalty under zero tolerance.
The suspension is at least 45 days, and an ignition interlock device is required.
The six month interlock period is for adults who fail a test; under 21 it is at least one year.

questions.q: You and another driver arrive at a four-way stop at the same moment. The other driver is on your right. Who goes first?
options: You, because the vehicle on the left goes first at a four-way stop
Whichever driver is going straight rather than turning
The driver in the larger or heavier vehicle
The other driver, since the vehicle on the right goes first
questions.ref: P. 36: at a four-way stop the first to arrive goes first; if more than one vehicle arrives at the same time, the vehicle on the right goes first.
questions.why: At a four-way stop, if two vehicles arrive at the same time, the vehicle on the right goes first. (Driver's Manual, page 36)
wrong: The vehicle on the right goes first, not the one on the left.
The manual's rule is based on who is on the right, not on who is going straight.
Vehicle size does not matter; the vehicle on the right goes first.

questions.q: Assuming no signs apply, which parking position does NOT violate the manual's no-parking rules?
options: Parked 12 feet from a fire hydrant and 6 inches from the curb
Parked 20 feet away from a stop sign on the corner
Parked 15 feet from a pedestrian safety zone in the block
Parked 18 inches away from the curb on a quiet street
questions.ref: P. 37: do not park within 25 feet of a stop sign or pedestrian safety zone, within 10 feet of a hydrant, or more than one foot from the curb.
questions.why: You may not park within 10 feet of a fire hydrant or more than one foot from the curb, so 12 feet from a hydrant and 6 inches from the curb is fine. (Driver's Manual, page 37)
wrong: You may not park within 25 feet of a stop sign, so 20 feet is too close.
You may not park within 25 feet of a pedestrian safety zone, so 15 feet is too close.
You may not park more than one foot from the curb, and 18 inches is more than a foot.

questions.q: A three-sided, pennant-shaped sign posted on the left side of a two-lane, two-way road means:
options: A school zone is ahead
You must yield to oncoming traffic
A no-passing zone begins
A railroad crossing is ahead
questions.ref: P. 46: the pennant shape marks the beginning of a no-passing zone and is on the left side of a two-lane, two-way road.
questions.why: The pennant-shaped sign, posted on the left side of a two-lane, two-way road, marks the beginning of a no-passing zone. (Driver's Manual, page 46)
wrong: School zones are marked by a five-sided pentagon sign.
A yield sign is a downward-pointing triangle, not a pennant.
A railroad crossing ahead is shown by a round sign.

questions.q: On a two-lane road the center of the roadway has two yellow lines: a solid line on the oncoming side and a dashed line on your side. What does this allow?
options: You may not pass, because any solid yellow line prohibits passing
You may pass if it is safe, because the dashed line is on your side
You may pass only when turning left into a driveway
The lines mark a shared center left-turn lane
questions.ref: P. 44: a dashed yellow line alongside a solid yellow line means passing is permitted on the side of the broken line, but not on the side of the solid line.
questions.why: When a dashed yellow line runs next to a solid yellow line, passing is allowed on the side of the dashed line but not on the side of the solid line. (Driver's Manual, page 44)
wrong: A solid line only stops passing for traffic on its own side; your side has the dashed line.
The dashed line on your side lets you pass when it is safe, not only for left turns.
A shared center left-turn lane has a solid and dashed yellow line on each side of the lane, not one pair at the center.

questions.q: You approach an intersection with a flashing red traffic light. You must:
options: Come to a full stop and proceed when it is safe
Slow down and proceed with caution through the intersection
Stop only if there is cross traffic approaching
Stop only if pedestrians are crossing in front of you
questions.ref: P. 45: a flashing red light means the same as a stop sign: full stop, then proceed when safe (slow and proceed with caution describes a flashing yellow).
questions.why: A flashing red light means the same as a stop sign, so come to a full stop and go when it is safe. (Driver's Manual, page 45)
wrong: Slowing down and going ahead with caution is what a flashing yellow light means.
You must stop at a flashing red light every time, whether or not cross traffic is coming.
You must make a full stop at a flashing red light even when no pedestrians are crossing.

questions.q: A Connecticut learner's permit is valid until you obtain a driver's license or for how long after the date it is issued, whichever comes first?
options: 1 year
18 months
2 years
180 days
questions.ref: P. 5 NOTE: the permit is valid until you obtain a driver's license or 2 years from the date issued, whichever comes first.
questions.why: A learner's permit is valid until you get a driver's license or for 2 years from the date it is issued, whichever comes first. (Driver's Manual, page 5)
wrong: The permit lasts up to 2 years, not 1 year.
The permit lasts up to 2 years, not 18 months.
180 days is a road test waiting period, not how long the permit is valid.

questions.q: A 16-year-old obtains a learner's permit. Which requirement applies to the teen's parent or legal guardian?
options: Complete two hours of instruction with the teen on laws for drivers under 18 and teen driving dangers
Complete the full 30 hours of classroom instruction alongside the teen at the driving school
Have held a license for at least ten years before supervising any of the teen's practice sessions
Sign off on a mandatory 100 hours of behind-the-wheel practice before the road test is scheduled
questions.ref: Pp. 6-7: parent/guardian must complete two hours of instruction (included in the 8-hour program); 100 hours is only recommended (p. 30).
questions.why: A parent or legal guardian of a 16- or 17-year-old permit holder must complete two hours of instruction with the teen on the laws for drivers under 18 and the dangers of teen driving. (Driver's Manual, page 6)
wrong: The 30 hour classroom course is for the teen; the parent's requirement is a two-hour class.
The manual has no ten year rule; a person who supervises practice must be at least 20 and licensed four or more years.
The law requires 40 hours of practice; 100 hours is only recommended. (page 30)

questions.q: Dana, 17, received her driver's license three months ago. Which person may she carry as a passenger?
options: Her 15-year-old brother, because he is immediate family
Her best friend, a licensed 17-year-old driver
Her cousin, who is 19 and has been licensed for two years
Her parent, who holds a valid driver's license
questions.ref: P. 8: in the first six months, only a licensed instructor, parents/guardian (one with a valid license), or one person 20+ licensed 4+ years; immediate family is added only in months seven through twelve.
questions.why: In the first six months of a license, a teen may carry a licensed driving instructor, a parent or guardian with a valid license, or one person 20 or older licensed for four or more years. (Driver's Manual, page 8)
wrong: Immediate family members are allowed only in months seven through twelve, and Dana has had her license three months.
Teen friends are not allowed as passengers during the first year of the license.
The adult passenger must be at least 20 and licensed four or more years in a row, so a 19-year-old does not qualify.

questions.q: A 16-year-old driver is convicted of a first violation of the passenger restrictions. What is the penalty?
options: A 60-day suspension and a $175 license restoration fee
A 30-day suspension and a $175 license restoration fee
A 6-month suspension and a $175 license restoration fee
A 90-day suspension and a $175 license restoration fee
questions.ref: P. 34 table: GDL violations (passenger restrictions, curfew, etc.) carry a 30-day suspension for a 1st offense; 6 months for 2nd and subsequent offenses.
questions.why: A first violation of the teen passenger restrictions brings a 30-day suspension and a 175 dollar license restoration fee. (Driver's Manual, page 34)
wrong: 60 days is the first-offense suspension for speeding 20 miles per hour over the limit.
A 6-month suspension applies to a second or later passenger restriction violation.
The manual's table lists 30 days for a first passenger restriction violation, not 90.

questions.q: You are wearing your seat belt, but your adult front-seat passenger refuses to buckle up. What does Connecticut law say about the passenger?
options: The passenger is breaking the law and could be cited and fined $75
Nothing, because only the driver must wear a belt in Connecticut
The passenger may ride unbuckled because the car has front airbags
The passenger gets only a warning, since adults are allowed to choose
questions.ref: Pp. 12-13: if either the driver or the passenger fails to wear a seat belt, each could be cited and fined $75; belts are required even with airbags.
questions.why: In Connecticut it is illegal to drive or to be a passenger without wearing a safety belt. A person who does not wear one could be cited and fined 75 dollars. (Driver's Manual, page 12)
wrong: The law covers passengers too. It is illegal to be a passenger without a safety belt.
Belts are required even if the vehicle has airbags. Airbags do not protect you in side or rear crashes or rollovers.
There is no choice for adults. Every passenger must wear a safety belt, and the fine is 75 dollars.

questions.q: Studded tires are permitted in Connecticut during which period?
options: October 1 through March 31
December 1 through April 15
November 1 through March 15
November 15 through April 30
questions.ref: P. 25: studded tires are permitted in Connecticut from November 15th through April 30th.
questions.why: Studded tires are allowed in Connecticut from November 15th through April 30th. (Driver's Manual, page 25)
wrong: The season starts November 15th and ends April 30th, not October 1 to March 31.
The season starts November 15th, not December 1, and ends April 30th.
The season runs to April 30th, and it starts November 15th, not November 1.

questions.q: The insurance company reports that coverage on your registered vehicle was canceled, and DMV sends you a warning notice. If you do not respond to the notice, what happens?
options: The vehicle's registration is suspended
Your driver's license is suspended for 45 days
The vehicle is towed and impounded
The insurance compliance fine is waived
questions.ref: P. 13: failure to respond to the warning notice will result in suspension of the registration; responding and showing proof of insurance avoids further action.
questions.why: If you do not respond to the DMV's insurance warning notice, your vehicle's registration will be suspended. (Driver's Manual, page 13)
wrong: The manual says the registration is suspended, not your driver's license.
The manual's penalty is a registration suspension, not towing.
The fine is not waived; you avoid more trouble only by responding, showing proof of insurance, and paying the fine.

questions.q: After completing a sharp turn, how should you straighten the steering wheel?
options: Let it slide back through your fingers as the vehicle straightens out
Release the wheel briefly and let it center itself as the vehicle straightens
Straighten it out by hand; letting it slip through your fingers is dangerous
Push it back to center with one hand at the 12 o'clock position
questions.ref: P. 14: when you complete a turn, straighten the steering wheel by hand; letting it slip through your fingers could be dangerous.
questions.why: When you finish a turn, straighten the steering wheel by hand, because letting it slip through your fingers could be dangerous. (Driver's Manual, page 14)
wrong: The manual says letting the wheel slip through your fingers could be dangerous.
Letting go of the wheel means you are not steering; straighten it by hand instead.
The manual says to straighten the wheel by hand, not to push it with one hand from the top.

questions.q: A driver is tailgating you on a two-lane road with no right lane available. What should you do?
options: Brake sharply a few times to discourage the driver from following so closely behind you
Speed up until the gap between you and the other driver is large enough
Drive onto the shoulder and stop so that the other driver can go by you
Wait until the road ahead is clear, then slowly reduce speed so the driver goes around you
questions.ref: P. 22: if there is no right lane, wait until the road ahead is clear, then reduce speed slowly; never slow down quickly to discourage a tailgater.
questions.why: If you are tailgated with no right lane, wait until the road ahead is clear, then slow down gradually so the tailgater goes around you. (Driver's Manual, page 22)
wrong: Never slow down quickly to discourage a tailgater, because it raises your risk of being hit from behind.
Speeding up does not solve tailgating, and the manual says to reduce speed slowly instead.
Unless officials tell you to, never drive on the shoulder. (page 20)

questions.q: A driver behind you is clearly trying to pass on a two-lane road. What does the manual recommend?
options: Slow down to allow room in front of you, which lets the pass finish sooner
Speed up slightly so that the passing driver stays behind you
Move toward the centerline so the driver can see farther ahead of you
Hold your speed and sound your horn at the driver who is behind you
questions.ref: P. 21: when the driver behind you wants to pass, use a four-second following distance; slow down to allow room in front and to allow the pass to be completed sooner.
questions.why: When the driver behind you wants to pass, slow down to allow room in front of you, which also helps the pass finish sooner. (Driver's Manual, page 21)
wrong: Never speed up when you are being passed; it makes passing more dangerous.
Crowding the centerline is unsafe; it is safest to drive in the center of your lane. (page 22)
The manual says to slow down, and honking at the passing driver can provoke trouble.

questions.q: You approach a hill that blocks your view of the road ahead. You should not start to pass if you are within how far of the hill or curve?
options: 400 feet
One-quarter of a mile
One-third of a mile
One-half mile
questions.ref: P. 24: you must see at least one-third of a mile (about 10 seconds) ahead; do not start to pass within one-third of a mile of a hill or curve.
questions.why: You must be able to see at least one-third of a mile ahead, so do not start to pass within one-third of a mile of a hill or curve. (Driver's Manual, page 24)
wrong: 400 feet is the stopping distance at 50 miles per hour, not the passing rule for hills.
A quarter of a mile is the 12 second look-ahead distance; the hill and curve rule is one-third of a mile.
The manual's rule is one-third of a mile, not one-half mile.

questions.q: You are in the middle of an intersection when you hear a siren and see an emergency vehicle approaching from behind. What should you do?
options: Stop immediately where you are
Drive through the intersection, then pull over to the right and stop
Pull to the left side of the intersection and stop
Continue driving at your normal speed until the vehicle passes you
questions.ref: P. 37: if you are in an intersection, drive through the intersection before you pull over to the right edge of the road and stop.
questions.why: If you are in an intersection when an emergency vehicle comes, drive through the intersection first, then pull over to the right and stop. (Driver's Manual, page 37)
wrong: Stopping in the intersection could block the emergency vehicle; clear the intersection first.
You must pull over to the right edge of the road, not the left.
You must pull over and stop until the emergency vehicle has passed.

questions.q: A school bus is stopped with its red lights flashing. In which situation are you NOT required to stop?
options: The bus is traveling toward you and a median or physical barrier separates the roadway
You are approaching an intersection where the bus is stopped with its red lights flashing
The bus is on the opposite side of an undivided two-lane road with no median or barrier
The bus is on your side of the road and no children are visible yet near the bus
questions.ref: P. 37: stop for a stopped school bus with red lights flashing on your side, the opposite side, or at an intersection; not required if a median or physical barrier separates the roadway.
questions.why: You do not have to stop when the school bus is traveling toward you and a median or other physical barrier separates the roadway. (Driver's Manual, page 37)
wrong: You must stop for a school bus stopped at an intersection you are approaching.
Without a median or barrier, you must stop even when the bus is on the opposite side.
You must stop for a bus on your side whether or not you can see children.

questions.q: At an intersection with no painted crosswalk lines, a pedestrian steps to the curb and raises a hand toward your vehicle. What must you do?
options: Proceed, since pedestrians must wait for a marked crosswalk before crossing
Tap your horn and continue if the pedestrian has not yet entered the road
Speed up to clear the intersection before the pedestrian steps off the curb
Slow or stop and grant the right-of-way, since every intersection has a crosswalk
questions.ref: P. 16: there is a crosswalk at every intersection; drivers must slow or stop and grant the right-of-way when a pedestrian steps to the curb and indicates intent to cross by raising a hand.
questions.why: There is a crosswalk at every intersection, even without painted lines, and you must slow or stop and yield when a pedestrian at the curb raises a hand to cross. (Driver's Manual, page 16)
wrong: Every intersection has a crosswalk, even if it is not marked with painted lines.
Raising a hand at the curb shows intent to cross, and you must yield.
Speeding up to beat a pedestrian is dangerous; you must slow or stop and yield.

questions.q: You are waiting to pull out from a side street when an approaching motorcycle has its turn signal flashing toward your street, but it has not begun to turn. What should you do?
options: Pull out right away, since the motorcycle is signaling a turn toward your street
Flash your headlights at the rider and then pull out in front of the motorcycle
Wait until the motorcycle actually begins to turn, since its signal may be stuck on
Sound your horn briefly and then pull out ahead of it
questions.ref: Pp. 18, 21: do not assume a motorcycle is turning because its signal is flashing; do not pull out until you see it actually beginning to turn.
questions.why: Do not assume a motorcycle is turning just because its signal is flashing, since the signal may not cancel by itself; wait until it actually begins to turn. (Driver's Manual, page 18)
wrong: Motorcycle signals may not self-cancel, so a flashing signal does not prove it will turn.
Flashing your lights does not make it safe; wait until you see the motorcycle start to turn.
Honking does not make it safe to pull out; wait until the motorcycle actually turns.

questions.q: You are driving toward a person riding a horse along the edge of a public road. What should you do?
options: Reduce your speed, or stop if necessary, and do not sound your horn
Sound your horn lightly so the horse and rider hear you coming up behind them
Pass as quickly as possible to limit the time you are near the horse
Flash your high beams at the rider to signal that you are approaching
questions.ref: P. 18: reduce speed (or stop) when approaching a horse, drive at a reasonable distance, and it is illegal to sound your horn or cause loud noises near a horse.
questions.why: When you approach a horse, reduce your speed or stop if needed, and it is illegal to sound your horn or make loud noises near it. (Driver's Manual, page 18)
wrong: Sounding your horn near a horse is illegal.
You must slow down and drive at a reasonable speed and distance near a horse, not rush past it.
The manual's rule is to slow down and avoid frightening the horse, not to signal with your lights.

questions.q: Your tires hydroplane on a wet road. Which action is correct?
options: Brake firmly to try to regain traction as quickly as possible
Ease off the gas and keep the steering wheel straight
Steer sharply toward the edge of the road to get out of the water
Accelerate gently to power through the standing water
questions.ref: P. 25: if tires lose traction on water, ease off the gas, keep the steering wheel straight, and do not try to stop or turn until the tires grip again.
questions.why: If your tires lose traction on water, ease your foot off the gas and keep the steering wheel straight. (Driver's Manual, page 25)
wrong: Do not try to stop until your tires are gripping the road again.
Do not turn while hydroplaning unless it is an emergency, and then only slowly, or you will skid.
Speed causes hydroplaning, so ease off the gas instead.

questions.q: After an angry exchange with another driver, a hostile motorist begins to follow you. What should you do?
options: Drive home so you can call the police from there once you are safely inside
Make eye contact and gesture to show you are not intimidated by the driver
Pull over on the shoulder and wait for the driver to pass by you
Drive to a police station or other public, well-lit place where you can get help
questions.ref: P. 26: do not make eye contact; if a motorist pursues you, do not go home - drive to a police station, convenience store, or other public, well-lit location.
questions.why: If a hostile motorist follows you, do not go home; drive to a police station, convenience store, or other public, well-lit place where you can get help. (Driver's Manual, page 26)
wrong: The manual says if a motorist pursues you, do not go home.
Do not make eye contact or gesture, because it can push the other driver to violence.
The manual says to drive to a public, well-lit place, not to stop and wait on the shoulder.

questions.q: A 35-year-old driver arrested for DUI refuses to take a blood, breath, or urine test. What is the consequence?
options: No penalty, since there is no test result
License suspension of at least 30 days with no ignition interlock requirement
License suspension of at least 45 days and an ignition interlock device for at least one year
License suspension of at least 45 days and an ignition interlock device for at least six months
questions.ref: P. 33: regardless of age, refusing a test means suspension for at least 45 days and an IID for at least one year (six months applies to a failed test by an adult).
questions.why: Regardless of age, refusing a test brings a license suspension of at least 45 days and an ignition interlock device for at least one year. (Driver's Manual, page 33)
wrong: Refusing the test is itself penalized, even without a test result.
The suspension is at least 45 days, and an ignition interlock device is required.
Six months is the interlock period for an adult who fails a test; refusing means at least one year.

questions.q: Under Connecticut's Operator Retraining Program, which driver must complete a certified retraining program?
options: A 22-year-old with two moving violations
A 22-year-old with one moving violation
A 30-year-old with two moving violations
A 45-year-old with one moving violation
questions.ref: P. 35: age 24 or younger with two or more moving or suspension violations must complete the program; age 25 or older needs three or more.
questions.why: Anyone 24 or younger with two or more moving or suspension violations must complete the operator retraining program. (Driver's Manual, page 35)
wrong: Drivers 24 or younger need two or more violations, not one.
Drivers 25 or older need three or more violations before retraining is required.
A 45-year-old needs three or more violations, not one.

questions.q: Which statement about driving in a roundabout is correct?
options: Traffic already in the roundabout must yield to vehicles waiting to enter it
Entering traffic must yield to circulating traffic and pedestrians in the crosswalk
You should stop inside the roundabout to let a vehicle enter from another road
You should use your left turn signal as you reach your intended exit
questions.ref: P. 37: entering traffic yields to circulating traffic and pedestrians; do not stop within the roundabout to allow others to enter; use the right turn signal at your exit.
questions.why: Traffic entering a roundabout must yield to traffic already circulating and to pedestrians in the crosswalk. (Driver's Manual, page 37)
wrong: Entering traffic yields to circulating traffic, not the other way around.
Do not stop inside the roundabout to let traffic enter from another road.
Use your right turn signal when you are about to reach your exit, not your left.

questions.q: Your brakes suddenly stop working while you are driving. What should you try first?
options: Pull the parking brake handle sharply
Shift to a lower gear
Turn the ignition to the lock position
Pump the brake pedal several times
questions.ref: P. 39: pump the brake pedal; if that fails, slowly use the parking brake; then shift to lower gears. Turning the ignition to lock while moving locks the steering (p. 40).
questions.why: If your brakes fail, first pump the brake pedal several times, which often builds up enough pressure to stop. (Driver's Manual, page 39)
wrong: The parking brake comes second, and you should pull it slowly so you do not lock the wheels and skid.
Shifting to a lower gear is the third step, after pumping the brakes and using the parking brake.
Turning the ignition to lock while moving locks the steering, and you lose control. (page 40)

questions.q: You reach an intersection where the traffic signal is completely dark because it is not working. What does Connecticut law require?
options: Slow down and proceed as if the light were flashing yellow
Stop as though the intersection were controlled by a stop sign
Yield to cross traffic but continue without stopping if the way is clear
Follow the lead of the vehicle ahead of you
questions.ref: Pp. 15, 25: state law requires a driver at an intersection with an inoperative stop light to stop as though controlled by a stop sign.
questions.why: Connecticut law requires you to stop at a broken traffic light as though the intersection had a stop sign. (Driver's Manual, pages 15 and 25)
wrong: The law says to treat a broken light as a stop sign, not a flashing yellow.
You must come to a full stop, as at a stop sign, even when the way looks clear.
Each driver must stop as at a stop sign, whatever the car ahead does.

questions.q: A double solid white line on the pavement between lanes means:
options: Lane changing is allowed when it is safe
The lane on your left is reserved for buses
Lane changing is prohibited
Passing is allowed on the left side only
questions.ref: P. 44, Other Markings: a double solid white line prohibits lane changing.
questions.why: A double solid white line prohibits lane changing. (Driver's Manual, page 44)
wrong: Dashed white lines allow lane changes; a double solid white line forbids them.
Bus lanes are marked with signs and the words transit or bus, not by a double white line.
A double solid white line prohibits changing lanes, including to pass.

questions.q: While you are waiting to turn left, the signal changes to a steady yellow left-pointing arrow. What does this mean?
options: The protection of the green arrow is ending; prepare to stop
A green arrow is about to appear, so wait for it to turn green
You must treat the signal as a four-way stop and then proceed
You should speed up to finish the turn before the light changes
questions.ref: P. 45: a yellow arrow means the protection of a green arrow is ending; if you are turning in the direction of the arrow, you should prepare to stop.
questions.why: A yellow arrow means the protection of the green arrow is ending, so if you are turning that way, prepare to stop. (Driver's Manual, page 45)
wrong: A yellow arrow comes after the green arrow, as its protection is ending.
A flashing red light, not a yellow arrow, is treated like a stop sign.
The manual says to prepare to stop, not speed up.

questions.q: A parent is supervising a learner's permit holder. Where must the parent sit, and who is responsible for the vehicle's safe operation?
options: In the back seat behind the driver; only the permit holder is responsible
In the front passenger seat; only the permit holder is responsible for it
In the back seat behind the driver; only the supervising parent is responsible
In the front passenger seat; the parent and the driver share responsibility
questions.ref: P. 5: the instructor must sit in the front passenger seat, alert and ready to take over; safe operation is the responsibility of both the instructor and the driver.
questions.why: The person giving instruction must sit in the front passenger seat, alert and ready to take over, and safe operation is the responsibility of both that person and the driver. (Driver's Manual, page 5)
wrong: The instructor must sit in the front passenger seat, and both people share responsibility.
The seat is right, but responsibility is shared by the instructor and the driver.
The instructor must sit up front, and the driver is also responsible.

questions.q: Connecticut requires 16- and 17-year-old license applicants to have at least how many hours of behind-the-wheel, on-the-road training?
options: 30 hours
40 hours
100 hours
8 hours
questions.ref: Pp. 6-7, 30: all 16-17 year old applicants must have at least 40 hours of behind-the-wheel training (100 hours is only recommended).
questions.why: All 16- and 17-year-old applicants must have at least 40 hours of behind-the-wheel, on-the-road training. (Driver's Manual, page 7)
wrong: 30 hours is the classroom requirement, not behind-the-wheel time.
100 hours is recommended, but the legal minimum is 40. (page 30)
8 hours is the safe driving practices course or a part of school training, not the full requirement.

questions.q: An applicant for a license is blind in one eye. What does Connecticut require?
options: The other eye must be at least 20/20 with a visual field of 180 degrees or more
The applicant cannot be licensed under any circumstances
The other eye must be at least 20/40 with a visual field of 100 degrees or more
The other eye must be at least 20/70 with a visual field of at least 70 degrees
questions.ref: P. 5: if the applicant is blind in one eye, the other eye must be at least 20/40 with a minimal visual field of 100 degrees or more.
questions.why: If an applicant is blind in one eye, the other eye must be at least twenty forty with a visual field of at least 100 degrees. (Driver's Manual, page 5)
wrong: The standard is twenty forty with 100 degrees, not twenty twenty with 180 degrees.
A person blind in one eye can still be licensed if the other eye meets the standard.
The standard is twenty forty with at least 100 degrees, not twenty seventy with 70 degrees.

questions.q: Which requirement applies to a person who is 18 or older and has never held a license in Connecticut or any other state?
options: Take an 8-hour safe driving practices course and present a certificate of attendance
Complete 30 hours of classroom instruction and 40 hours of behind-the-wheel training
Complete two hours of parent training together with a parent or legal guardian
Wait 180 days after receiving the permit before being allowed to take the road test
questions.ref: P. 7: applicants 18+ without a prior license must take an 8-hour course on safe driving practices and present a certificate; 30/40-hour and parent training apply to 16-17 year olds.
questions.why: Anyone 18 or older who has never held a license must take an 8-hour safe driving practices course and present a certificate. (Driver's Manual, page 7)
wrong: The 30 hour classroom and 40 hour driving rules are for 16- and 17-year-olds.
Parent training applies to parents of 16- and 17-year-olds.
Applicants 18 or older wait 90 days, not 180.

questions.q: Why should you make sure there are no loose objects on the floor of your vehicle before you drive?
options: Loose objects can trigger the airbag sensors at the wrong time
Items on the floor reduce your vehicle's fuel economy on long trips
Objects on the floor make the horn less effective as a warning
An object could roll under the brake pedal and prevent you from stopping
questions.ref: P. 12, Loose Objects: ensure no objects on the floor could roll under the brake pedal and prevent you from stopping, or hit someone in a sudden stop or crash.
questions.why: Make sure nothing is on the floor that could roll under the brake pedal and stop you from braking. (Driver's Manual, page 12)
wrong: The manual's concern is objects hitting someone or blocking the brake pedal, not airbag sensors.
The manual's concern is safety, not fuel economy.
The manual does not connect loose objects to the horn; the danger is blocking the brake pedal.

questions.q: A licensed 17-year-old receives a phone call and wants to use a hands-free earpiece while driving. Which statement is correct?
options: Not allowed; drivers 16 or 17 may not use any cell phone, even hands-free
Allowed, because drivers may use hands-free accessories in Connecticut
Allowed only while the vehicle is stopped at a traffic light
Allowed only when a parent is seated in the front passenger seat
questions.ref: Pp. 8, 13: drivers who are 16 or 17 are not permitted to use any cell phone or mobile electronic device, including hands-free.
questions.why: Drivers who are 16 or 17 may not use any cell phone or mobile electronic device, even a hands-free one. (Driver's Manual, page 13)
wrong: Hands-free use is allowed only for drivers 18 and older.
Teen drivers may not use a phone while driving, even when stopped at a light.
Having a parent in the car does not change the teen cell phone ban.

questions.q: Where is a rear-facing child restraint system NOT permitted to be placed in Connecticut?
options: In the rear seat directly behind the driver, with the harness secured
In the front seat of a vehicle with a functional passenger-side airbag
In the center of the rear seat of the vehicle, away from the doors
In the rear seat of a vehicle that also has side airbags
questions.ref: P. 12: the law prohibits placing a rear-facing child restraint in the front seat of a vehicle with a functional passenger side airbag.
questions.why: The law bans putting a rear-facing child seat in the front seat of a vehicle with a working passenger-side airbag. (Driver's Manual, page 12)
wrong: The rear seat is allowed; the ban is on the front seat with a working passenger airbag.
The center of the rear seat is allowed; the ban is on the front seat with a working airbag.
The manual's ban is about the front passenger airbag, not side airbags in the rear.

questions.q: You are stopped at an intersection, and a parked truck blocks your view of the cross street. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn and then proceed through the intersection
Accelerate quickly to clear the intersection before traffic arrives
Edge forward slowly until you can see the cross street
Back up so that you can improve your view of the cross street
questions.ref: P. 15: if your view of a cross street is blocked, edge forward slowly until you can see; crossing drivers can then see the front of your vehicle.
questions.why: If your view of the cross street is blocked, edge forward slowly until you can see, which also lets crossing drivers see the front of your car. (Driver's Manual, page 15)
wrong: Honking does not show you whether traffic is coming; edge forward slowly until you can see.
Speeding into an intersection you cannot see is dangerous.
Backing up in a travel lane is illegal and unsafe. (page 24)

questions.q: You need to move across three lanes of a multi-lane highway to reach your exit. What is the safest approach?
options: Wait until all lanes are clear and then move across at once
Change one lane at a time, checking mirrors and blind spots
Signal once and cross all three lanes in a single movement
Speed up and cross two lanes at a time to reduce your exposure
questions.ref: P. 23: take one lane at a time, like going up or down stairs; waiting for all lanes to clear can tie up traffic and cause a crash.
questions.why: When you need to cross several lanes, take them one at a time, like going up or down stairs one step at a time. (Driver's Manual, page 23)
wrong: Waiting for all lanes to clear can tie up traffic and even cause a crash.
Crossing several lanes at once is unsafe, because it is hard to be sure all of them are clear.
The manual says one lane at a time, not two.

questions.q: Why should you avoid swinging wide to the left before making a right turn?
options: It is prohibited on any road with three or more lanes of traffic in one direction of travel
Oncoming drivers will assume that you are about to stop in the roadway ahead of them
It requires you to come to a complete stop in the road before completing the turn
The driver behind may think you are changing lanes or turning left and pass on the right
questions.ref: P. 24: if you swing wide, the driver behind may think you are changing lanes or turning left and may try to pass you on the right.
questions.why: If you swing wide before a right turn, the driver behind you may think you are changing lanes or turning left and try to pass you on the right. (Driver's Manual, page 24)
wrong: The manual's reason is about confusing the driver behind you, not a rule about three-lane roads.
The manual's concern is the driver behind, not oncoming drivers.
Swinging wide does not require a stop; the danger is confusing the driver behind you.

questions.q: You are waiting at a railroad crossing that has more than one track, and a train has just passed. What should you do?
options: Wait until the train is well down the track, since another train may be hidden
Cross as soon as you can clearly see the far side of the tracks
Follow the vehicle ahead of you across the tracks as it goes
Cross quickly before another train has time to arrive at the crossing
questions.ref: P. 15: at crossings with more than one track, wait until the passing train is well down the track; it may hide an approaching train.
questions.why: At a crossing with more than one track, wait until the train is well down the track, because it may hide another train coming. (Driver's Manual, page 15)
wrong: A clear view of the far side is not enough, since another train may be hidden.
Following another car across does not protect you from a hidden second train.
Rushing across is dangerous; wait until the passing train is well down the track.

questions.q: A motorcycle is passing your vehicle on a multi-lane road. What should you do?
options: Speed up slightly to stay ahead of it
Slow down sharply to give it more room
Maintain your lane position and speed
Move to the edge of your lane and flash your headlights
questions.ref: P. 18: when a motorcycle is passing, maintain your lane position and speed; never speed up or interfere with its ability to pass safely.
questions.why: When a motorcycle is passing you, keep your lane position and speed so the rider can finish the pass. (Driver's Manual, page 18)
wrong: Never speed up when a motorcycle is passing you.
The manual says to keep your speed, and sudden braking can cause a crash.
Keep your lane position, and do not interfere with the rider's ability to pass.

questions.q: What is the purpose of Connecticut's Vulnerable User's Law?
options: It requires all pedestrians and bicyclists to wear reflective clothing when using any road at night
It lowers the speed limit on any road that is used by pedestrians or bicyclists
It bans trucks and buses from roads that are used by vulnerable users
It sets higher penalties for drivers who fail to use reasonable care and cause serious injury or death
questions.ref: P. 16: the Vulnerable User's Law provides higher penalties for drivers who fail to exercise reasonable care and cause serious injury or death of a vulnerable user.
questions.why: The Vulnerable User's Law sets higher penalties for drivers who fail to use reasonable care and cause serious injury or death to a vulnerable user. (Driver's Manual, page 16)
wrong: The law is about driver penalties, not clothing rules for pedestrians and bicyclists.
The law raises penalties for careless drivers; it does not change speed limits.
Garbage trucks and tank vehicles are themselves listed as vulnerable users, not banned.

questions.q: You drive through a highway work zone and, after passing the first warning sign, you do not see any workers. What should you do?
options: Resume normal speed right away, since no workers are in sight ahead
Keep observing posted signs until you see the 'End Road Work' sign
Resume normal speed once you pass the first set of orange cones
Slow down only when you actually see workers wearing bright vests
questions.ref: P. 16: some work zones are mobile; just because you do not see workers does not mean they are not there - observe posted signs until 'End Road Work'.
questions.why: Some work zones are mobile, so even if you see no workers, keep obeying the posted signs until you see the 'End Road Work' sign. (Driver's Manual, page 16)
wrong: Not seeing workers does not mean they are not there.
The work zone continues until the 'End Road Work' sign, not just past the first cones.
Workers could be present at any point, so slow down and obey posted limits the whole way.

questions.q: A bicyclist is riding near the center of a narrow lane ahead of you. What is the best response?
options: Slow down and pass only when you can give at least three feet of clearance
Sound your horn so the bicyclist moves over to the right side of the lane
Pass immediately with about two feet of clearance between you and the bicycle
Speed up and pass before the oncoming traffic gets any closer to you
questions.ref: P. 17: when a lane is too narrow, bicyclists 'take the lane'; pass only with at least three feet; avoid sounding your horn; there may be hazards not visible to motorists.
questions.why: When passing a bicyclist, slow down and pass only when you can give at least three feet of space. (Driver's Manual, page 17)
wrong: Sounding your horn may startle the rider into your path, and bicyclists may take the lane when it is narrow.
The minimum passing distance is three feet, not two.
Rushing past a bicyclist with oncoming traffic near is unsafe; take one hazard at a time. (page 22)

questions.q: In which situation may a driver cross a double yellow line to pass?
options: To pass a line of traffic moving at normal speed when the road ahead looks clear
To pass any vehicle if no oncoming vehicle is visible
To pass a slow-moving farm tractor when you can see far enough ahead
To pass a vehicle at an intersection or railroad crossing
questions.ref: P. 18: state law permits passing slow-moving traffic, pedestrians, parked vehicles, animals, bicycles, mopeds and scooters in no-passing zones if you can see far enough ahead to pass safely.
questions.why: State law allows passing slow-moving vehicles in a no-passing zone, crossing the double yellow line, if you can see far enough ahead to pass safely. (Driver's Manual, page 18)
wrong: The exception is for slow-moving traffic, not traffic moving at normal speed.
The exception covers slow-moving or stopped vehicles, not any vehicle.
Passing at intersections and railroad crossings is dangerous, because vehicles or trains may enter your path. (page 23)

questions.q: You notice a vehicle ahead drifting over lane lines and changing speeds for no apparent reason. What should you do?
options: Stay close behind the vehicle and flash your lights to alert the driver
Pass immediately and move back into the lane close in front of the vehicle
Keep a two-second following distance so that you can react to its movements quickly
Keep plenty of room and a 3 to 4 second following distance, and be careful when passing
questions.ref: P. 27: watch for vehicles that drift or travel at inconsistent speeds; give a distracted driver plenty of room and a 3 to 4 second following distance.
questions.why: Drifting and changing speeds are signs of a distracted driver, so give them plenty of room and a 3 to 4 second following distance. (Driver's Manual, page 27)
wrong: Following closely leaves you no room to react if the distracted driver does something sudden.
Be very careful passing a distracted driver, who may drift in front of you.
The manual says 3 to 4 seconds for a distracted driver, not two.

questions.q: You have just had an argument and are very angry, but you need to go somewhere. What does the manual recommend?
options: Drive immediately and use the trip itself to work off the anger you feel
Cool off first and stay off the road until you are calm, or have someone else drive
Drive on a freeway where there is less traffic to distract you from the anger
Drive faster than the flow of traffic to arrive sooner and calm down quickly
questions.ref: P. 28: if you are angry or excited, give yourself time to cool off and stay off the road until calm; have someone else drive; do not drive faster than the flow of traffic.
questions.why: If you are angry or excited, give yourself time to cool off and stay off the road until you are calm, or have someone else drive. (Driver's Manual, page 28)
wrong: Anger affects your driving, so the manual says to stay off the road until you calm down.
The manual says to cool off before driving, on any road.
The manual says not to drive faster than the flow of traffic.

questions.q: According to the manual, a driver under 21 years old in Connecticut could be considered impaired after:
options: Having only one drink of alcohol
Having two drinks within one hour
Having three drinks within two hours
Having more than one drink per hour
questions.ref: P. 33: in Connecticut, people under 21 years old could be considered impaired after having only one drink of alcohol.
questions.why: In Connecticut, people under 21 could be considered impaired after only one drink of alcohol. (Driver's Manual, page 33)
wrong: The manual says even one drink can count as impaired for someone under 21.
The manual says one drink can be enough to be considered impaired under 21.
The manual's rule is about one drink total, not drinks per hour.

questions.q: A 17-year-old is adjudicated as a youthful offender. For which offense can a person under 18 NOT be considered a youthful offender?
options: Reckless driving on a public road
Street racing on a public road
Driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs
Operating a motor vehicle while under suspension
questions.ref: P. 35: a person under 18 cannot be considered a youthful offender for negligent homicide, evading responsibility with death/serious injury, or DUI; the others can be adjudicated and reported to DMV.
questions.why: A person under 18 cannot be treated as a youthful offender for driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs. (Driver's Manual, page 35)
wrong: Reckless driving can be handled as youthful offender status, with the record reported to DMV.
Street racing can be handled as youthful offender status, with the record reported to DMV.
Driving under suspension can be handled as youthful offender status, with the record reported to DMV.

questions.q: You are making a legal U-turn on a street where U-turns are allowed. Into which lane should you move?
options: The inside (left-hand) lane traveling in the opposite direction
The outside (right-hand) lane traveling the opposite way
Whichever lane is open in the opposite direction of travel
The center turn lane, if one is available on that street
questions.ref: P. 37: when making a U-turn, signal left, stop, check for traffic, and proceed into the outside or right-hand lane traveling in the opposite direction.
questions.why: When making a U-turn, signal left, stop, check for traffic, and go into the outside, or right-hand, lane going the opposite way. (Driver's Manual, page 37)
wrong: The manual says to enter the outside, or right-hand, lane, not the inside lane.
You should go into the outside, or right-hand, lane, not just any open lane.
The manual says to finish in the outside, or right-hand, lane, not a center turn lane.

questions.q: Your windshield wipers are on because of steady rain. What does Connecticut law require?
options: Turn on your headlights
Use your parking lights only
Use your high beams to see farther
Headlights are optional unless it is dark
questions.ref: P. 38: if you turn on your wipers, turn on your headlights - it's the law; parking lights are for parked vehicles only.
questions.why: If you turn on your wipers, you must turn on your headlights; it's the law. (Driver's Manual, page 38)
wrong: Parking lights are only for parked vehicles.
In rain, high beams reflect back and cause glare, so use low beams.
The law says headlights go on whenever wipers are on, day or night.

questions.q: A white, X-shaped 'Railroad Crossing' crossbuck sign has the same meaning as which sign?
options: Stop sign
Merge sign
Do Not Enter sign
Yield sign
questions.ref: P. 52: the railroad crossbuck has the same meaning as a Yield sign; you must yield to crossing trains.
questions.why: The white X-shaped railroad crossbuck means the same as a yield sign, so you must yield to trains. (Driver's Manual, page 52)
wrong: The crossbuck has the same meaning as a yield sign, not a stop sign.
A merge sign warns that two lanes become one, which is different from a crossbuck.
Do not enter means you may not go in at all, which is not what a crossbuck means.

questions.q: A HAWK pedestrian signal is displaying a flashing red. What should you do?
options: Proceed with caution, since flashing red is the same as a yield sign
Wait until the signal turns green before proceeding
Stop, and proceed only after pedestrians have cleared the crosswalk
Stop only if a pedestrian is visible in the crosswalk at the time
questions.ref: P. 45: flashing red on a HAWK signal means it is about to deactivate; drivers must stop but may proceed when pedestrians have cleared the crosswalk.
questions.why: A flashing red HAWK signal means it is about to shut off, so you must stop but may go once pedestrians have cleared the crosswalk. (Driver's Manual, page 45)
wrong: You must stop at a flashing red HAWK signal, not just yield.
A HAWK signal has no green; you may go once pedestrians clear the crosswalk.
Drivers must stop at a flashing red HAWK signal and wait for the crosswalk to clear.

questions.q: Yellow or white diagonal stripes painted on the pavement are used to mark:
options: Fixed obstructions
A reversible lane
The beginning of a passing zone
A reserved bus lane
questions.ref: P. 44, Other Markings: yellow or white diagonal stripes are used to mark fixed obstructions.
questions.why: Yellow or white diagonal stripes on the pavement mark fixed obstructions. (Driver's Manual, page 44)
wrong: Reversible lanes are usually marked by double dashed yellow lines.
Passing zones are shown by center line markings and signs, not diagonal stripes.
Bus lanes are marked by signs and the words transit or bus.

questions.q: Which vehicle may be used for a Connecticut road test?
options: A properly insured long-term leased vehicle with proof of insurance naming the registrant
A rented car, even if the applicant has no valid driver's license, as long as it is insured
Any registered vehicle that the unlicensed applicant drives alone to the test location
A vehicle with an expired registration if the vehicle is fully insured
questions.ref: P. 7: long-term leased vehicles with proper proof of insurance may be used; without a valid license you cannot test in a rented vehicle; a non-licensed operator cannot drive to the test alone; valid registration is required.
questions.why: A long-term leased vehicle may be used for the road test if it has proof of insurance that identifies the vehicle and the lease company. (Driver's Manual, page 7)
wrong: If you do not have a valid driver's license, you cannot test in a rented vehicle.
A non-licensed operator cannot drive to the test location alone.
The test vehicle must have a valid registration as well as proof of insurance.

questions.q: Home training for a 16-year-old applicant must be given by an instructor who meets which requirement?
options: At least 18 years old and licensed for two years with a clean record
At least 21 years old and licensed for five or more consecutive years
At least 20 years old and licensed for four or more years without a suspension
At least 25 years old and licensed for three or more years
questions.ref: P. 6: home instructors must be at least 20 years of age, have held a license for four or more years prior to training, and not have been suspended during that period.
questions.why: A home training instructor must be at least 20 years old and have held a license for four or more years with no suspension during that time. (Driver's Manual, page 6)
wrong: The instructor must be at least 20 and licensed four or more years, not 18 with two years.
The minimum age is 20, not 21, and the license time is four years, not five.
The minimum age is 20, and the license must have been held four or more years, not three.

questions.q: Which trip is NOT an exception to the 11 p.m. to 5 a.m. curfew for a 16- or 17-year-old driver?
options: Traveling to a job
Driving to a friend's house to spend time together
Acting as the assigned driver in a Safe Ride Program
Traveling because of a medical necessity
questions.ref: P. 8: the curfew does not apply when traveling for employment, school, religious activities, medical necessity, or as an assigned driver in the Safe Ride Program.
questions.why: Visiting a friend is not a curfew exception; the exceptions are employment, school, religious activities, medical necessity, and Safe Ride Program driving. (Driver's Manual, page 8)
wrong: Traveling for employment is an exception to the curfew.
Being an assigned driver in the Safe Ride Program is an exception to the curfew.
Medical necessity is an exception to the curfew.

questions.q: A 17-year-old is convicted of a second offense of using a cell phone while driving. What is the penalty?
options: A 30-day suspension and a $175 license restoration fee
A 6-month suspension and a $175 license restoration fee
A 60-day suspension and a $175 license restoration fee
A 90-day suspension and a $175 license restoration fee
questions.ref: P. 34 table: cell phone/text messaging is a 30-day suspension for a 1st offense, 90-day for a 2nd, and 6 months for a 3rd.
questions.why: For a teen, a second cell phone offense brings a 90-day suspension and a 175 dollar license restoration fee. (Driver's Manual, page 34)
wrong: 30 days is the penalty for a first cell phone offense.
6 months is the penalty for a third cell phone offense.
60 days is the first-offense penalty for speeding 20 miles per hour over the limit.

questions.q: Your vehicle has an automatic shoulder belt. What else should you do?
options: Nothing more, because the automatic belt provides full protection
Buckle the lap belt only when driving on highways
Buckle the lap belt too, or you could slide out of the belt
Buckle the lap belt only if the vehicle lacks airbags
questions.ref: P. 12: if you have an automatic shoulder belt, be sure to buckle your lap belt as well; otherwise you could slide out of the belt and be hurt or killed.
questions.why: With an automatic shoulder belt, buckle the lap belt as well, or you could slide out of the belt and be hurt or killed in a crash. (Driver's Manual, page 12)
wrong: The shoulder belt alone does not fully protect you; you must also buckle the lap belt.
The lap belt should be buckled on every trip, not just on highways.
Belts must be worn even with airbags, so the lap belt is always needed.

questions.q: A vehicle fails its emissions inspection. How long does the owner have to fix the problem and have the emissions rechecked?
options: 30 days
60 days
45 days
90 days
questions.ref: P. 11: if the vehicle does not pass an emissions inspection, you will be given 60 days to have the problem fixed and the emissions rechecked.
questions.why: If a vehicle fails its emissions inspection, the owner has 60 days to fix the problem and have it rechecked. (Driver's Manual, page 11)
wrong: The manual gives 60 days, not 30.
The manual gives 60 days, not 45.
The manual gives 60 days, not 90.

questions.q: Which statement about airbags and safety belts is correct?
options: Belts must be worn even with airbags, which do not protect in side or rear hits
Airbags make safety belts optional for drivers who are in the front seat
Airbags keep you behind the wheel if your vehicle is struck from the side or rear
Safety belts are needed only on highway trips and long distance travel
questions.ref: P. 12: safety belts must be worn even if the vehicle has airbags; airbags don't protect you in side/rear hits or rollovers and won't keep you behind the wheel.
questions.why: State law requires seat belts even with airbags, because airbags do not protect you if you are hit from the side or rear or roll over. (Driver's Manual, page 12)
wrong: State law requires seat belts even if the vehicle has airbags.
An airbag will not keep you behind the wheel in a side or rear crash; belts do that.
Over half of all traffic deaths happen within 25 miles of home, so belts are needed on every trip. (page 13)

questions.q: You are on an entrance ramp and must wait for an opening in highway traffic. What should you do?
options: Drive to the end of the ramp and stop until there is a gap
Merge at ramp speed and expect traffic to slow for you
Speed up as much as possible on the ramp and force an opening
Slow down on the ramp to leave room to speed up before merging
questions.ref: P. 20: do not drive to the end of the ramp and stop; if you must wait for space, slow down on the ramp so you have room to speed up before merging.
questions.why: If you must wait for space on a ramp, slow down on the ramp so you have room to speed up before you merge. (Driver's Manual, page 20)
wrong: Stopping at the end of the ramp leaves no room to reach traffic speed, and drivers behind may hit you.
Try to enter at the speed of traffic, and never assume others will make space for you.
Do not force your way into an opening that is too small.

questions.q: You are on a highway and plan to take an exit ramp. When should you begin to slow down?
options: After you have moved onto the exit ramp
As soon as you see the exit sign, while still on the main road
Well before the exit, tapping your brakes on the main road
Only after you reach the end of the ramp
questions.ref: P. 21: keep up with the speed of traffic on the main road; if the road has exit ramps, do not slow down until you move onto the exit ramp.
questions.why: Keep up with the speed of traffic on the main road, and do not slow down until you move onto the exit ramp. (Driver's Manual, page 21)
wrong: Slowing on the main road can cause a rear-end crash; wait until you are on the ramp.
On roads with exit ramps, do not slow down until you are on the ramp.
You must slow down on the ramp, not wait until the end of it.

questions.q: You must back out of a parking space. Which is the best way to back safely?
options: Rely on your rearview mirror alone to see directly behind the vehicle
Rely on both side mirrors to check behind you
Look over your right shoulder through the rear window
Back quickly to clear the space for other traffic
