questions.ref: P. 24: turn around and look over your right shoulder through the rear window; do not depend on mirrors; back slowly because the vehicle is harder to steer.
questions.why: When backing, turn and look over your right shoulder directly through the rear window. (Driver's Manual, page 24)
wrong: You cannot see directly behind your vehicle with your rearview mirror.
Side mirrors cannot show you what is directly behind your vehicle.
Back slowly, because your vehicle is much harder to steer in reverse.

questions.q: You approach a roadside crash where police are directing traffic. What should you do?
options: Slow down to see whether anyone at the scene needs help from you
Stop on the shoulder for a moment to watch what is happening
Slow to a crawl so that you can get a good look at the damage
Keep your eyes on the road and get past quickly and safely
questions.ref: Pp. 24, 41: do not slow down to look at a crash ('rubbernecking'); keep your eyes on the road; do not stop at an accident unless involved or help has not arrived.
questions.why: Do not slow down to look at a crash; keep your eyes on the road and get past as quickly and safely as you can. (Driver's Manual, page 24)
wrong: Do not stop at a crash unless you are involved or help has not arrived, and police are already there. (page 41)
Stopping to watch can block rescue vehicles and cause another crash.
Slowing down to look, called rubbernecking, can cause you to crash.

questions.q: Which statement about school zones is correct?
options: The slower speed limit applies only while a crossing guard is on duty at the crosswalk
Obey the slower posted school-zone speed limit; children may be present outside school hours
You must yield to students only when a crossing guard signals you to do so
Children are present in school zones only during school hours
questions.ref: P. 16: school hours are not the only time children are present; you must obey the slower posted speed limit or be fined; stop and yield to students who are crossing or if a guard signals.
questions.why: You must obey the slower posted school zone speed limit, and children can be present even outside school hours. (Driver's Manual, page 16)
wrong: The manual says to obey the slower posted school zone limit, and children are there at other times too.
You must stop and yield to students who are crossing, even without a crossing guard.
The manual says school hours are not the only time children are present.

questions.q: After passing a tractor-trailer on the highway, when should you return to the right lane?
options: As soon as your car has passed the truck's cab
Once you are about one car length ahead of the truck's cab
When you can see the whole front of the truck in your inside mirror
When the truck driver flashes his headlights to signal you to merge
questions.ref: P. 19: when passing, look for the entire front of the truck in your rearview mirror before pulling in front; return to the right lane when you can see the front of the truck in your inside mirror.
questions.why: After passing a truck, signal and return to the right lane when you can see the front of the truck in your inside mirror. (Driver's Manual, page 19)
wrong: Cutting in right after the cab puts you in the truck's front No-Zone, where you could be rear-ended.
One car length is too close; wait until you can see the front of the truck in your mirror.
The manual's rule is to use your own mirror, not to wait for a signal from the truck driver.

questions.q: A bus has stopped at the curb ahead and now signals to re-enter your lane, traveling in the same direction as you. What should you do?
options: Yield the right-of-way to the bus
Speed up to pass before it pulls out
Sound your horn so the bus waits
Maintain your speed, since the bus must yield to traffic
questions.ref: Pp. 18, 37: drivers must yield the right-of-way to a bus traveling in the same direction when the bus appropriately signals.
questions.why: Drivers must yield the right-of-way to a bus traveling in the same direction when the bus signals. (Driver's Manual, pages 18 and 37)
wrong: The law says you must yield to the signaling bus, not race it.
Honking does not change the rule; you must yield to the bus.
The bus does not have to yield here; drivers must yield to a bus that signals.

questions.q: You are approaching a right turn, and there is a bike lane along the curb. Which is correct?
options: Move into the bike lane well before the intersection to prepare for your turn
Yield to bicyclists; you may turn across the bike lane but not drive in it beforehand
Speed up so you can turn ahead of any bicyclist who is in the lane
Stay in the travel lane and turn without yielding, since bicyclists must yield to cars
questions.ref: P. 17: you must yield to bicycles in the bike lane; you may turn across a bicycle lane but may not drive in the bicycle lane when approaching a turn.
questions.why: You must yield to bicycles in a bike lane, and you may turn across the lane but may not drive in it as you approach a turn. (Driver's Manual, page 17)
wrong: You may not drive in the bike lane when approaching a turn.
Racing a bicyclist to the turn is dangerous; you must yield to them.
Drivers must yield to bicyclists in a bike lane before turning across it.

questions.q: Which statement about sharing the road with motorcycles is correct?
options: You may pass a motorcycle in its lane if you give it extra room
A motorcycle's flashing turn signal always means it is about to turn
You should use your high beams when approaching a motorcycle so it can see you
A motorcyclist is entitled to a full lane, so you should not pass within that lane
questions.ref: P. 18: motorcycle operators have the right to a complete lane; do not pass a motorcycle in the same lane; do not assume a flashing signal means a turn; always dim headlights approaching a motorcycle.
questions.why: Motorcyclists have the right to a complete traffic lane, so do not pass a motorcycle in the same lane. (Driver's Manual, page 18)
wrong: Do not pass a motorcycle in its own lane at all, because the rider needs space to react.
Motorcycle signals may not cancel by themselves, so a flashing signal does not prove a turn.
Always dim your headlights when approaching a motorcycle, because high beams can blind the rider.

questions.q: Your vehicle begins to skid on a slippery road. What should you do?
options: Stay off the brake and steer where you want the vehicle to go
Brake as hard as you can to stop the skid quickly
Turn the steering wheel away from the direction you want to go
Accelerate firmly to regain traction with the road surface
questions.ref: P. 40: if your vehicle begins to skid, stay off the brake and steer in the direction you want the vehicle to go, correcting your steering as it straightens.
questions.why: If your car starts to skid, stay off the brake and steer in the direction you want the car to go. (Driver's Manual, page 40)
wrong: Braking during a skid does not work until the car slows and can make the skid worse.
Steer in the direction you want the car to go, not away from it.
The manual says skids happen from going too fast, and it does not say to speed up.

questions.q: You run over a shoulder rumble strip while driving at night. What should you do?
options: Treat it as a harmless warning and continue to the next exit before resting
Turn up the radio and open a window and keep going
Pull off the road at a safe place immediately and check your alertness
Slow down and keep driving in the right lane until you arrive
questions.ref: P. 28: if you run over a shoulder rumble strip, pull off the road at a safe place immediately and check your alertness level.
questions.why: If you run over a shoulder rumble strip, pull off the road at a safe place right away and check how alert you are. (Driver's Manual, page 28)
wrong: The manual says to pull off immediately, not wait for the next exit.
Turning up the radio and opening the window are warning signs of fatigue, not fixes.
The manual says to pull off immediately, not keep driving.

questions.q: Which statement about drugs and driving is correct?
options: Only illegal drugs can affect your driving ability
Cold and allergy drugs bought over the counter can cause drowsiness
Prescription drugs never affect reflexes when taken as directed
Taking a non-prescription drug along with alcohol is safe
questions.ref: P. 33: many prescription and over-the-counter drugs (colds, hay fever, allergies) can make a person drowsy; never drink alcohol while taking other drugs.
questions.why: Many over-the-counter drugs, such as those for colds and allergies, can make you drowsy and affect your driving. (Driver's Manual, page 33)
wrong: Prescription and over-the-counter drugs can also affect your driving.
Some prescription drugs can affect your reflexes, judgment, vision and alertness, like alcohol.
Never drink alcohol while taking other drugs, which could multiply its effects.

questions.q: Which first-offense violation carries the longest suspension for a 16- or 17-year-old driver?
options: Speeding 20 mph over the limit, with a 60-day suspension
Using a cell phone, with a 30-day suspension
Violating the passenger restrictions, with a 30-day suspension
Reckless driving, with a 6-month suspension
questions.ref: P. 34 table: 1st offense - GDL violation 30 days, cell phone 30 days, speeding (20 over) 60 days, reckless driving 6 months.
questions.why: A first reckless driving offense brings a 6-month suspension, the longest first-offense suspension in the teen table. (Driver's Manual, page 34)
wrong: A 60-day suspension is shorter than the 6-month suspension for reckless driving.
A 30-day suspension is shorter than the 6-month suspension for reckless driving.
A 30-day suspension is shorter than the 6-month suspension for reckless driving.

questions.q: Compared with the distance it takes to stop at 30 mph, stopping at 60 mph takes:
options: Twice the distance
Over three times the distance
About one and a half times the distance
The same distance if you have good tires and brakes
questions.ref: P. 36: stopping at 60 mph does not take twice the distance it takes at 30 mph, but over three times the distance.
questions.why: Stopping at 60 miles per hour takes over three times the distance it takes at 30 miles per hour, not just twice. (Driver's Manual, page 36)
wrong: The manual says it does not take twice the distance, as one might think, but over three times.
It takes over three times the distance, much more than one and a half times.
Higher speed always takes more distance to stop, even with good tires and brakes.

questions.q: At a crash scene, a person is injured but is not in a burning vehicle and is not in immediate danger of being hit. What should you do?
options: Move the person to the shoulder so the injury does not block traffic
Give the person a little water to drink to help prevent shock
Lay the person across the back seat and drive straight to a hospital
Be sure police and emergency help are called, and do not move the person
questions.ref: P. 41: get help; do not move the injured unless in a burning vehicle or immediate danger; do not give anything to drink, not even water; cover with a blanket to prevent shock.
questions.why: Make sure police and emergency help are called, and do not move an injured person unless they are in a burning vehicle or in immediate danger. (Driver's Manual, page 41)
wrong: Moving an injured person can make their injuries worse.
Do not give injured persons anything to drink, not even water.
Do not move the injured person; call for police and emergency help instead.

questions.q: Which color of sign shows services along the roadway, such as rest areas, gas stations, and hospitals?
options: Green
Brown
Blue
Orange
questions.ref: Pp. 47, 51: blue signs tell you about services along the roadway; green signs are guide signs; brown signs mark parks and recreation; orange signs are work-area warnings.
questions.why: Blue signs are guide signs that tell you about services along the road, such as rest areas, gas stations, and hospitals. (Driver's Manual, pages 47 and 51)
wrong: Green signs tell you where you are, which way to go, and the distance.
Brown signs are for parks and recreation.
Orange signs warn of construction and maintenance work.

questions.q: A reversible lane has an overhead signal displaying a steady yellow X. What does it mean?
options: Use of the lane is changing; move out of it as soon as it is safe
The lane is reserved for turning vehicles in either direction
You may continue to use the lane that is beneath the signal
You may not enter the lane under any circumstances at all
questions.ref: P. 44: steady yellow X means the use of the lane is changing and you should move out as soon as it is safe; flashing yellow X is for turning only; red X means you cannot use it.
questions.why: A steady yellow X means the use of the lane is changing, so move out of it as soon as it is safe. (Driver's Manual, page 44)
wrong: A flashing yellow X, not a steady one, means the lane is only for turning.
A green arrow means you can use the lane; a steady yellow X means get out of it.
A red X means you cannot use the lane.

questions.q: A yellow diamond-shaped sign shows two lanes of traffic about to become one. Who is responsible for merging smoothly?
options: Only drivers in the right lane
Only drivers in the lane that is ending
Whichever driver is traveling faster
Drivers in both lanes
questions.ref: P. 49, Merge sign: two lanes of traffic are about to become one; drivers in both lanes are responsible for merging smoothly.
questions.why: At a merge sign, two lanes are about to become one, and drivers in both lanes are responsible for merging smoothly. (Driver's Manual, page 49)
wrong: Drivers in both lanes share the job of merging smoothly.
The driver in the ending lane is not the only one responsible; both lanes are.
Speed does not decide it; drivers in both lanes are responsible.

questions.q: A 17-year-old learner's permit holder is driving with a 19-year-old friend, who has held a license for five years, in the front passenger seat. Which statement is correct?
options: This is allowed, because the friend has held a license for more than four years.
This is not allowed, because the instructor must be at least 20 years old and have held a license for four or more consecutive years.
This is allowed as long as the friend sits in the front passenger seat and stays alert.
This is not allowed, because a permit holder may never carry any passenger other than a licensed driving instructor from a driving school, whatever the passenger's age.
questions.ref: pp. 5-6, Learner's Permit Passenger Restrictions: the only non-instructor passenger allowed is one person at least 20 years old who has held a license for four or more consecutive years.
questions.why: Besides a licensed driving instructor, a teen permit holder may carry only one person giving instruction who is at least 20 and has held a license for four or more years in a row. (Driver's Manual, page 6)
wrong: Years of licensed driving are not enough; the person must also be at least 20 years old.
Seating does not matter here, because a 19-year-old cannot supervise a teen permit holder.
One qualified person at least 20 years old may also ride along, not only a driving school instructor.

questions.q: How long is a Connecticut learner's permit valid?
options: Until you obtain a driver's license or 1 year from the date it is issued, whichever comes first
For 180 days from the date it is issued, regardless of whether you get a license
Until you obtain a driver's license or 4 years from the date it is issued, whichever comes first
Until you obtain a driver's license or 2 years from the date it is issued, whichever comes first
questions.ref: p. 5, Obtaining a Learner's Permit NOTE: valid until you obtain a license or 2 years from issue, whichever comes first.
questions.why: A learner's permit is valid until you get a driver's license or 2 years from the date it is issued, whichever comes first. (Driver's Manual, page 5)
wrong: The permit lasts up to 2 years, not 1 year.
180 days is a road test waiting period, and the permit lasts up to 2 years.
The permit lasts up to 2 years, not 4 years.

questions.q: A 16-year-old completes 30 hours of classroom instruction and 40 hours of behind-the-wheel training through a licensed Connecticut commercial driving school. How long after the learner's permit is issued must the teen wait before taking the road test?
options: 120 days
90 days
180 days
60 days
questions.ref: p. 6, Commercial Driving School or Secondary School Training: those who complete driver education through a commercial or secondary school must wait 120 days after permit issuance (all others 180).
questions.why: Teens who finish driver education at a commercial driving school or high school program must wait 120 days after the permit is issued before the road test. (Driver's Manual, page 6)
wrong: The 90 day wait is for applicants who are 18 or older.
180 days is the wait for teens who did not train through a commercial or high school program.
The manual has no 60 day wait; the wait after school training is 120 days.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an exception to the 11 p.m. to 5 a.m. driving curfew for 16- and 17-year-old drivers?
options: Traveling for employment
Traveling because of a medical necessity
Driving to a friend's house to watch a movie
Serving as an assigned driver in the Safe Ride Program
questions.ref: p. 8, Hour Restrictions (Curfew): exceptions are employment, school, religious activities, medical necessity, or Safe Ride Program assigned driver.
questions.why: Visiting a friend is not a curfew exception; the exceptions are employment, school, religious activities, medical necessity, and Safe Ride Program driving. (Driver's Manual, page 8)
wrong: Traveling for employment is an exception to the curfew.
Medical necessity is an exception to the curfew.
Being an assigned driver in the Safe Ride Program is an exception to the curfew.

questions.q: During the 'penny test' you place Lincoln's head into a tread groove at the lowest-looking spot on your tire, and part of Lincoln's head is covered by the tread. What does this indicate?
options: You have a safe amount of tread
The tire is worn and should be replaced immediately
The tire is overinflated
The tire pressure should be checked against the door jamb label
questions.ref: p. 11, Tires: if any part of Lincoln's head is covered by the tread, you are driving with a safe amount of tread.
questions.why: In the penny test, if any part of Lincoln's head is covered by the tread, you have a safe amount of tread. (Driver's Manual, page 11)
wrong: A covered head means the tread is still deep enough, so the tire is not worn out.
The penny test checks tread depth, not whether a tire is overinflated.
Tire pressure is checked with a gauge; the penny test only checks tread depth.

questions.q: A 25-year-old driver is stopped at a red light and wants to send a text message on a hand-held phone. Under Connecticut law, this is:
options: Legal, because the vehicle is not moving
Legal, as long as the driver is wearing a seat belt
Legal, because only drivers under 18 are covered by the cell phone law and adults may use any device whenever the vehicle is not in motion
Illegal, because hand-held use is also prohibited while temporarily stopped for traffic or a signal
questions.ref: p. 13, Cell Phone Laws: hand-held devices may not be used while operating a vehicle, including when temporarily stopped because of traffic, road conditions, or a traffic control sign or signal.
questions.why: Hand-held phones are banned while driving, including when you are temporarily stopped for traffic or a signal. (Driver's Manual, page 13)
wrong: Being stopped at a light does not make hand-held phone use legal.
Wearing a seat belt has nothing to do with the cell phone law.
The hand-held ban applies to drivers of all ages, even when stopped at a light.

questions.q: A registered vehicle owner's insurance lapses and the DMV sends a warning notice. If the owner fails to respond to the notice, what happens?
options: The insurance company automatically reinstates the policy
The registration is suspended
The owner's driver's license is suspended for 45 days
The vehicle is towed and the owner is fined $75
questions.ref: p. 13, Insurance Laws: failure to respond to your warning notice will result in suspension of the registration.
questions.why: If you do not respond to the DMV's insurance warning notice, your vehicle's registration will be suspended. (Driver's Manual, page 13)
wrong: The manual says nothing about automatic reinstatement; the penalty is a registration suspension.
The manual says the registration is suspended, not your driver's license.
The manual's penalty is a registration suspension; the 75 dollar fine is for seat belt violations.

questions.q: You move into the middle of an opening in traffic when merging so that both you and the vehicle behind you have a two-second following distance. How large was the opening?
options: About three seconds
About six seconds
About four seconds
About ten seconds
questions.ref: p. 20, Space to Merge: you need an opening of about four seconds; in the middle of it you and the vehicle behind each have a two-second following distance.
questions.why: You need an opening of about four seconds to merge, and moving into the middle of it leaves two seconds in front and behind. (Driver's Manual, page 20)
wrong: Half of three seconds is only one and a half seconds, so the opening is about four seconds.
Half of six seconds is three seconds, not two.
Ten seconds is the time needed to pass at 55 miles per hour, not to merge.

questions.q: You are driving on a highway and realize you just missed your exit. What should you do?
options: Continue on to a place where you can safely turn around
Stop on the shoulder and back up to the exit
Slow down in the right lane and back up with your emergency flashers on
Stop in the travel lane until traffic clears, then back up to the exit
questions.ref: p. 24, Backing: never back in any travel lane; if you miss your turn or exit, do not back up but go on to where you can safely turn around.
questions.why: If you miss your exit, do not back up; go on to a place where you can safely turn around. (Driver's Manual, page 24)
wrong: Backing up on a highway is illegal and unsafe, even on the shoulder.
Never back up in a travel lane, even with flashers on.
Do not stop in travel lanes for any reason, and never back up there.

questions.q: You are making a left turn at an intersection and an oncoming vehicle is also waiting to turn left. Which guidance from the manual applies?
options: Cut the corner as tightly as possible so that the oncoming driver cannot turn left across the front of your vehicle
Swing wide into the oncoming driver's turning path so that vehicles approaching from the left have more room to pass you
Stop in the middle of the intersection until the oncoming driver has finished turning, then complete your own turn
Avoid cutting the corner so sharply that you run into someone approaching from the left, but leave room for oncoming vehicles to turn left in front of you
questions.ref: p. 24, Turning, Left turns: avoid cutting the corner so sharply that you run into someone approaching from the left, but leave room for oncoming vehicles to turn left in front of you.
questions.why: When turning left, do not cut the corner so sharply that you hit someone coming from the left, but leave room for oncoming vehicles to turn left in front of you. (Driver's Manual, page 24)
wrong: Cutting the corner sharply can cause a crash with someone approaching from the left.
Swinging into the other driver's path can cause a crash; leave them room to turn.
Both drivers can turn at once if you leave room for the oncoming driver to turn in front of you.

questions.q: You are following a slow vehicle on a two-lane road and approaching a hill that blocks your view of the road ahead. Which is correct?
options: Pass quickly, since you cannot see any oncoming vehicle and the slow vehicle is holding up the traffic behind it
Pass if the hill is more than 800 feet away
Treat the hill like an oncoming vehicle and do not start to pass within one-third of a mile of it
Pass on the shoulder to stay clear of the lane markings
questions.ref: p. 24, Hills and Curves: treat a hill or curve like an oncoming vehicle; do not start to pass within one-third of a mile (about 10 seconds). Also p. 23: never pass on the shoulder.
questions.why: Treat a hill or curve like an oncoming vehicle, and do not start to pass within one-third of a mile of it. (Driver's Manual, page 24)
wrong: Assume an oncoming vehicle is just out of sight over a hill.
800 feet is too short; you need about one-third of a mile.
Never pass on the shoulder, paved or not. (page 23)

questions.q: Under Connecticut's Vulnerable User's Law, which of the following is NOT listed as a vulnerable user?
options: A person riding or driving an animal
A motorcyclist
A highway worker
A wheelchair user
questions.ref: p. 16, Vulnerable Users: lists pedestrians, bicyclists, wheelchair users, persons riding/driving an animal, highway workers, garbage trucks, tank vehicles, U.S. mail vehicles and express delivery carriers.
questions.why: The vulnerable user list includes pedestrians, bicyclists, wheelchair users, people riding or driving animals, and highway workers, but not motorcyclists. (Driver's Manual, page 16)
wrong: A person riding or driving an animal is on the vulnerable user list.
Highway workers are on the vulnerable user list.
Wheelchair users are on the vulnerable user list.

questions.q: An ice cream truck in your lane has its flashing lights on and has extended its stop signal arm and crossing arm. What must you do?
options: Stop at least 10 feet away, pass at no more than 5 mph, and yield to any pedestrian crossing
Stop at least 25 feet away and wait until the truck turns off its lights and retracts its stop arm
Slow to 15 mph and pass with caution
Stop at least 10 feet away and remain stopped until the truck leaves
questions.ref: p. 18, Ice Cream Trucks: stop at least 10 feet away; then you may proceed at a reasonable speed, up to 5 mph, yielding to any pedestrian.
questions.why: You must stop at least 10 feet from the ice cream truck, then pass at up to 5 miles per hour while yielding to pedestrians. (Driver's Manual, page 18)
wrong: The stopping distance is 10 feet, and you may pass slowly after stopping.
You must stop first, and then pass at no more than 5 miles per hour.
After stopping, you may pass at up to 5 miles per hour; you do not wait for the truck to leave.

questions.q: A bicyclist is riding in the travel lane ahead of you, and you want to make sure the rider knows you are there. What does the manual say about using your horn?
options: Give a long blast on the horn before you reach the bicyclist so the rider moves to the far right edge of the road
Tap the horn lightly twice as you pass so the bicyclist knows which side of the lane you are using
Do not sound your horn close to a bicyclist unless you have good cause, because it may startle the rider into steering into your path
Sound the horn only after you have passed, so the bicyclist does not drift left into the lane behind you
questions.ref: p. 17, Bicyclists (as a driver): do not sound your horn close to bicyclists unless you have good cause, since it may startle them and cause them to steer into your path and crash.
questions.why: Do not sound your horn close to a bicyclist unless you have good cause, because it may startle the rider into your path. (Driver's Manual, page 17)
wrong: A loud horn may startle the bicyclist into your path, and they may have a good reason to ride in the lane.
The manual says not to sound your horn close to bicyclists without good cause.
The manual's advice is to avoid honking near bicyclists, not to honk after passing.

questions.q: You are following a tractor-trailer on a dark highway at night. Which practice does the manual call for?
options: Use your high beams so you can see around the truck and spot debris that the truck has already driven over safely
Flash your high beams at the truck driver to show that you are close behind and would like to pass the truck
Keep your lights on low beam, because high beams glaring in the truck's large side mirrors can blind the truck driver
Follow closely in the truck's rear blind area so that your headlights do not reach the truck's side mirrors
questions.ref: p. 20, Keep a Safe Following Distance Behind Trucks: never use your high beams when following a truck at night; the glare in the large side mirrors can blind the truck driver.
questions.why: Never use your high beams when following a truck at night, because the glare in its large side mirrors can blind the driver. (Driver's Manual, page 20)
wrong: High beams behind a truck can blind the driver through the side mirrors.
Flashing high beams can blind the truck driver, and passing should be done only when it is safe.
Following closely behind a truck means driving blind, and you should stay at least three seconds back.

questions.q: You are approaching a person riding a horse along the edge of a road. What should you do?
options: Tap your horn lightly to let the rider know you are there, so the horse is not startled
Slow down, or stop if necessary, and do not sound your horn or make loud noises
Maintain your speed and keep as far from the horse as possible
Speed up to pass quickly before the horse notices you
questions.ref: p. 18, Horses: reduce speed (or stop if necessary); it is illegal to sound your horn or cause loud or unusual noises when approaching or passing a horse.
questions.why: When you approach a horse, slow down or stop if needed, and it is illegal to sound your horn or make loud noises. (Driver's Manual, page 18)
wrong: Sounding your horn near a horse is illegal.
You must reduce your speed near a horse, not keep it.
You must slow down near a horse, not speed up.

questions.q: The posted speed limit is 50 mph, and packed snow covers the road. According to the manual, about how fast should you drive?
options: About 25 mph
About 40 mph
About 35 mph
About 10 mph
questions.ref: p. 25, Slippery Roads: on packed snow you should cut your speed in half (on a wet road reduce by about 10 mph).
questions.why: On packed snow, cut your speed in half, so 50 miles per hour becomes about 25. (Driver's Manual, page 25)
wrong: 40 is a 10 mile per hour cut, which is the advice for wet roads, not packed snow.
35 is not half of 50; on packed snow you cut your speed in half.
Slowing to a crawl is the advice for ice, not packed snow.

questions.q: While driving late at night, you run over a shoulder rumble strip. What should you do?
options: Turn up the radio and continue to your destination
Drink caffeine and continue driving without stopping
Open the window and keep driving for another hour before resting
Pull off the road at a safe place immediately and check your alertness level
questions.ref: p. 28, Fatigue: if you run over a shoulder rumble strip, pull off the road at a safe place immediately and check your alertness level.
questions.why: If you run over a shoulder rumble strip, pull off the road at a safe place right away and check how alert you are. (Driver's Manual, page 28)
wrong: Turning up the radio is a warning sign of fatigue, not a fix.
Caffeine wears off, and the manual says not to rely on it.
Opening the window is a warning sign of fatigue, and you should pull off now.

questions.q: An adult driver over 21 is arrested for DUI and fails a blood, breath, or urine test. What is the minimum license suspension, and for how long is an ignition interlock device (IID) required?
options: At least 30 days, with an IID for at least six months
At least 90 days, with an IID for at least two years
At least 45 days, with an IID for at least six months
At least 45 days, with an IID for at least one year
questions.ref: p. 33, Alcohol and the Law: failing the test brings a suspension of at least 45 days and an IID for at least six months or possibly more (one year applies to under-21 and test refusal).
questions.why: An adult who fails a test faces a suspension of at least 45 days and an ignition interlock device for at least six months. (Driver's Manual, page 33)
wrong: The minimum suspension is 45 days, not 30.
The manual's minimums are 45 days and six months, not 90 days and two years.
One year is the interlock period for drivers under 21 or anyone who refuses the test.

questions.q: A 22-year-old driver has been convicted of two moving violations. What does Connecticut require?
options: Nothing, until the driver has three or more convictions
Completion of the DMV-certified operator retraining program
A mandatory 90-day license suspension
Retraining is required only for drivers under 18
questions.ref: p. 35, Operator Retraining Program: anyone age 24 or younger who commits two or more moving violations must complete the program (25+ needs three or more).
questions.why: Anyone 24 or younger with two or more moving violations must complete the DMV-certified operator retraining program. (Driver's Manual, page 35)
wrong: Three violations is the rule for drivers 25 or older; at 22, two is enough.
The manual's rule here is the retraining program, not a 90-day suspension.
Retraining applies to anyone 24 or younger with two or more violations, not just teens.

questions.q: On dry pavement with good tires and brakes, about how far does it take to react and bring a vehicle to a complete stop at 30 mph?
options: About 100 feet
About 400 feet
About 300 feet
About 200 feet
questions.ref: p. 36, Stopping: at 30 mph it can take about 200 feet to stop (about 400 feet at 50 mph).
questions.why: At 30 miles per hour on dry pavement, it can take about 200 feet to react and stop. (Driver's Manual, page 36)
wrong: 100 feet is too short; the manual says about 200 feet.
About 400 feet is the stopping distance at 50 miles per hour.
The manual says about 200 feet at 30 miles per hour, not 300.

questions.q: When are you NOT required to stop for a school bus with its red lights flashing?
options: When the bus is traveling toward you and a median or physical barrier separates the roadway
When the bus is on the opposite side of an undivided road and no children are in sight
When you are approaching an intersection where the bus is stopped
When no children are visible along the side of the road
questions.ref: p. 37, Right-of-Way: you must stop whether the bus is on your side, the opposite side, or at an intersection; not required if the bus is traveling toward you and a median or physical barrier separates the roadway.
questions.why: You do not have to stop when the school bus is traveling toward you and a median or other physical barrier separates the roadway. (Driver's Manual, page 37)
wrong: Without a median or barrier, you must stop even if the bus is on the other side.
You must stop for a school bus stopped at an intersection you are approaching.
You must stop even if you see no children.

questions.q: A steady yellow X is displayed over the lane you are driving in on a road with reversible lanes. What does it mean?
options: The lane is only for turning, and you should stay in it until you reach the next intersection ahead
Use of the lane is changing, and you should move out of it as soon as it is safe
You may continue to use the lane at any speed
You may not use the lane
questions.ref: p. 44, Reversible Lanes: a steady yellow X means the use of the lane is changing and you should move out as soon as safe (flashing yellow X = turning only; red X = cannot use).
questions.why: A steady yellow X means the use of the lane is changing, so move out of it as soon as it is safe. (Driver's Manual, page 44)
wrong: A flashing yellow X means the lane is only for turning; a steady yellow X means get out.
A steady yellow X means move out of the lane, not keep using it.
A red X means you cannot use the lane.

questions.q: On a two-lane road, the center line has a solid yellow line on your side and a dashed yellow line on the other side. What does this mean for you?
options: You may pass whenever the oncoming lane is clear
You may pass only during daylight hours when the road ahead is clear of oncoming traffic
You may not pass, since passing is permitted only on the broken-line side
You may pass if you signal first
questions.ref: pp. 43-44, Center Lines: a dashed yellow line alongside a solid yellow line means passing is permitted on the side of the broken line, but not on the side of the solid line.
questions.why: With a solid yellow line on your side and a dashed line on the other, you may not pass; passing is allowed only on the dashed line side. (Driver's Manual, page 44)
wrong: A solid yellow line on your side means you may not pass, even with a clear lane.
Daylight does not matter; the solid line on your side means no passing.
Signaling does not allow you to cross a solid yellow line on your side to pass.

questions.q: A three-sided sign shaped like a pennant is posted on the left side of a two-lane, two-way road. What does it indicate?
options: A school zone ahead
A railroad crossing ahead
A yield situation ahead
The beginning of a no-passing zone
questions.ref: p. 46, Shapes, Pennant: No Passing Zone; posted on the left side at the beginning of a no-passing zone.
questions.why: The pennant-shaped sign, posted on the left side of a two-lane, two-way road, marks the beginning of a no-passing zone. (Driver's Manual, page 46)
wrong: School zones are marked by a five-sided pentagon sign.
A railroad crossing ahead is shown by a round sign.
A yield sign is a downward-pointing triangle.

questions.q: An applicant is blind in one eye. What is the minimum vision requirement for the other eye?
options: At least 20/20, with no visual field requirement
At least 20/40, with no visual field requirement
At least 20/40, with a minimal visual field of 100 degrees or more
At least 20/70, with a visual field of 100 degrees or more
questions.ref: p. 5, The Vision Test: if blind in one eye, the other must be at least 20/40 with a minimal visual field of 100 degrees or more.
questions.why: If an applicant is blind in one eye, the other eye must be at least twenty forty with a visual field of at least 100 degrees. (Driver's Manual, page 5)
wrong: The standard is twenty forty, not twenty twenty, and there is a visual field requirement.
Twenty forty is right, but a visual field of at least 100 degrees is also required.
The eye must be at least twenty forty; twenty seventy is too weak.

questions.q: A 17-year-old has had a driver's license for eight months. Assuming there are enough seat belts, which passenger may the teen carry?
options: The teen's younger brother
A classmate who is also 17
A neighbor who is 16
A teammate going to practice
questions.ref: p. 8, Passenger Restrictions: during months seven through twelve the only additional passengers allowed are members of the driver's immediate family.
questions.why: In months seven through twelve of a teen license, the only extra passengers allowed are members of the driver's immediate family, such as a brother. (Driver's Manual, page 8)
wrong: A classmate is not immediate family, so teen friends are not allowed in the first year.
A neighbor is not immediate family, so this passenger is not allowed in the first year.
A teammate is not immediate family, so this passenger is not allowed in the first year.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of hours of behind-the-wheel, on-the-road training required of all 16- and 17-year-old license applicants?
options: 8 hours
30 hours
100 hours
40 hours
questions.ref: p. 7: all 16/17-year-old applicants must have at least 40 hours behind-the-wheel training (p. 30 only recommends 100 hours).
questions.why: All 16- and 17-year-old applicants must have at least 40 hours of behind-the-wheel, on-the-road training. (Driver's Manual, page 7)
wrong: 8 hours is the safe driving practices course or a part of school training, not the full requirement.
30 hours is the classroom requirement, not behind-the-wheel time.
100 hours is recommended, but the legal minimum is 40. (page 30)

questions.q: A 17-year-old is convicted of violating the driving curfew for the second time. What is the penalty?
options: A 30-day suspension, a $175 restoration fee, and court fines for the offense
A 6-month suspension or until age 18, whichever is longer
A 90-day suspension
A 1-year suspension
questions.ref: p. 34, suspension table: GDL violations (curfew) bring a 30-day suspension for the 1st offense and a 6-month suspension or until age 18, whichever is longer, for 2nd and subsequent offenses.
questions.why: A second or later teen curfew violation brings a 6-month suspension or until age 18, whichever is longer, plus a 175 dollar restoration fee. (Driver's Manual, page 34)
wrong: A 30-day suspension is the penalty for a first curfew violation.
90 days is the second-offense penalty for cell phone use, not curfew violations.
A 1-year suspension is for a second reckless driving or street racing offense.

questions.q: A driver whose car has an automatic shoulder belt and front airbags says there is no need to buckle the lap belt. What is true?
options: The driver is right, since airbags and the shoulder belt together give full protection in any kind of crash
The driver is right, but should buckle the lap belt on highways
The lap belt must be buckled too, or the driver could slide out of the belt and be hurt or killed
Airbags make safety belts unnecessary at speeds below 25 mph
questions.ref: p. 12, Seat Belt Laws: with an automatic shoulder belt, buckle the lap belt as well; state law requires belts even with airbags.
questions.why: With an automatic shoulder belt, you must buckle the lap belt too, or you could slide out and be hurt or killed. (Driver's Manual, page 12)
wrong: Airbags do not protect you in side or rear crashes or rollovers, and you still need the lap belt.
The lap belt is needed on every trip, not just on highways.
Even at 25 miles per hour a crash is like riding a bike full speed into a brick wall, so belts are always needed. (page 13)

questions.q: A parent is driving an 18-month-old child who weighs 32 pounds. Which restraint is required?
options: A rear-facing car seat, because the more restrictive requirement applies when categories differ
A forward-facing seat with a 5-point harness, because the child is over 30 pounds and the weight category controls
A booster seat
A regular seat belt with the lap belt only
questions.ref: pp. 12-13, Child Safety Requirements: if age and weight fall in two categories (under 2 but over 30 lb), the more restrictive requirement (rear-facing seat) applies.
questions.why: When a child's age and weight fall into two categories, such as under two but over 30 pounds, the more restrictive rule applies, which is a rear-facing seat. (Driver's Manual, page 12)
wrong: Weight does not control; when categories differ, the stricter one, rear-facing, applies.
Booster seats are for older and heavier children, not a child under two.
A seat belt alone is never right for a child under two.

questions.q: Gases from a leaky exhaust can cause death inside a vehicle in a very short time. If you must sit in your vehicle with the motor running for a long time, what should you do?
options: Keep the windows closed so exhaust cannot get in
Park inside a closed garage for protection from the weather
Turn on the emergency flashers
Open a window
questions.ref: p. 12, Exhaust System: never run the motor in a closed garage; if you sit in a vehicle with the motor running for a long time, open a window.
questions.why: If you sit in a vehicle with the motor running for a long time, open a window, because exhaust leaks can kill quickly. (Driver's Manual, page 12)
wrong: The manual says to open a window, since many exhaust leaks cannot be heard.
Never run the motor in a closed garage.
Emergency flashers do nothing to protect you from exhaust gases.

questions.q: In which of these situations does the manual say you may need a four-second following distance?
options: You are driving on a dry road in light daytime traffic
You are pulling a trailer, which increases your stopping distance
You are the first vehicle stopped at a green light
You are driving alone on a straight, dry highway in clear daylight with light traffic
questions.ref: p. 21, When to use the 'four-second' rule: includes slippery roads, following motorcycles, pulling a trailer, low visibility, and others; the three-second rule is the baseline.
questions.why: Pulling a trailer is one of the times to use a four-second following distance, because the extra weight increases your stopping distance. (Driver's Manual, page 21)
wrong: A dry road in light traffic is a normal condition, where the three-second rule applies.
Being the first car stopped at a light is not on the manual's list of four-second situations.
Clear, dry, light traffic is a normal condition, where the three-second rule applies.

questions.q: You are in the right lane of a multi-lane highway and need to cross three lanes to reach your exit. What does the manual advise?
options: Check once and cross all three lanes at once to spend less time in traffic
Wait until all of the lanes are clear, then cross them together
Take the lanes one at a time
Flash your headlights and cross all lanes in one move
questions.ref: p. 23, Changing Lanes: if you want to change several lanes, take them one at a time; waiting for all lanes to be clear can tie up traffic and cause a crash.
questions.why: When you need to cross several lanes, take them one at a time. (Driver's Manual, page 23)
wrong: Crossing several lanes at once is unsafe, because it is hard to be sure all of them are clear.
Waiting for all lanes to clear can tie up traffic and even cause a crash.
Flashing your lights does not make it safe to cross several lanes at once.

questions.q: At 55 mph, about how much clear distance do you need to complete a pass safely, counting the oncoming vehicle that is also approaching?
options: About 400 feet
About 800 feet
About 200 feet
Over 1,600 feet (about one-third of a mile)
questions.ref: p. 23, Rules of Passing: at 55 mph you need about 10 seconds; you travel over 800 feet and so does the oncoming vehicle, so you need over 1,600 feet.
questions.why: At 55 miles per hour you travel over 800 feet in the 10 seconds a pass takes, and so does an oncoming car, so you need over 1,600 feet. (Driver's Manual, page 23)
wrong: About 400 feet is the stopping distance at 50 miles per hour, far too short for passing.
800 feet covers only your own travel and ignores the oncoming car.
About 200 feet is the stopping distance at 30 miles per hour.

questions.q: On the highway, 12 seconds of look-ahead distance is about:
options: Four city blocks, or a quarter of a mile
One city block
Half a mile
Eight city blocks
questions.ref: p. 14, Look Ahead: in the city 12 seconds is about one block; on the highway about four city blocks (a quarter of a mile).
questions.why: On the highway, looking 12 seconds ahead is about four city blocks, or a quarter of a mile. (Driver's Manual, page 14)
wrong: One block is the 12 second distance in the city, not on the highway.
Half a mile is too far; the manual says a quarter of a mile.
Eight blocks is too far; the manual says about four blocks.

questions.q: You are in the middle of an intersection when you hear the siren of an approaching fire engine. What should you do?
options: Stop immediately where you are
Pull to the left edge of the road and stop
Continue driving at the same speed until the fire engine passes
Drive through the intersection, then pull over to the right and stop
questions.ref: p. 37, Right-of-Way: if you are in an intersection, drive through the intersection before you pull over (to the right) and stop.
questions.why: If you are in an intersection when an emergency vehicle comes, drive through the intersection first, then pull over to the right and stop. (Driver's Manual, page 37)
wrong: Stopping in the intersection could block the fire engine; clear the intersection first.
You must pull over to the right edge of the road, not the left.
You must pull over and stop, then stay stopped until the emergency vehicle passes.

questions.q: A vehicle is pulled over on the side of a multi-lane highway ahead of you. What does the 'Move Over Law' require?
options: Slow down below the posted speed limit and move over one lane when it is safe
Stop completely until the vehicle leaves
Maintain your speed and sound your horn
Move over only if the vehicle is a police vehicle or tow truck with its lights flashing
questions.ref: p. 16, Move Over Law: when any vehicle is pulled over on any part of a highway, slow down (below the posted limit) and move over one lane when safe.
questions.why: When any vehicle is pulled over on a highway, slow down below the posted speed limit and move over one lane when it is safe. (Driver's Manual, page 16)
wrong: The law asks you to slow down and move over, not to stop.
You must slow down, and honking is not part of the law.
The law applies to any vehicle that is pulled over, not only police or tow trucks.

questions.q: A pedestrian at the curb of an intersection with no painted crosswalk lines moves the front of a stroller into the entrance of the crosswalk. What must you do?
options: Proceed, because the crosswalk is not marked with painted lines and the pedestrian has not yet stepped into the roadway itself
Proceed, because the pedestrian has not stepped into the roadway
Slow or stop and yield, since every intersection has a crosswalk and the pedestrian has indicated intent to cross
Sound your horn to warn the pedestrian and then continue
questions.ref: p. 16, Pedestrians: there is a crosswalk at every intersection even if unmarked; a pedestrian indicates intent by moving any extension of the body, including a stroller, into the crosswalk entrance.
questions.why: Every intersection has a crosswalk, even without painted lines, and moving a stroller into the crosswalk entrance shows intent to cross, so you must slow or stop and yield. (Driver's Manual, page 16)
wrong: Every intersection has a crosswalk, even if it is not painted, and a stroller counts as showing intent.
Putting a stroller into the crosswalk entrance counts as showing intent to cross.
Honking does not let you skip yielding; you must slow or stop for the pedestrian.

questions.q: You are driving down a rainy street and see a pedestrian with an umbrella held in front of the face stepping toward the curb. What does the manual say about people in this situation?
options: They are required to stop at the curb and wait until you have passed, so you may keep your speed and lane position
They are considered to have seen you once you tap your horn lightly, so you may then continue past without slowing
They may not be able to see you and could enter your path without knowing you are there, so give them extra room
They have the right-of-way only in painted crosswalks, so you need not adjust for them at unmarked corners
questions.ref: p. 24, Visibility, Others Who Cannot See You: pedestrians with umbrellas in front of their faces or hats pulled down may enter your path without knowing you are there; p. 22 says to give pedestrians extra space.
questions.why: Pedestrians with umbrellas in front of their faces may not see you and could step into your path, so give them extra room. (Driver's Manual, pages 22 and 24)
wrong: The manual warns that such pedestrians may enter your path without knowing you are there.
A horn tap does not mean they saw you, and you must still be ready to yield.
There is a crosswalk at every intersection, marked or not. (page 16)

questions.q: You are about to pull out onto a road and see an approaching motorcycle with its left turn signal flashing but it has not begun to turn. What should you do?
options: Pull out, because the signal shows the motorcycle is turning
Tap your horn and pull out
Speed up to get in front of the motorcycle
Wait until you see the motorcycle actually begin to turn
questions.ref: p. 18, Motorcycles: do not assume a motorcycle is turning when its signal flashes; signals may not self-cancel. Do not pull out until you see it actually begin to turn.
questions.why: Do not assume a motorcycle is turning just because its signal is flashing; wait until you see it actually begin to turn. (Driver's Manual, page 18)
wrong: Motorcycle signals may not cancel by themselves, so a flashing signal does not prove a turn.
Honking does not make it safe to pull out; wait until the motorcycle turns.
Racing in front of a motorcycle is dangerous; wait until it actually turns.

questions.q: While driving in heavy rain, you feel your tires lose traction with the road surface. What should you do?
options: Brake firmly to regain traction
Turn the steering wheel sharply to find a grip
Ease your foot off the gas pedal and keep the steering wheel straight
Accelerate to drive out of the water
questions.ref: p. 25, Water on the Roadway: if you lose traction, ease your foot off the gas, keep the steering wheel straight, and do not try to stop or turn until the tires grip again.
questions.why: If your tires lose traction on water, ease your foot off the gas and keep the steering wheel straight. (Driver's Manual, page 25)
wrong: Do not try to stop until your tires are gripping the road again.
Turning sharply can cause a skid; turn only in an emergency, and then slowly.
Speed causes hydroplaning, so ease off the gas instead.

questions.q: A hostile driver, angry after a confrontation, is pursuing you. What should you do?
options: Drive to a police station or other public, well-lit place where you can get help
Drive home and call the police from there once you are safely inside with the doors locked
Pull over and speak with the other driver
Make eye contact to show you are not afraid
questions.ref: p. 26, Eye Contact: do not make eye contact; if a motorist pursues you, do not go home; drive to a police station, convenience store, or other public, well-lit location.
questions.why: If a hostile driver pursues you, do not go home; drive to a police station or another public, well-lit place where you can get help. (Driver's Manual, page 26)
wrong: The manual says if a motorist pursues you, do not go home.
The manual says to get out of the way and not engage the other driver.
Do not make eye contact, because it can be seen as a challenge.

questions.q: Which of the following has about the same amount of alcohol as one standard alcohol drink?
options: An 8-oz. glass of wine
A 16-oz. mug of beer
3 oz. of 80-proof liquor
A 5-oz. glass of wine
questions.ref: p. 33, Alcohol and You: a drink is 1.5 oz of 80-proof liquor, 12 oz of beer, or a 5 oz glass of wine.
questions.why: One alcohol drink is a 5 ounce glass of wine, 12 ounces of beer, or 1.5 ounces of 80-proof liquor. (Driver's Manual, page 33)
wrong: A drink of wine is 5 ounces, so 8 ounces is more than one drink.
A drink of beer is 12 ounces, so 16 ounces is more than one drink.
A drink of liquor is 1.5 ounces, so 3 ounces is two drinks.

questions.q: A group of friends is going to a party where alcohol will be served. Which plan does the manual recommend?
options: Let the person who has had the fewest drinks drive, after waiting an hour and drinking coffee to sober up
Go with two or more people and agree which one will not drink, rotating the designated driver, or use public transportation or a cab
Agree that anyone who feels fine after a single drink may drive, because only larger amounts affect judgment
Stop drinking two hours before leaving and let each driver take a cold shower and get fresh air before driving
questions.ref: p. 33, Alcohol and You: arrange to go with two or more persons, agree which one will not drink and rotate as designated driver, or use public transportation or a cab.
questions.why: Go with two or more people and agree on one who will not drink, taking turns as designated driver, or use public transportation or a cab. (Driver's Manual, page 33)
wrong: Coffee does not sober you up; only time does.
Any amount of alcohol can affect your driving, and under 21 one drink can count as impaired.
Cold showers and fresh air do not sober you up; only time does.

questions.q: Which of the following parking spots is illegal?
options: Parked 20 feet from a stop sign
Parked 12 feet from a fire hydrant
Parked 30 feet from a pedestrian safety zone
Parked in a designated parking area
questions.ref: p. 37, No-Parking Zones: do not park within 25 feet of a stop sign or pedestrian safety zone, or within 10 feet of a fire hydrant.
questions.why: You may not park within 25 feet of a stop sign, so 20 feet is too close. (Driver's Manual, page 37)
wrong: The rule is to stay at least 10 feet from a hydrant, so 12 feet is legal.
The rule is to stay 25 feet from a pedestrian safety zone, so 30 feet is legal.
The manual says to always park in a designated area if possible.

questions.q: The engine dies while you are driving on a road. What should you do?
options: Turn the ignition to the lock position so the engine can be restarted, then steer toward the shoulder
Keep a strong grip on the steering wheel, which may be hard to turn but still can be turned, and pull off the roadway
Shift into park right away and release the wheel, because the steering will lock until the engine restarts
Stop in the travel lane and turn on the flashers, because the brakes will not work when the engine is off
questions.ref: p. 40, Power Failure: keep a strong grip on the steering wheel (it may be difficult to turn but is possible) and pull off the roadway; the brakes will still work but you may have to push very hard.
questions.why: If the engine dies, keep a strong grip on the steering wheel, which may be hard to turn but still works, and pull off the roadway. (Driver's Manual, page 40)
wrong: Never turn the ignition to lock while moving, or the steering will lock.
The wheel can still be turned, so keep a strong grip and pull off the road.
The brakes still work, though you may have to push very hard, so pull off the road.

questions.q: A HAWK signal over a crosswalk is displaying a flashing red. What must drivers do?
options: Proceed with caution, because the signal is not activated
Stop and wait for the signal to turn green
Slow down and proceed with caution
Stop, and proceed only when pedestrians have cleared the crosswalk
questions.ref: p. 45, HAWK Signals: flashing red means the signal is about to deactivate; drivers must stop but may proceed when pedestrians have cleared the crosswalk.
questions.why: A flashing red HAWK signal means it is about to shut off, so you must stop but may go once pedestrians have cleared the crosswalk. (Driver's Manual, page 45)
wrong: A dark HAWK signal means it is not activated; flashing red means you must stop.
A HAWK signal has no green; you may go once pedestrians clear the crosswalk.
Slowing down is not enough; you must stop at a flashing red HAWK signal.

questions.q: A blue Emergency Notification System sign at a highway-rail grade crossing provides:
options: A train schedule for that crossing
A 24/7/365 telephone number to report problems at the crossing
Advance notice that the crossing is closed
A list of train schedules and the nearest rail stations for that crossing
questions.ref: p. 51, Railroad Crossing Signs: a blue Emergency Notification System sign gives a 24/7/365 telephone number to report problems or emergencies.
questions.why: The blue Emergency Notification System sign gives a phone number, answered 24 hours a day every day of the year, to report problems or emergencies at the crossing. (Driver's Manual, page 51)
wrong: The sign gives a phone number to report problems, not a train schedule.
The sign gives a phone number for reporting problems, not a closure notice.
The sign gives a phone number for reporting problems, not schedules or station lists.

questions.q: What does a double solid white pavement line mean?
options: Lane changing is prohibited
Lane changing is allowed when it is safe
The lane is reserved for high occupancy vehicles
Passing is allowed on either side
questions.ref: p. 44, Other Markings: a double solid white line prohibits lane changing.
questions.why: A double solid white line prohibits lane changing. (Driver's Manual, page 44)
wrong: Dashed white lines allow lane changes; a double solid white line forbids them.
HOV lanes are marked with a diamond-shaped marker and signs.
A double solid white line prohibits changing lanes, so you may not pass across it.

questions.q: A 19-year-old with no previous license applies for a Connecticut learner's permit. What is the minimum time the permit must be held before the road test?
options: 120 days
180 days
30 days
90 days
questions.ref: p. 7, Applicants 18 Years of Age or Older: must hold a learner's permit for at least 90 days before the road test.
questions.why: A person 18 or older must hold a learner's permit for at least 90 days before taking the road test. (Driver's Manual, page 7)
wrong: 120 days is the wait for teens who finish driver education at a school.
180 days is the wait for teens who do not train through a school program.
The manual's minimum is 90 days, not 30.

questions.q: Which statement about the vehicle used for a Connecticut road test is correct?
options: A rented vehicle may be used by an applicant with no valid license if the rental company provides proof of insurance
A long-term leased vehicle may be used if its insurance identifies the vehicle and the lease company
An unlicensed applicant may drive alone to the test location if it is nearby
A vehicle with no valid registration may be used if it is insured
questions.ref: p. 7, The Road Test: vehicle must have valid registration and proof of insurance; long-term leased vehicles properly insured may be used; no rentals without a valid license; unlicensed operator cannot drive to the test alone.
questions.why: A long-term leased vehicle may be used for the road test if its insurance identifies the vehicle and the lease company. (Driver's Manual, page 7)
wrong: If you do not have a valid driver's license, you cannot test in a rented vehicle.
A non-licensed operator cannot drive to the test location alone, even nearby.
The test vehicle must have a valid registration as well as proof of insurance.

questions.q: How many hours of instruction must a parent or legal guardian complete with a teen who obtains a learner's permit?
options: Four hours, covering the effects of alcohol and drugs on drivers and the penalties for violations
Eight hours, covering all material in the driver's manual
Two hours, on the laws governing drivers under 18 and the dangers of teen driving
Thirty hours, covering classroom instruction
questions.ref: p. 6, Parent Training Requirements: two hours of instruction concerning the laws governing drivers under 18 and the dangers of teen driving.
questions.why: A parent or legal guardian of a 16- or 17-year-old permit holder must complete two hours of instruction with the teen. It covers the laws for drivers under 18 and the dangers of teen driving. (Driver's Manual, page 6)
wrong: Four hours on alcohol and drugs is part of the eight-hour safe driving course, not the parent training.
The parent class is two hours, not eight, and it does not cover the whole manual.
Thirty hours is the classroom course for teens, not the parent training.

questions.q: A 17-year-old is convicted for the second time of using a hands-free phone while driving. What is the penalty?
options: A 90-day suspension and a $175 license restoration fee
A 30-day suspension and a $175 license restoration fee
A 60-day suspension and a $175 license restoration fee
A 6-month suspension and a $175 license restoration fee
questions.ref: p. 34, suspension table: cell phone use brings 30 days (1st), 90 days (2nd), and 6 months (3rd). Drivers 16/17 may not use even hands-free devices (p. 8).
questions.why: For a 16- or 17-year-old, cell phone use brings a 30-day suspension the first time and a 90-day suspension the second time. Teens may not use even a hands-free phone. (Driver's Manual, page 34)
wrong: Thirty days is the penalty for a first offense, not a second.
No cell phone offense carries 60 days. That number is for a first speeding offense.
Six months is the penalty for a third offense.

questions.q: You want to check your tire pressure with a gauge. Where does the manual say you can find the recommended psi?
options: On the tire sidewall, which always lists the exact pressure that you should inflate the tire to
On the dashboard panel next to the warning light that shows the tire pressure symbol
On the registration card that you are required to keep in the vehicle at all times
In the vehicle owner's manual or on the driver's side door jamb of the vehicle
questions.ref: p. 11, Tires: the recommended psi is located in the vehicle owner's manual or the driver's side door jamb; use a tire pressure gauge to check it.
questions.why: The recommended tire pressure is listed in the vehicle owner's manual or on the driver's side door jamb. Use a tire pressure gauge to check it. (Driver's Manual, page 11)
wrong: The manual points you to the owner's manual or the door jamb, not the tire sidewall.
The manual does not say the dashboard lists the recommended pressure.
The registration card does not list tire pressure. The manual names the owner's manual or door jamb.

questions.q: A vehicle bounces a lot after a bump or a stop and is hard to control. According to the manual, which parts may need to be replaced?
options: Worn brake pads and rotors in the braking system
A leaking muffler or exhaust pipe in the exhaust system
New shocks or other suspension parts
Cracked wiper blades or a damaged washer bottle
questions.ref: p. 12, Suspension System: if the vehicle bounces a lot after a bump or a stop, or is hard to control, you may need new shocks or other suspension parts; have a mechanic check it.
questions.why: If a vehicle bounces a lot after a bump or a stop, or is hard to control, it may need new shocks or other suspension parts. Have a mechanic check it. (Driver's Manual, page 12)
wrong: Brake trouble shows up as noise, an odd smell, pulling to one side, or a pedal that sinks to the floor.
The exhaust system handles engine gases and noise, not bouncing.
Wipers and washer fluid help you see. They do not affect how the car bounces.

questions.q: When you finish a sharp turn using the hand-over-hand technique, how should you straighten the steering wheel?
options: Let the wheel slip back through your fingers to save time
Straighten it by hand rather than letting it slip through your fingers
Release the wheel so it straightens itself
Pull it back with one hand while shifting
questions.ref: p. 14, Steering, Hand-over-Hand: when you complete a turn, straighten out the wheel by hand; letting it slip through your fingers could be dangerous.
questions.why: After a hand-over-hand turn, straighten the steering wheel by hand. Letting it slip through your fingers could be dangerous. (Driver's Manual, page 14)
wrong: The manual warns that letting the wheel slip through your fingers could be dangerous.
Letting go of the wheel means losing control. Straighten it by hand.
The manual says to straighten the wheel by hand, not while shifting with one hand.

questions.q: You are driving on a road with exit ramps and want to exit. When should you begin to slow down?
options: As soon as you signal, while still in the main lane
A quarter mile before the exit
As soon as you can see the exit sign
Not until you have moved onto the exit ramp
questions.ref: p. 21, Space to Leave: keep up with the speed of traffic on the main road; do not slow down until you move onto the exit ramp.
questions.why: Keep up with the speed of traffic while you are on the main road. Do not slow down until you have moved onto the exit ramp. (Driver's Manual, page 21)
wrong: Slowing in the main lane surprises drivers behind you. Wait until you are on the ramp.
The manual gives no quarter-mile rule. Stay at traffic speed until you are on the ramp.
Seeing the sign is too early. Keep pace with traffic until you reach the ramp.

questions.q: You are on a two-lane road with no right lane and a driver is following you very closely. What should you do?
options: Wait until the road ahead is clear, then reduce your speed slowly
Brake hard for a moment to make the tailgater back off
Speed up to stay ahead of the tailgater
Stop on the road and let the tailgater pass
questions.ref: p. 22, Being Tailgated: if no right lane, wait until the road ahead is clear and reduce speed slowly; never slow down quickly to discourage a tailgater.
questions.why: If you are tailgated and there is no right lane, wait until the road ahead is clear, then slow down gradually. This encourages the tailgater to go around you. (Driver's Manual, page 22)
wrong: Never slow down quickly to discourage a tailgater. It raises your risk of being hit from behind.
Speeding up does not help. The manual says to slow down gradually when the road ahead is clear.
Do not stop in a travel lane for any reason. It is dangerous.

questions.q: You are driving on a road with two lanes in your direction and you are not passing or turning left. Which lane should you use?
options: The left lane, since it is for faster traffic
Either lane, as long as you signal your lane changes and do not exceed the posted speed limit at any time
The right lane, since Connecticut law requires it with fewer than three lanes in your direction
The left lane if you are traveling faster than the cars to your right
questions.ref: p. 23, On Multi-Lane roads: when direction of travel is less than three lanes, Connecticut law requires you to drive in the right lane except when passing.
questions.why: When your direction of travel has fewer than three lanes, Connecticut law requires you to drive in the right lane except when passing. (Driver's Manual, page 23)
wrong: The left lane is for passing slower vehicles, not for everyday travel.
Signaling and staying under the limit do not make it okay. The law requires the right lane here.
Being faster does not let you stay left. Use the left lane only to pass, then return to the right.

questions.q: A bicyclist is riding slowly in the travel lane on a two-lane road marked with a double solid yellow line. When may you pass?
options: Never, because crossing a double solid yellow line to pass any vehicle, including a bicycle, is always illegal
Only if you can see far enough ahead to pass safely and leave at least three feet of space
Only after sounding your horn to warn the bicyclist
Only if the bicyclist moves onto the shoulder
questions.ref: pp. 17-18: you may pass slow moving vehicles, including bicyclists, in a no passing zone if you can do so safely (cross the double yellow only if you can see far enough ahead), with a minimum of three feet.
questions.why: You may pass slow vehicles, including bicyclists, in a no-passing zone if you can see far enough ahead to do it safely. You must leave at least three feet when passing a bicycle. (Driver's Manual, pages 17 and 18)
wrong: State law allows crossing a double yellow line to pass a bicycle when it is safe.
The manual says not to sound your horn near bicyclists. It can startle them.
The bicyclist does not have to move to the shoulder. You may pass safely with three feet of space.

questions.q: Why should you resist the temptation to pass on the right of a truck that is approaching an intersection?
options: Trucks always have the right-of-way at intersections
The rear wheels of a truck follow a longer path than its front wheels
Trucks cannot make right turns without stopping first
If the truck turns right, you could be caught between the truck and the curb
questions.ref: p. 20, Trucks Make Wide Right Turns: resist passing on the right of a truck approaching an intersection; if the driver turns right you could be caught between the truck and the curb. (Rear wheels follow a shorter path.)
questions.why: Do not pass on the right of a truck near an intersection. If the truck turns right, you could be caught between the truck and the curb. (Driver's Manual, page 20)
wrong: The manual does not give trucks the right-of-way at intersections. The danger is getting trapped by a wide turn.
The rear wheels of a truck follow a shorter path than the front wheels, not a longer one.
The manual does not say trucks must stop before turning right. They swing wide to make the turn.

questions.q: A school bus ahead has stopped with its red lights flashing, and they have just stopped flashing. What should you do?
options: Watch for children along the road and wait until they have left the roadway and it is safe
Proceed immediately, since the bus lights have stopped flashing and the children are already on board
Proceed as soon as the bus starts to move
Proceed slowly while sounding your horn
questions.ref: p. 37, Right-of-Way: after the school bus lights stop flashing, watch for children and do not proceed until they have completely left the roadway and it is safe.
questions.why: After a school bus's red lights stop flashing, watch for children along the road. Do not go until they have completely left the roadway and it is safe. (Driver's Manual, page 37)
wrong: Children may still be near the road. Wait until they have fully left the roadway.
The bus moving is not the signal. Wait until the children are out of the road.
Honking is not the rule. Wait until the children have left the roadway and it is safe.

questions.q: You see an orange triangle on the back of a vehicle. What does it mean?
options: The vehicle is disabled and stopped on the road
The vehicle is carrying hazardous materials and is required to stop at all railroad crossings
A slow-moving vehicle, such as a farm tractor, usually traveling 25 mph or less
The vehicle is an emergency vehicle responding to a call
questions.ref: p. 18, Slow Moving Vehicles: farm tractors, animal-drawn and roadway maintenance vehicles usually go 25 mph or less and display an orange triangle slow-moving decal.
questions.why: An orange triangle marks a slow-moving vehicle. Farm tractors, animal-drawn vehicles, and road maintenance vehicles usually go 25 miles per hour or less. (Driver's Manual, page 18)
wrong: A disabled vehicle uses emergency flashers. The orange triangle means slow-moving.
The manual does not use the orange triangle for hazardous materials. It means slow-moving.
Emergency vehicles use sirens and flashing lights. The triangle means slow-moving.

questions.q: You are following a motorcyclist on a road with potholes and loose gravel. What does the manual say to expect?
options: The rider will hold a steady line, because motorcycles handle gravel and potholes just as safely as cars do
The rider will stop completely and wait for you to pass, so you should move up close behind to be ready
The rider will move onto the shoulder, so you should speed up to keep pace in the vacated lane
The rider may suddenly change lanes or speed to avoid the hazard, so you should allow room for the motorcyclist to maneuver
questions.ref: p. 18, Motorcycles: obstacles minor to a motorist, such as potholes and gravel, can be deadly to a motorcyclist; be prepared for sudden changes in lanes or speed and allow room to maneuver.
questions.why: Potholes and gravel that seem minor to a car can be deadly to a motorcyclist. Expect sudden changes in lane or speed, and leave the rider room to maneuver. (Driver's Manual, page 18)
wrong: These hazards are much more dangerous for motorcycles than for cars.
Moving up close is unsafe. Leave extra room behind a motorcycle.
Speeding up is unsafe. Leave the rider room to maneuver.

questions.q: Why can the pavement on a bridge be icy even when other pavement is not?
options: Bridges are always shaded by trees and tall buildings along the water
Bridges have no earth underneath to insulate them
Bridges are never treated with road salt
Water from rivers freezes on the pavement
questions.ref: p. 25, Slippery Roads: bridges do not have earth underneath to insulate them, so they can be colder and icier than other roadways.
questions.why: Bridges have no earth underneath to insulate them from the cold. So they can be colder and icier than other roads. (Driver's Manual, page 25)
wrong: The manual does not mention trees or buildings. The reason is that no earth insulates the bridge.
The manual does not say bridges are never salted. The reason is the missing earth underneath.
The manual does not blame river water. Bridges ice up because nothing insulates them from below.

questions.q: According to the manual, people with untreated obstructive sleep apnea are how many times more likely to fall asleep at the wheel?
options: 7 times
2 times
6 times
10 times
questions.ref: p. 28, Fatigue: untreated obstructive sleep apnea makes drivers 7 times more likely to fall asleep at the wheel (night shift work increases the risk by nearly 6 times).
questions.why: People with untreated obstructive sleep apnea are 7 times more likely to fall asleep at the wheel. (Driver's Manual, page 28)
wrong: The manual's number is 7 times, not 2.
Nearly 6 times is the added risk for night shift workers, not sleep apnea.
The manual's number is 7 times, not 10.

questions.q: After drinking several beers at a party, you want to drive home in an hour. What will sober you up?
options: Drinking several cups of strong coffee
Taking a cold shower
Only the passage of time
Walking outside in the fresh air
questions.ref: p. 33, Alcohol and You: there is no way to sober up quickly; coffee, fresh air, exercise, or cold showers will not help; time is the only thing.
questions.why: There is no way to sober up quickly. Coffee, fresh air, exercise, and cold showers do not help. Only time will sober you up. (Driver's Manual, page 33)
wrong: The manual says coffee will not sober you up.
The manual says a cold shower will not sober you up.
The manual says fresh air will not sober you up.

questions.q: A driver completes the DMV operator retraining program and commits another moving violation 18 months later. What results?
options: No suspension, because more than one year has passed
A license suspension of at least 30 days
A suspension of at least 45 days
A suspension of at least 90 days
questions.ref: p. 35, Operator Retraining Program: an additional moving violation within three years of completion results in a suspension of at least 30 days.
questions.why: After completing operator retraining, another moving violation within three years brings a suspension of at least 30 days. Eighteen months falls inside that window. (Driver's Manual, page 35)
wrong: The window is three years, not one. Eighteen months is still inside it.
The manual's minimum is 30 days, not 45.
The manual's minimum is 30 days, not 90.

questions.q: You are driving in a roundabout and a driver on another approach is waiting to enter. What should you do?
options: Keep moving; do not stop within the roundabout to allow that driver to enter
Stop and wave the driver into the roundabout
Stop, because entering traffic has the right-of-way
Slow to a crawl until the driver enters
questions.ref: p. 37, Roundabouts: entering traffic must yield to circulating traffic; do not stop within the roundabout to allow traffic to enter from another leg.
questions.why: Drivers entering a roundabout must yield to traffic already circulating. Do not stop inside the roundabout to let traffic in from another road. (Driver's Manual, page 37)
wrong: Stopping to wave someone in breaks the rule. Do not stop within the roundabout.
