questions.q: You are following a car and pass the same sign two seconds after the rear of that car passed it. What does the manual say to do?
options: Nothing, because two seconds is a safe following distance at any speed
Drop back and recount at another spot until you are no closer than three seconds
Speed up so that you pass the car and no longer follow it
Drop back to exactly four seconds, which is the required distance on dry roads
questions.ref: p.21 Space Ahead: if you pass the mark before finishing the count you are following too closely; drop back and recount until following no closer than three seconds.
questions.why: If you pass the mark before you finish counting three seconds, you are too close. Drop back and count again until you are no closer than three seconds. (Driver's Manual, page 21)
wrong: Two seconds is too close. The rule is at least three seconds.
Speeding up to pass is not the fix. Drop back to three seconds.
Three seconds is the basic rule. Four seconds is for special cases like slippery roads.

questions.q: Before you change into the next lane on a road with several lanes in your direction, what else does the manual say to check besides the lane you want to enter?
options: The shoulder, because a vehicle parked there may pull back onto the road and take the lane you want to enter
The far lane, because someone in that lane may be planning to move into the same lane you want to enter
The oncoming lanes, because a driver there may cross over into the lane that you are planning to enter
The lane behind you only, because traffic in the far lane cannot possibly reach the lane you want to enter
questions.ref: p. 23, Changing Lanes: check the far lane (if there is one), as someone in that lane may be planning to move into the same lane that you want to enter.
questions.why: Before changing lanes, check the far lane if there is one. Someone there may be planning to move into the same lane you want. (Driver's Manual, page 23)
wrong: The manual's extra check is the far lane, not the shoulder.
The manual's extra check is the far lane, not oncoming traffic.
Traffic in the far lane can move into your target lane, so you must check it.

questions.q: A freight train has just cleared a crossing that has more than one track. What should you do before crossing?
options: Cross immediately, since the train that passed has already cleared the crossing area
Look only in the direction the train came from, then cross when it is clear
Stop on the tracks for a moment to look carefully in both directions
Wait until the passing train is well down the track, since it may hide a second train
questions.ref: p.15 Railroad Crossings: at crossings with more than one track, wait until the passing train is well down the track; the train that just passed may hide another one.
questions.why: At crossings with more than one track, wait until the passing train is well down the track. It may be hiding another train. (Driver's Manual, page 15)
wrong: A second train may be hidden behind the first. Wait before crossing.
Look both ways and wait. Another train could come from either direction.
Never stop on the tracks. Make sure you can cross without stopping.

questions.q: Signs in a work zone warn that your lane ends ahead. What does the manual advise?
options: Merge as soon as possible, at first notice of the approaching work zone
Stay in the closing lane to the end, then take turns merging
Speed up to pass slower vehicles before the lane ends
Stop before the lane closure until a flagger waves you ahead
questions.ref: p.16 Work Zones: merge as soon as possible; move to the appropriate lane at first notice of an approaching work zone.
questions.why: In a work zone, merge as soon as possible. Move to the right lane at first notice of the work zone ahead. (Driver's Manual, page 16)
wrong: The manual says to merge as soon as possible, not at the end of the lane.
Speeding in a work zone is dangerous. Slow down and merge early.
Stopping is not the advice. Merge early and follow any flagger's directions.

questions.q: You are about to overtake a bicyclist on a narrow road when a vehicle approaches from the opposite direction. What should you do?
options: Speed up and pass before the vehicles meet, leaving as much room as you can for the bicyclist
Sound your horn to warn the bicyclist, then pass while the oncoming car approaches
Slow down and let the oncoming vehicle pass first, then give the bicyclist three feet
Pass with at least one foot of clearance, since the oncoming car limits your space
questions.ref: p.22 Space to the Side: take hazards one at a time; slow down and let the oncoming vehicle pass first, and allow at least three feet when passing a bicycle.
questions.why: Take hazards one at a time. Slow down, let the oncoming vehicle pass first, then pass the bicyclist with at least three feet of space. (Driver's Manual, page 22)
wrong: Racing to pass squeezes you between two hazards at once.
Do not honk close to bicyclists. It can startle them into your path.
One foot is too close. You must leave at least three feet.

questions.q: A bike lane runs along the curb and you are about to turn right. What is the correct way to handle the turn?
options: Merge into the bike lane early so you are next to the curb for the turn
Yield to bicyclists, then turn across the lane without driving in it beforehand
Turn from the travel lane without checking, since bicyclists must yield to turning vehicles
Drive in the bike lane for the last half block, then turn
questions.ref: p.17 Bicyclists: you must yield to bicycles in the bike lane; you may turn across a bicycle lane but may not drive in it when approaching a turn.
questions.why: Yield to bicyclists in the bike lane first. You may turn across a bike lane, but you may not drive in it as you approach the turn. (Driver's Manual, page 17)
wrong: You may not drive in the bike lane when approaching a turn.
Drivers must yield to bicyclists in the bike lane, not the other way around.
Driving in the bike lane before a turn is not allowed.

questions.q: A tractor-trailer is approaching an intersection with its right turn signal on, and you are in the lane to its right. What should you do?
options: Do not pass on its right, or you could be caught between the truck and the curb
Pass on the right quickly before the truck starts its turn
Move up beside its rear wheels, since rear wheels follow a shorter path than the front wheels
Stay alongside the cab so the driver can see you in the side mirror
questions.ref: p.20 Trucks Make Wide Right Turns: resist the temptation to pass on the right of a truck approaching an intersection; you could be caught between the truck and the curb.
questions.why: Do not pass on the right of a truck near an intersection. If it turns right, you could be caught between the truck and the curb. (Driver's Manual, page 20)
wrong: Racing past on the right is exactly what the manual warns against.
The rear wheels' shorter path is why trucks swing wide, so that spot is dangerous.
Staying beside the cab puts you in the truck's side blind spot.

questions.q: You are about to back out of your driveway. Why does the manual say to be extra watchful?
options: Delivery vehicles are required to stop behind your vehicle so that the driver has a clear view of the road ahead
Pedestrians on the sidewalk are required to wait until your vehicle has fully entered the road
Other drivers on the road must give you the right-of-way because you are entering from a driveway
Children may run behind or be playing behind your vehicle, where you cannot see them from the driver's seat
questions.ref: p. 16, Children at Play and School Zones: always be extra watchful when backing in or out of a driveway; children may run behind or be playing behind your vehicle.
questions.why: Always be extra watchful when backing in or out of a driveway. Children may run or play behind your vehicle, where you cannot see them. (Driver's Manual, page 16)
wrong: The manual has no rule like this for delivery vehicles.
The manual says nothing about pedestrians having to wait. The reason is children you cannot see.
Drivers entering from a driveway must yield to traffic already on the road.

questions.q: An orange triangle on the back of a vehicle identifies it as:
options: A vehicle carrying hazardous materials
A school bus that is about to stop
A slow-moving vehicle, such as a farm tractor, usually going 25 mph or less
A vehicle that is required to stop at railroad crossings
questions.ref: p.18 Slow Moving Vehicles: farm tractors, animal-drawn and roadway maintenance vehicles usually go 25 mph or less and should have a slow-moving decal (an orange triangle).
questions.why: An orange triangle marks a slow-moving vehicle, such as a farm tractor. These usually go 25 miles per hour or less. (Driver's Manual, page 18)
wrong: The manual does not use the orange triangle for hazardous materials.
School buses use flashing red lights, not an orange triangle.
The triangle means slow-moving, not a vehicle that must stop at railroad crossings.

questions.q: Heavy rain begins and it feels like your tires have lost traction with the road. What should you do?
options: Ease off the gas and keep the wheel straight until the tires grip again
Brake hard and steer toward the shoulder as quickly as you can to get off the road
Steer sharply back and forth to regain grip on the wet pavement
Accelerate gently to power through the water until traction returns
questions.ref: p.25 Water on the Roadway: ease your foot off the gas, keep the wheel straight, and do not try to stop or turn until your tires are gripping the road again.
questions.why: If your tires lose traction, ease off the gas and keep the wheel straight. Do not try to stop or turn until the tires grip again. (Driver's Manual, page 25)
wrong: Hard braking and sharp steering can cause a skid. Wait until the tires grip.
Steering back and forth can cause a skid. Keep the wheel straight.
Speeding up makes hydroplaning worse. Ease off the gas.

questions.q: You feel very angry after an argument and need to drive somewhere. What does the manual suggest?
options: Turn up the radio, since music helps when you are angry or excited
Give yourself time to cool off, such as a short walk or nap, before driving
Take a longer route so that the extra time on the road helps you calm down
Drive in the left lane, away from other traffic, until the anger passes
questions.ref: p.28 Emotions: if you are angry or excited, give yourself time to cool off and stay off the road until calm (listening to the radio is suggested for being worried or down).
questions.why: If you are angry or excited, give yourself time to cool off, such as a short walk or nap. Stay off the road until you are calm. (Driver's Manual, page 28)
wrong: The radio tip is for being worried or down, not angry.
The manual says to stay off the road until you calm down.
The manual says to stay off the road until you calm down.

questions.q: Which driver would be REQUIRED to complete the DMV-certified operator retraining program?
options: A 22-year-old with one moving violation
A 30-year-old with two moving violations
A 25-year-old with two moving violations
A 22-year-old with two moving violations
questions.ref: p.35 Operator Retraining: age 24 or younger with two or more moving violations must complete it; age 25 or older requires three or more convictions.
questions.why: Anyone age 24 or younger with two or more moving violations must complete the operator retraining program. (Driver's Manual, page 35)
wrong: One violation is not enough. It takes two at this age.
Drivers 25 or older need three or more violations, not two.
At 25, it takes three or more violations, not two.

questions.q: After a night of drinking, a driver says a cold shower and several cups of coffee will sober him up. According to the manual:
options: Coffee will help, but only when combined with fresh air
A cold shower will help after about 30 minutes
Time is the only thing that will sober you up
Exercise will lower his blood alcohol content within an hour
questions.ref: p.33 Alcohol and You: there is no way to sober up quickly; coffee, fresh air, exercise, or cold showers will not help; time is the only thing.
questions.why: There is no way to sober up quickly. Coffee, fresh air, exercise, and cold showers do not help. Only time will sober you up. (Driver's Manual, page 33)
wrong: Coffee and fresh air do not help, even together.
A cold shower does not help, no matter how long you wait after.
Exercise does not sober you up. Only time does.

questions.q: On a dry road with good tires and brakes, you can see only 300 feet ahead. According to the manual's stopping distances, which speed may be unsafe?
options: 30 mph
50 mph
25 mph
20 mph
questions.ref: p.36 How Well Can You See: about 400 feet to stop at 50 mph and about 200 feet at 30 mph; if you cannot see 400 feet ahead you may not be driving safely at 50 mph.
questions.why: At 50 miles per hour, it can take about 400 feet to stop. If you can see only 300 feet ahead, 50 may not be safe. (Driver's Manual, page 36)
wrong: At 30 miles per hour, you need about 200 feet, which fits within 300.
The manual says about 200 feet at 30 miles per hour, so a slower speed fits within 300 feet.
The manual says about 200 feet at 30 miles per hour, so this slower speed fits within 300 feet.

questions.q: You intend to turn into a driveway just beyond an intersection. When should you signal?
options: Wait until you reach the intersection, then signal
Signal as soon as you can see the driveway
Signal one full block before the intersection so drivers behind you have time
Do not signal; driveways do not require a signal
questions.ref: p.39 Turn Signals: if there are streets, driveways, or intersections between you and where you want to turn, wait until you have reached that point before signaling.
questions.why: If an intersection or driveway lies between you and your turn, wait until you reach that point before signaling. Signaling too early can confuse other drivers. (Driver's Manual, page 39)
wrong: Signaling as soon as you see the driveway is too early. Wait until you reach the intersection.
A block early is too soon. Drivers may think you are turning at the intersection.
You should always signal when you change direction, including into a driveway.

questions.q: You are approaching a railroad crossing you have never seen a train use before. What does the manual advise?
options: Keep your normal speed and watch only for flashing lights or gates, because a crossing where you have never seen a train is rarely used
Slow down and look only in the direction of the nearest approaching traffic, since trains travel with traffic
Slow down and look up and down the tracks, because assuming no train is coming is one of the leading causes of fatalities at crossings
Stop and shift to a lower gear before the tracks so that you do not have to shift while crossing
questions.ref: p. 15, Railroad Crossings: slow down and look up and down the tracks; even if you have never seen a train at that crossing, do not assume none are coming, one of the leading causes of fatalities.
questions.why: Slow down and look up and down the tracks at every crossing. Assuming no train is coming is one of the leading causes of crossing deaths. (Driver's Manual, page 15)
wrong: Never assume a crossing is unused. That belief is a leading cause of deaths.
Look both ways. A train can come from either direction.
The manual's advice here is to slow down and look up and down the tracks, not to stop and shift.

questions.q: A steady yellow X is displayed over a reversible lane you are driving in. What does it mean?
options: The lane may be used only for turning
The lane is open to you, so continue
The lane is closed and you must stop at once
Use of the lane is changing; move out of it when safe
questions.ref: p.44 Reversible Lanes: a steady yellow X means use of the lane is changing and you should move out as soon as safe (a flashing yellow X means turning only).
questions.why: A steady yellow X over a reversible lane means its use is changing. Move out of it as soon as it is safe. (Driver's Manual, page 44)
wrong: A flashing yellow X means turning only. A steady one means move out.
A green arrow means the lane is open to you.
A red X means you cannot use the lane. A steady yellow X means move out when safe.

questions.q: Connecticut freeway mileposts are placed every mile. Where does zero usually start?
options: At the south and west borders of the state
At the north and east borders of the state
At Hartford
At the south and east borders of the state
questions.ref: p.51 Destination and Distance Signs: mileposts are placed every mile; zero usually starts at the south and west borders of the state.
questions.why: Mileposts are placed every mile, and zero usually starts at the south and west borders of the state. (Driver's Manual, page 51)
wrong: The manual says south and west, not north and east.
Mileposts start at the state border, not at Hartford.
The manual says south and west, not south and east.

questions.q: Which applicant must complete the 8-hour Safe Driving Practices course before getting a Connecticut license?
options: A 40-year-old who has never held a license in any state
A 40-year-old who holds a valid license issued by another state
An 18-year-old who previously held a Connecticut license
A 45-year-old Connecticut resident renewing a valid license
questions.ref: p.4 and p.7: anyone who has not previously held a license in Connecticut or does not hold a valid license from another state must take the 8-hour Safe Driving Practices course.
questions.why: Anyone who has never held a Connecticut license and does not hold a valid license from another state must take the 8-hour Safe Driving Practices course. (Driver's Manual, pages 4 and 7)
wrong: A valid license from another state means the course is not required.
Someone who held a Connecticut license before is not covered by this rule.
Renewing a valid license does not require the course.

questions.q: Which statement about the road test is TRUE?
options: A permit holder may drive alone to the test location if the vehicle is registered
An applicant without a valid license may use a rented vehicle if the rental is fully insured
If the vehicle is unsafe, no test is given and the applicant reschedules for no fee
A long-term leased vehicle may be used without proof of insurance since the lessor owns it
questions.ref: p.7 The Road Test: an unsafe vehicle means no evaluation and a no-fee reschedule; a non-licensed operator cannot drive to the test alone; no rented vehicle without a valid license; leased vehicles need proof of insurance.
questions.why: If the test vehicle is unsafe, no road test is given. The applicant reschedules for no fee. (Driver's Manual, page 7)
wrong: A driver without a license cannot drive to the test location alone.
Without a valid license, you cannot test in a rented vehicle.
A leased vehicle must have proof of insurance to be used for the test.

questions.q: A 16-year-old licensed driver is convicted of a second violation of a Graduated Driver's License restriction, such as the curfew. What suspension applies?
options: 30 days
6 months, or until age 18, whichever is longer
90 days
1 year
questions.ref: p.34 suspension table: GDL violations are 30 days for a first offense and 6 months or until age 18, whichever is longer, for second and subsequent offenses.
questions.why: A first Graduated Driver's License violation, such as breaking curfew, brings a 30-day suspension. A second brings 6 months or until age 18, whichever is longer. (Driver's Manual, page 34)
wrong: Thirty days is the penalty for a first offense.
Ninety days is a second-offense penalty for cell phone use or speeding, not this.
One year is for repeat reckless driving or street racing.

questions.q: A limited driver's license has a restriction allowing driving only 'during the period of daylight.' What does the manual say that means?
options: From exactly sunrise to exactly sunset, with no extra time
From one full hour before sunrise to one full hour after sunset
From 5 a.m. until the 11 p.m. curfew begins
From half an hour before sunrise to half an hour after sunset
questions.ref: p.9 Limited Licenses: restriction to daylight begins half an hour before sunrise and ends half an hour after sunset.
questions.why: On a limited license, daylight driving starts half an hour before sunrise and ends half an hour after sunset. (Driver's Manual, page 9)
wrong: The window includes an extra half hour on each end.
The extra time is half an hour, not a full hour.
The 11 p.m. to 5 a.m. curfew is a teen rule, not a daylight restriction.

questions.q: Which statement about underinflated or unbalanced tires is correct?
options: They wear the tires evenly but reduce fuel economy a little
They improve traction on wet roads while reducing fuel economy
They cause faster tire wear, lower fuel economy, and harder steering and stopping
They affect only fuel economy and have no effect on steering or stopping distance
questions.ref: p.11 Tires: unbalanced tires and low pressure cause faster tire wear, reduce fuel economy, and make the vehicle harder to steer and stop.
questions.why: Unbalanced tires and low tire pressure cause faster tire wear and lower fuel economy. They also make the vehicle harder to steer and stop. (Driver's Manual, page 11)
wrong: They wear tires faster, not evenly.
The manual does not say they improve traction. They make steering and stopping harder.
They also make the vehicle harder to steer and stop.

questions.q: What adjustment does the manual suggest for your side mirrors?
options: Set them so that when you lean forward slightly, you can see the side of your vehicle
Set them so you can see the side of your vehicle while sitting upright without leaning
Angle them inward so they show the same view as the rear view mirror
Set them to show only the road behind your rear bumper
questions.ref: p.12 Mirrors: a good adjustment for the side mirrors is to set them so that when you lean forward slightly, you can see the side of your vehicle.
questions.why: A good side mirror setting lets you see the side of your vehicle when you lean forward slightly. (Driver's Manual, page 12)
wrong: The manual says to lean forward slightly to see the side of your car.
Side mirrors should show the sides. The rear view mirror shows behind you.
Side mirrors should show the sides, not only the road behind the bumper.

questions.q: Which driver may legally use a hand-held cell phone while driving?
options: A 30-year-old driver stopped at a red light
A 22-year-old using it only at a stop sign
A 50-year-old driver calling a friend to say he is on his way
A 35-year-old peace officer
questions.ref: p.13 Cell Phone Laws: drivers 18 and older who are peace officers, firefighters, or ambulance drivers may use hand-held phones; use is also barred when temporarily stopped.
questions.why: Drivers 18 or older who are peace officers, firefighters, or ambulance drivers may use hand-held phones. (Driver's Manual, page 13)
wrong: Hand-held use is banned even when stopped at a red light.
Hand-held use is banned even when stopped at a stop sign.
A regular call to a friend is not an emergency, so hand-held use is banned.

questions.q: You are stopped at a stop sign and parked vehicles block your view of the cross street. What should you do?
options: Pull forward quickly to look past the vehicles
Edge forward slowly until you can see
Wait for the driver in the next lane to go first
Sound your horn and proceed slowly
questions.ref: p.15 Intersections: if your view of a cross street is blocked, edge forward slowly until you can see so crossing drivers can see the front of your vehicle.
questions.why: If your view of a cross street is blocked, edge forward slowly until you can see. This lets crossing drivers see your car first. (Driver's Manual, page 15)
wrong: Pulling forward quickly does not give crossing drivers time to see you. Edge forward slowly.
Waiting for another driver does not let you see the cross street. Edge forward slowly.
The manual says to edge forward slowly, not to honk.

questions.q: While passing, when does the manual say it is safe to return to your lane?
options: When both headlights of the passed vehicle show in your rear-view mirror
As soon as your front bumper is even with the passed vehicle's rear bumper
When you have counted three seconds after passing
When the passed vehicle's roof appears in your rear-view mirror
questions.ref: p.23 Return to your lane: when you can see both headlights of the vehicle you just passed in your rear-view mirror, it is safe to return.
questions.why: When you can see both headlights of the car you passed in your rear-view mirror, it is safe to return to your lane. (Driver's Manual, page 23)
wrong: That is far too close. Wait until both headlights show in your mirror.
The manual's test is seeing both headlights, not counting seconds.
The manual's test is seeing both headlights, not the roof.

questions.q: You are on a multi-lane road and realize you are beside and slightly behind another vehicle. What should you do?
options: Stay in position, since driving beside a vehicle gives you the most room
Sound your horn to warn the other driver
Speed up or drop back so the other driver can see you more easily
Move closer to the vehicle so it sees you in its mirror
questions.ref: p.22 Blind Spots: avoid driving on either side and slightly to the rear of another vehicle; speed up or drop back so the other driver can see you.
questions.why: Avoid driving beside and slightly behind another vehicle, because you are in its blind spot. Speed up or drop back so the driver can see you. (Driver's Manual, page 22)
wrong: That position is the other driver's blind spot.
Honking is not the advice. Move out of the blind spot.
Moving closer is unsafe. The other driver may pull into you.

questions.q: Where should your hands be placed on the steering wheel according to the manual?
options: Left hand between 10 and 12 o'clock and right hand between 12 and 2 o'clock
Both hands at the top of the wheel, between 11 and 1 o'clock
Left hand between 4 and 6 o'clock and right hand between 6 and 8 o'clock
Left hand between 8 and 10 o'clock and right hand between 2 and 4 o'clock
questions.ref: p.14 Steering: both hands on opposite sides of the wheel, left hand between 8 and 10 o'clock and right hand between 2 and 4 o'clock.
questions.why: Hold the wheel on opposite sides, with your left hand between 8 and 10 o'clock and your right hand between 2 and 4 o'clock. (Driver's Manual, page 14)
wrong: The manual says 8 to 10 and 2 to 4, not near the top.
The manual says 8 to 10 and 2 to 4, not at the top.
The manual says 8 to 10 and 2 to 4, not at the bottom.

questions.q: When is a driver permitted to pass in a no-passing zone?
options: When passing any vehicle that is traveling below the posted speed limit on that road
When passing a slow-moving vehicle or bicycle and you can see far enough ahead
When no oncoming vehicle is in sight and the road ahead looks clear
When the driver behind you is honking or flashing headlights at you
questions.ref: p.18 Slow Moving Vehicles: state law permits passing slow moving traffic, pedestrians, parked or standing vehicles, animals, bicycles, mopeds and scooters in no-passing zones if you can see far enough ahead to pass safely.
questions.why: State law allows passing slow vehicles, bicycles, and similar traffic in a no-passing zone. You must be able to see far enough ahead to pass safely. (Driver's Manual, pages 17 and 18)
wrong: Going under the limit is not enough. It must be a slow-moving vehicle, bicycle, or similar.
No oncoming car in sight is not enough. The exception is only for slow vehicles and similar.
A honking driver behind you does not let you pass in a no-passing zone.

questions.q: Why does the manual tell drivers to be especially alert for elderly and disabled pedestrians?
options: They are not covered by right-of-way rules in crosswalks, so drivers must proceed first and let them cross behind
They are required to cross only at painted crosswalks, and drivers can expect them to stay within those lines
They may have poor vision and hearing and may move slowly, and they are among the most frequent victims in auto-pedestrian collisions
They often use white canes, so drivers should sound the horn to alert them before passing
questions.ref: p. 16, Pedestrians: be especially alert for children, the elderly and disabled pedestrians; they are the most frequent victims, and elderly and disabled pedestrians may have poor vision and hearing and may move slowly.
questions.why: Children, the elderly, and disabled pedestrians are the most frequent victims in pedestrian crashes. Elderly and disabled pedestrians may have poor vision and hearing and may move slowly. (Driver's Manual, page 16)
wrong: Drivers must yield to all pedestrians in crosswalks.
There is a crosswalk at every intersection, even unmarked ones.
Do not honk near a pedestrian with a white cane. It can confuse or frighten them.

questions.q: According to the manual, nearly 40 percent of motorcycle crashes with another vehicle were caused by the other vehicle doing what?
options: Turning left in front of the motorcyclist
Following the motorcycle too closely in heavy traffic
Changing lanes without signaling or checking mirrors
Backing out of a driveway into the motorcyclist's lane
questions.ref: p.18 Motorcycles: nearly 40 percent were caused by the other vehicle turning left in front of the motorcyclist.
questions.why: Nearly 40 percent of motorcycle crashes with another vehicle were caused by the other vehicle turning left in front of the motorcyclist. (Driver's Manual, page 18)
wrong: The manual's 40 percent figure is about left turns, not following too closely.
The manual's 40 percent figure is about left turns, not lane changes.
The manual's 40 percent figure is about left turns, not backing out.

questions.q: You see a truck driver attempting to back from the street into a loading area. What should you do?
options: Drive around the truck quickly on the left
Stop to give the driver a chance to back up safely
Sound your horn so the driver sees you
Slow down and drive around it, staying close to its rear
questions.ref: p.20 Trucks Need Space While Backing Up: stop to give them a chance; never attempt to drive around a backing truck.
questions.why: If a truck is backing into a loading area, stop and give the driver a chance to do it safely. Never drive around a backing truck. (Driver's Manual, page 20)
wrong: Never drive around a backing truck. You may leave the driver's view.
The manual says to stop, not to honk.
Never drive around a backing truck, and never stay close to its rear.

questions.q: Which is a correct practice when getting out of a vehicle parked at the curb?
options: Get out on the street side so you can watch oncoming traffic
Open the door before checking, since other drivers must avoid it
Leave the door open while you unload, so others will see it
Check traffic first and, if you can, get out on the curb side
questions.ref: p.37 Parking: check traffic before you open the door; get out on the curbside if you can; shut the door as soon as you can after getting out.
questions.why: Check traffic before you open the door, and get out on the curb side if you can. Shut the door as soon as you can. (Driver's Manual, page 37)
wrong: Get out on the curb side when you can. Use the street side only if you must, after checking.
Always check traffic before you open the door.
Shut the door as soon as you can after getting out.

questions.q: When are studded tires permitted in Connecticut?
options: From October 1st through March 31st
From December 1st through March 15th
From November 15th through April 30th
All year, if the driver needs them for ice
questions.ref: p.25 Slippery Roads: studded tires are permitted in Connecticut from November 15th through April 30th.
questions.why: Studded tires are permitted in Connecticut from November 15th through April 30th. (Driver's Manual, page 25)
wrong: The dates are November 15th through April 30th.
The dates are November 15th through April 30th.
Studded tires are not allowed all year because they can damage roads.

questions.q: During a long trip, your tires pass over a shoulder rumble strip. What should you do?
options: Pull off at a safe place immediately and check your alertness
Turn up the radio and continue to the next exit
Steer back into the lane and continue, because the strip did its job
Drive faster to reach your destination before fatigue gets worse
questions.ref: p.28 Rumble strips: if you run over a shoulder rumble strip, pull off the road at a safe place immediately and check your alertness level.
questions.why: If you run over a shoulder rumble strip, pull off the road at a safe place right away and check how alert you are. (Driver's Manual, page 28)
wrong: Turning up the radio is a warning sign of fatigue, not a fix.
The strip is a warning. Pull off safely and check your alertness.
Driving faster when tired raises your crash risk. Pull off safely.

questions.q: A 17-year-old commits one of the following offenses. Which one CANNOT be considered under youthful offender status?
options: Reckless driving, even without any crash
Street racing on a public highway
Operating a vehicle while under suspension
Driving under the influence (DUI)
questions.ref: p.35 Youthful Offender Status: someone under 18 who commits negligent homicide, evades responsibility after a death or serious injury, or drives under the influence cannot be a youthful offender.
questions.why: Someone under 18 who drives under the influence of alcohol or drugs cannot be treated as a youthful offender. (Driver's Manual, page 35)
wrong: Reckless driving can be handled as youthful offender status.
Street racing can be handled as youthful offender status.
Operating under suspension can be handled as youthful offender status.

questions.q: You are pulled over by a police vehicle at night. Which action does the manual recommend?
options: Get out and walk back to the officer's vehicle with your license in hand
Turn on the interior light after stopping, before the officer approaches
Reach for your license and registration as the officer approaches
Turn off all lights, including the interior light, to avoid glare
questions.ref: p.35 Stopping for Police Vehicles: if at night, turn on the interior light after stopping and before the officer approaches; get license and registration only when requested; remain in the vehicle.
questions.why: If you are stopped at night, turn on the interior light after you stop and before the officer walks up. (Driver's Manual, page 35)
wrong: Stay in your vehicle unless the officer asks you to get out.
Get your license and registration only when the officer asks.
Police recommend turning the interior light on at night, not off.

questions.q: Which describes the correct way to make a legal U-turn?
options: Give a right turn signal and finish in the left lane nearest the median
Make it from the right lane without signaling
Give a left turn signal, stop, check for approaching traffic, then proceed into the outside (right-hand) lane traveling the opposite way
Make it at an opening in the median of an expressway
questions.ref: p.37 U-Turns: never make a U-turn on an expressway; give a left turn signal, stop, check traffic, and proceed into the outside or right-hand lane in the opposite direction.
questions.why: For a U-turn, give a left signal, stop, and check for traffic. Then go into the outside, or right-hand, lane going the opposite way. (Driver's Manual, page 37)
wrong: Use a left signal and finish in the outside or right-hand lane.
You must signal and check for traffic first.
Never make a U-turn on an expressway.

questions.q: Your gas pedal sticks and the engine keeps going faster and faster. After keeping your eyes on the road, what should you do first?
options: Turn the ignition key to the 'lock' position
Quickly shift to neutral
Pull the parking brake handle all the way up
Pump the brake pedal several times
questions.ref: p.40 Gas Pedal Sticks: keep your eyes on the road, quickly shift to neutral, pull off the road when safe, then turn off the engine; never turn the ignition to 'lock' while moving.
questions.why: If the gas pedal sticks, keep your eyes on the road and quickly shift to neutral. Then pull off when safe and turn off the engine. (Driver's Manual, page 40)
wrong: Never turn the ignition to lock while moving. The steering will lock.
The parking brake is a step for brake failure, not a stuck gas pedal.
Pumping the brakes is for brake failure. For a stuck pedal, shift to neutral first.

questions.q: A center lane is marked on each side by a solid yellow line and a dashed yellow line, with left-turn arrows alternating from each direction. What is it?
options: A reversible lane that carries traffic one way at certain times of the day
A passing lane shared by traffic in either direction
An HOV lane for vehicles with more than one person
A shared center lane for left turns or U-turns, used by both directions
questions.ref: p.44 Shared Center Lane: reserved for left turns or permitted U-turns by vehicles traveling in both directions; marked by solid and dashed yellow lines on each side.
questions.why: A shared center lane is for left turns, or U-turns where allowed, by traffic from both directions. It has solid and dashed yellow lines on each side. (Driver's Manual, page 44)
wrong: Reversible lanes are usually marked with double dashed yellow lines.
The center lane is for left turns, not passing.
HOV lanes are marked with a white diamond.

questions.q: Which is correct about turning right at a red light?
options: You may turn after coming to a full stop and checking for oncoming traffic, unless a sign prohibits the turn
You may turn without stopping if no pedestrians are present
You may turn only where a sign specifically permits it
You may turn only after the red light changes to yellow
questions.ref: p.45 Red lights: you may turn right on red after a full stop and checking for oncoming traffic and no sign prohibiting it; also p.15 you may turn right at a red light after stopping unless prohibited.
questions.why: You may turn right on red after a full stop, if there is no oncoming traffic and no sign forbids it. Watch for pedestrians. (Driver's Manual, pages 15 and 45)
wrong: You must come to a full stop first.
Right on red is allowed unless a sign forbids it. You do not need a sign allowing it.
A yellow light means the light is about to turn red, so yellow does not follow red.

questions.q: A 'Wrong Way' sign is used to identify:
options: The beginning of a detour around a closed road
A lane that is reserved for turning vehicles
The point where a divided highway begins
A one-way street, expressway ramp, or the wrong side of a divided highway; do not drive past it, turn around
questions.ref: p.47 Wrong Way: used to identify a one-way street, expressway ramp or the wrong direction or wrong side of a divided highway; do not drive past this sign, turn around.
questions.why: A Wrong Way sign marks a one-way street, an expressway ramp, or the wrong side of a divided highway. Do not drive past it. Turn around. (Driver's Manual, page 47)
wrong: Detours are marked with an orange Detour sign.
Turn lanes are marked with lane use control signs.
The start of a divided highway has its own yellow warning sign.

questions.q: A 16-year-old is being home trained and must show a course completion certificate from an approved eight-hour course. At least how many of those hours must cover alcohol and drugs, the dangers of driving after using them, and the related penalties?
options: Two hours, matching the length of the parent training class
Six hours, leaving two hours for the parent training class
Four hours, as part of the approved eight-hour course
All eight hours, because the course is devoted to the topic
questions.ref: p.6 Home Training Program: the CS-1 a certificate must come from an approved eight-hour course that includes a minimum of four hours on the effects of alcohol and drugs, the dangers of driving after consuming them, and the related penalties.
questions.why: Home-trained applicants need an approved eight-hour course with at least four hours on alcohol and drugs, the dangers of driving after using them, and the penalties. (Driver's Manual, page 6)
wrong: The manual's minimum is four hours. Two hours is the parent class.
The manual's minimum is four hours, not six.
The manual's minimum is four hours. The course also includes the two-hour parent class.

questions.q: Nine months after receiving her license, a 16-year-old driver wants to carry a passenger. Which passenger is allowed in addition to those permitted during her first six months?
options: Her younger brother, a member of her immediate family
Her best friend, who is a licensed 17-year-old
A neighbor who is 20 years old and has held a license for two years
A cousin who is 19 years old
questions.ref: p.8 Passenger Restrictions: during months seven through twelve the only additional passengers allowed are members of the driver's immediate family.
questions.why: In months seven through twelve, the only extra passengers allowed are members of the driver's immediate family. (Driver's Manual, page 8)
wrong: Teen friends are not allowed in the first year.
A qualified adult must have held a license for four or more years. Two is not enough.
A 19-year-old cousin is too young to be a qualified adult and is not immediate family.

questions.q: A parent asks when a newly licensed teen is at the greatest risk of a crash. According to the DMV Commissioner's Advisory Committee on Teen Safe Driving, which period is the most dangerous?
options: The second six months, when immediate family passengers are first allowed
The month after the teen turns 18, when the restrictions end
The first month of holding a learner's permit, before any supervised practice
The first six months after the teen first receives a driver's license
questions.ref: p.4 Managing Your Teen's Driving Experience: most teen crashes occur during the first two years of having a license, and the first six months are the most dangerous for the newly licensed teen.
questions.why: Most teen crashes happen in the first two years of having a license. The first six months are the most dangerous for a new driver. (Driver's Manual, page 4)
wrong: The manual names the first six months as the most dangerous, not the second six.
The manual does not single out turning 18. It points to the first six months of licensing.
The danger the manual stresses is after licensing, not the permit stage.

questions.q: A 17-year-old with a learner's permit wants to practice driving. Which passenger arrangement is permitted?
options: An 18-year-old friend who has held a license for one year, sitting in the front seat
One person providing instruction, age 21, with an unsuspended license held for six straight years
Two friends, as long as there is a seat belt for each of them and one is a licensed driver
A 19-year-old sibling who has held a driver's license for five consecutive years
questions.ref: pp.5-6 Learner's Permit Passenger Restrictions: only a licensed instructor, or one person providing instruction who is at least 20 years old, has held a license four or more consecutive years and had no suspension in that period.
questions.why: A permit holder may carry one instructor who is at least 20, has held a license four or more years in a row, and has had no suspension in that time. (Driver's Manual, pages 5 and 6)
wrong: An 18-year-old is too young, and one year of licensing is not enough.
Permit holders may not carry friends as passengers.
A 19-year-old is too young. The instructor must be at least 20.

questions.q: A 17-year-old driver is stopped at a red light and uses a hands-free earpiece to talk to a friend. Under Connecticut law, this is:
options: Legal, because the device is hands-free
Legal, because the vehicle is temporarily stopped
Illegal, because drivers under 18 may not use any cell phone, even hands-free
Legal, as long as the call lasts less than two minutes
questions.ref: p.13 Cell Phone Laws: drivers who are 16 or 17 are not permitted to use any type of cell phone or mobile electronic device, including a hands-free device.
questions.why: Drivers who are 16 or 17 may not use any cell phone or mobile electronic device while driving, even a hands-free one (Driver's Manual, page 13).
wrong: Hands-free is allowed only for drivers 18 and older; 16 and 17 year olds may not use any phone.
Phone rules still apply when you are stopped at a light or in traffic.
There is no time limit exception; drivers under 18 may not use a phone at all.

questions.q: In the 'penny test' for tire wear, the tread is considered safe when:
options: All of Lincoln's head is visible above the tread
Lincoln's head is visible and the tires were balanced within the last month
You can read the date on the penny
Any part of Lincoln's head is covered by the tread
questions.ref: p.11 Tires: if any part of Lincoln's head is covered by the tread, you are driving with the safe amount of tread.
questions.why: Put Lincoln's head into the groove where the tread looks lowest. If any part of his head is covered by the tread, you have a safe amount of tread (Driver's Manual, page 11).
wrong: If all of his head shows, the tread is too low to grip the road well.
Tire balancing is not part of the penny test, which checks tread depth only.
The penny test looks at Lincoln's head, not the date.

questions.q: You are being tailgated on a two-lane road, and there is no right lane to move into. What does the manual say to do?
options: Brake sharply so the tailgater backs off and you regain your space cushion
Wait until the road ahead is clear, then reduce speed slowly so the tailgater drives around you
Speed up to stay ahead of the tailgater until you reach a road with a right lane
Turn on your hazard flashers and keep the same speed so the tailgater sees you
questions.ref: p.22 Being Tailgated: if there is no right lane, wait until the road ahead is clear, then reduce speed slowly; never slow down quickly to discourage a tailgater.
questions.why: If there is no right lane, wait until the road ahead is clear, then slow down gradually. This encourages the tailgater to drive around you (Driver's Manual, page 22).
wrong: The manual says never slow down quickly to discourage a tailgater, because it raises your risk of being hit from behind.
The manual does not say to speed up; it says to slow down gradually so the tailgater can pass.
Flashers are not the advice. Wait until the road ahead is clear, then slow down gradually so the tailgater passes.

questions.q: You judge that the gap in the next lane is a four-second opening and you merge into the middle of it. What following distance will you and the vehicle behind you each have?
options: One second
Three seconds
Two seconds
Four seconds
questions.ref: p.20 Space to Merge: if you move into the middle of a four-second opening, both you and the vehicle behind you have a two-second following distance.
questions.why: When you merge into the middle of a four-second opening, you and the vehicle behind you each end up with a two-second following distance (Driver's Manual, page 20).
wrong: Half of a four-second gap is two seconds, not one.
Half of a four-second gap is two seconds, not three.
Four seconds is the whole gap; splitting it gives each driver two seconds.

questions.q: You are driving on a road with three lanes in your direction, with a lot of traffic entering and exiting at nearby ramps, and you are not passing. Which lane does the manual suggest?
options: The center travel lane
The left-most lane, which is intended for passing slower vehicles
The right lane, so you are closest to the ramps
The shoulder, to give entering vehicles room to merge
questions.ref: p.20 Other Hints: on a road with three or more lanes in the same direction, use the center travel lane if there is a lot of entering or exiting traffic; never drive on the shoulder unless told to by officials.
questions.why: On a road with three or more lanes going your way, use the center lane when a lot of traffic is entering and exiting (Driver's Manual, page 20).
wrong: The left-most lane is for passing, and you are not passing.
The right lane is where the entering and exiting traffic is, so the manual suggests the center lane.
Never drive on the shoulder unless officials tell you to.

questions.q: You want to pass a slow vehicle on a two-lane road. According to the manual, you should NOT start to pass if you are within how far of a hill or curve?
options: 200 feet
400 feet
One-quarter mile
One-third of a mile
questions.ref: p.24 Hills and Curves: you should not start to pass if you are within one-third of a mile of a hill or curve.
questions.why: Treat a hill or curve like an oncoming car. Do not start to pass if you are within one-third of a mile of a hill or curve (Driver's Manual, page 24).
wrong: 200 feet is far too short; the distance is one-third of a mile.
400 feet is far too short; the distance is one-third of a mile.
The manual says one-third of a mile, not one-quarter.

questions.q: You are in the lane next to an ice cream truck that has flashing lights and its stop signal arm and crossing arm extended. No barrier separates the lanes. What must you do?
options: Stop at least 25 feet away, then continue at normal speed once the children have cleared
Stop at least 10 feet away, then pass at 5 mph or less, yielding to crossing pedestrians
Slow to 15 mph and pass while sounding your horn to warn children near the truck
Stop at least 20 feet away, then pass at up to 10 mph, yielding to any pedestrians
questions.ref: p.18 Ice Cream Trucks: stop at least 10 feet from the front or back of the truck; after stopping you may proceed at a reasonable speed, up to 5 mph, yielding to pedestrians.
questions.why: Stop at least 10 feet from the front or back of the ice cream truck. Then you may pass at up to 5 miles per hour, yielding to anyone crossing to or from the truck (Driver's Manual, page 18).
wrong: The stop distance is 10 feet, and after stopping you may go only up to 5 miles per hour, not normal speed.
You must stop first, and the top speed after stopping is 5 miles per hour; honking is not part of the rule.
The stop distance is 10 feet, and the top speed after stopping is 5 miles per hour, not 10.

questions.q: You are about to enter a loading-dock driveway when a tractor-trailer begins backing from the street into the loading area, partly blocking your lane. What should you do?
options: Drive quickly around the rear of the truck
Tap your horn to warn the driver
Stop and give the truck driver a chance to back in safely
Pull close to the truck's cab so the driver can see you
questions.ref: p.20 Trucks Need Space While Backing Up: if you see a truck driver attempting to back, stop to give them a chance; never attempt to drive around a backing truck.
questions.why: When a truck is backing into a loading area, stop and give the driver a chance to back in safely. Never try to drive around a backing truck (Driver's Manual, page 20).
wrong: Never drive around a backing truck; you may leave the driver's view and get hit.
The manual's rule is to stop and wait, not to honk.
Moving close to the truck can put you out of the driver's view; the manual says to stop.

questions.q: You are driving through a neighborhood. Which of the following is NOT one of the places where the manual says to take extra care for children, who are often the least predictable pedestrians?
options: Near car washes and gas station pumps
Near schools and school bus stops where children wait
Near playgrounds and parks where children gather
Near ice cream trucks, where children cross to buy treats
questions.ref: p.16 Children at Play and School Zones: take extra care to look out for children, especially near schools, bus stops, playgrounds, parks and ice cream trucks; car washes and gas stations are not listed.
questions.why: The manual says to take extra care near schools, bus stops, playgrounds, parks and ice cream trucks. Car washes and gas pumps are not on that list (Driver's Manual, page 16).
wrong: Schools and bus stops are on the manual's list.
Playgrounds and parks are on the manual's list.
Ice cream trucks are on the manual's list.

questions.q: Connecticut's Vulnerable User's Law provides higher penalties for drivers who fail to use reasonable care and cause serious injury or death to a vulnerable user. Which of the following is NOT listed as a vulnerable user?
options: A person riding or driving an animal
A highway worker
A wheelchair user
A taxi driver
questions.ref: p.16 Vulnerable Users: list includes pedestrians, bicyclists, wheelchair users, a person riding or driving an animal, highway workers, garbage trucks, tank vehicles, mail vehicles and express delivery carriers; taxis are not listed.
questions.why: Vulnerable users include pedestrians, bicyclists, wheelchair users, people riding or driving an animal, highway workers, and some work vehicles like garbage trucks and mail vehicles. Taxi drivers are not listed (Driver's Manual, page 16).
wrong: A person riding or driving an animal is on the list.
Highway workers are on the list.
Wheelchair users are on the list.

questions.q: A driver fails to yield the right-of-way to a bicyclist in an intersection and is cited. How does Connecticut treat the fine?
options: The fine is the same as for failing to yield to any other vehicle on the road
The fine is doubled for failure to yield the right-of-way to a bicyclist
The fine is waived if the bicyclist was not injured in the incident
The fine is doubled only if the bicyclist is under 16 years of age
questions.ref: p.17 Bicyclists, As a driver: fines are doubled for failure to yield right-of-way to a bicyclist.
questions.why: Fines are doubled for failing to yield the right-of-way to a bicyclist (Driver's Manual, page 17).
wrong: The fine is not the same; it is doubled for a bicyclist.
The manual says the fine is doubled, with no exception for when no one is hurt.
The manual's rule doubles the fine for any bicyclist, with no age condition.

questions.q: During a heavy rain at highway speed, you feel your tires lose traction with the road. What should you do?
options: Ease off the gas, keep the wheel straight, and do not brake or turn until the tires grip
Brake firmly to slow down as quickly as possible before the water gets deeper
Steer sharply toward the shoulder to get out of the standing water quickly
Accelerate gently to power through the water and regain traction
questions.ref: p.25 Water on the Roadway: if tires lose traction, ease off the gas, keep the steering wheel straight, and do not try to stop or turn until the tires grip the road again.
questions.why: If your tires lose traction on water, ease off the gas and keep the wheel straight. Do not try to stop or turn until the tires grip the road again (Driver's Manual, page 25).
wrong: Do not try to stop until the tires grip again.
Turning sharply can make you skid; keep the wheel straight.
Ease off the gas instead; going faster makes hydroplaning worse.

questions.q: On a long drive you notice you are yawning repeatedly, drifting from your lane, and missing signs. What is the best response?
options: Turn up the radio and roll down the window
Drink several cups of coffee and keep driving
Find a safe parking area and take a 15 to 20 minute nap
Keep driving until your next scheduled break, about two hours away
questions.ref: p.28 Ways to Prevent a Fatigue-Related Crash: stop driving; take a 15 to 20 minute nap in a safe parking area; turning up the radio or opening a window is itself a warning sign, and caffeine should not be relied on.
questions.why: Yawning, drifting from your lane, and missing signs are warning signs of fatigue. Stop driving and take a 15 to 20 minute nap in a safe parking area (Driver's Manual, page 28).
wrong: Turning up the radio or rolling down the window is itself a warning sign of fatigue, not a fix.
The manual says not to rely on caffeine to prevent fatigue, since it wears off.
When you see warning signs, the manual says to stop driving now, not keep going.

questions.q: A 35-year-old driver is arrested for driving under the influence and refuses to take the blood, breath, or urine test. What is the penalty?
options: A 30-day suspension and no interlock device
A suspension of at least 45 days and an ignition interlock device for at least six months
A 90-day suspension and an ignition interlock device for at least six months
A suspension of at least 45 days and an ignition interlock device for at least one year
questions.ref: p.33 Alcohol and the Law: regardless of age, refusing a test means suspension of at least 45 days and an ignition interlock device for at least one year (failing the test for an adult carries an IID of at least six months).
questions.why: At any age, refusing the test means a suspension of at least 45 days and an ignition interlock device for at least one year (Driver's Manual, page 33).
wrong: A refusal brings at least a 45 day suspension and an interlock device for at least one year.
Six months is the interlock minimum for an adult who fails the test; refusing requires at least one year.
The minimum suspension is 45 days, and the interlock device is required for at least one year.

questions.q: Which of the following contains about the same amount of alcohol as one regular 12-ounce beer?
options: An 8-ounce glass of wine
A 5-ounce glass of wine
3 ounces of 80-proof liquor
4 ounces of 80-proof liquor
questions.ref: p.33 Alcohol and You: an alcohol drink is 1.5 oz of 80-proof liquor, 12 oz of beer, or a 5 oz glass of wine.
questions.why: One drink is 12 ounces of beer, a 5 ounce glass of wine, or 1.5 ounces of 80 proof liquor (Driver's Manual, page 33).
wrong: One drink of wine is 5 ounces, not 8.
One drink of 80 proof liquor is 1.5 ounces, not 3.
One drink of 80 proof liquor is 1.5 ounces, not 4.

questions.q: You find a parking space that is 15 feet from a fire hydrant and 20 feet from a stop sign. Can you legally park there?
options: No, because it is within 25 feet of the stop sign
No, because you must be 25 feet from a hydrant
Yes, because both distances are far enough
Yes, because only 10 feet is required from a stop sign
questions.ref: p.37 No-Parking Zones: do not park within 25 feet of a stop sign; within 10 feet of a fire hydrant.
questions.why: Do not park within 25 feet of a stop sign. At 20 feet this spot is too close, even though 15 feet from the hydrant is fine (Driver's Manual, page 37).
wrong: The hydrant rule is 10 feet, so 15 feet from the hydrant is fine; the stop sign is the problem.
20 feet is too close to a stop sign; you need 25 feet.
The stop sign distance is 25 feet; 10 feet is the rule for fire hydrants.

questions.q: A tire suddenly blows out while you are driving. What should you do?
options: Brake hard to stop as quickly as possible, then pull onto the shoulder
Steer sharply toward the shoulder as soon as the tire goes, to get off the road quickly
Hold the wheel tightly, keep straight, ease off the gas and use the brakes lightly
Shift into neutral and coast to a stop in your lane of travel
questions.ref: p.39 Tire Blowout: hold the wheel tightly, keep going straight, slow gradually, take your foot off the gas and use the brakes lightly; do not stop on the road if possible.
questions.why: In a blowout, hold the wheel tightly and keep going straight. Take your foot off the gas, brake lightly, and slow down gradually (Driver's Manual, page 39).
wrong: Slow down gradually and brake lightly, not hard.
Keep the vehicle going straight; do not steer sharply.
The manual says to brake lightly and pull off the road, and not to stop on the road if at all possible.

questions.q: A small plaque showing a speed is mounted below a curve warning sign. According to the manual, what is it?
options: The minimum speed you must maintain through the curve, even in bad weather
An advisory speed plaque, showing the advisory speed for that condition
The speed limit for the whole roadway beyond the curve
The maximum speed for trucks and buses only
questions.ref: p.49 Advisory Speed Plaque: usually installed below another warning sign to indicate the advisory speed for a condition (see also p.50 Turns and Curves).
questions.why: An advisory speed plaque is usually placed below another warning sign. It shows the advised speed for that condition, such as a curve (Driver's Manual, page 49).
wrong: It is an advisory speed, not a minimum speed.
It applies to the condition the warning sign shows, not the whole road.
The manual does not limit it to trucks and buses; it is advice for all drivers.

questions.q: A bicycle sharrow, two chevrons painted above a bicycle symbol, is on the pavement of your lane. What does it mean?
options: The lane is reserved for bicycles only and motor vehicles may not enter
Passing is prohibited in this lane because bicycles may be present
Parking is permitted in this lane for bicycles only
The lane is shared, so vehicles or bicycles may be in it
questions.ref: p.44 Other Markings: a bicycle sharrow, two chevrons above a bicycle symbol, indicates the lane is shared; vehicle or bicycle traffic may be in the lane and it is an additional warning to watch for bicycles.
questions.why: A sharrow means the lane is shared. Cars or bicycles may be in it, so watch for bicycles (Driver's Manual, page 44).
wrong: A sharrow means the lane is shared, not bicycles only.
A sharrow is a warning to watch for bicycles, not a no passing marking.
A sharrow is about sharing the lane, not parking.

questions.q: At a HAWK pedestrian signal you see a flashing red light. What must you do?
options: Stop, then proceed once pedestrians have cleared the crosswalk
Stop and wait until the signal turns solid yellow
Slow down and proceed with caution
Proceed, because the signal has been deactivated
questions.ref: p.45 HAWK Signals: flashing red means the signal is about to deactivate; drivers must stop but may proceed when pedestrians have cleared the crosswalk.
questions.why: A flashing red HAWK signal means it is about to turn off. You must stop, but you may go once pedestrians have cleared the crosswalk (Driver's Manual, page 45).
wrong: You may go once pedestrians clear; solid yellow comes earlier in the cycle, not after.
You must stop first, not just slow down.
The signal is dark when it is off; flashing red still means you must stop first.

questions.q: A learner's permit applicant answers 19 of the 25 knowledge test questions correctly. What is the result?
options: Passes, because 18 correct is the minimum
Does not pass, because 20 correct answers are needed
Passes, because 19 of 25 is the requirement
Does not pass, because 23 correct answers are needed
questions.ref: p.5 The Knowledge Test: the test consists of 25 questions and you need 20 correct answers to pass.
questions.why: The knowledge test has 25 questions, and you need 20 correct answers to pass (Driver's Manual, page 5).
wrong: The passing mark is 20 correct, not 18.
19 is one short; you need 20 correct.
You need 20 correct answers, not 23.

questions.q: A first-time license applicant passes the road test and pays the license fee at the DMV office. What does the applicant receive?
options: The permanent license card, handed over at the counter on the same day
A temporary paper card, with the permanent card mailed within about 90 days of the test
A receipt only, with the learner's permit staying valid until the card arrives
A temporary paper card, with the permanent card mailed within 20 days
questions.ref: p.8 Pay for Your License: DMV mails the permanent license card; qualified applicants receive a temporary paper card at the office, and the permanent card arrives through the mail within 20 days.
questions.why: You get a temporary paper card at the office. The permanent card arrives in the mail within 20 days (Driver's Manual, page 8).
wrong: The permanent card is mailed; you get a temporary paper card at the office.
The permanent card arrives within 20 days, not 90.
You get a temporary paper card at the office, not just a receipt.

questions.q: A 19-year-old who has never held a license in any state obtains a learner's permit today. Which statement is correct?
options: She must hold the permit 90 days before the road test and take an 8-hour course
She may take the road test after 30 days because she is over 18 and the course is optional
She must hold the permit 120 days before the road test and complete a 30-hour course
She must hold the permit 180 days before the road test, with no safe driving course needed
questions.ref: p.7 Applicants 18 Years of Age or Older: must hold a learner's permit at least 90 days before the road test, and first-time applicants must take an 8-hour course on safe driving practices.
questions.why: Applicants 18 or older must hold a learner's permit for at least 90 days before the road test. If they were never licensed, they must also take an 8-hour safe driving course (Driver's Manual, page 7).
wrong: The wait is at least 90 days, and the 8-hour course is required for first-time drivers of any age.
The 120 day wait and 30 hour course are for 16 and 17 year olds; adults wait 90 days and take the 8-hour course.
Adults wait 90 days, and a first-time driver must take the 8-hour course.

questions.q: Which of the following is required of the parent or legal guardian of a 16-year-old who obtains a learner's permit?
options: Complete the full 30-hour classroom course alongside the teen at a driving school
Provide 8 hours of behind-the-wheel training with the teen before the road test
Complete two hours of instruction with the teen on teen driving laws and dangers
Take the knowledge test along with the teen and pass with 20 correct answers
questions.ref: p.6 Parent Training Requirements: a parent or guardian must complete two hours of instruction with the teen concerning laws governing drivers under age 18 and the dangers of teen driving.
questions.why: A parent or guardian of a 16 or 17 year old with a permit must complete two hours of instruction with the teen about teen driving laws and dangers (Driver's Manual, page 6).
wrong: The parent requirement is two hours of training, not the full 30 hour course.
The manual's parent requirement is two hours of instruction about teen laws and dangers.
Parents do not take the knowledge test; they complete two hours of instruction.

questions.q: A child is 20 months old and weighs 33 pounds. Which restraint does Connecticut require?
options: A forward-facing seat with a 5-point harness
A booster seat
An adult seat belt
A rear-facing car seat
questions.ref: p.12 Child Safety Requirements: if age and weight fall in two categories, the more restrictive requirement applies (under age 2 means rear-facing seat, even if weight exceeds 30 pounds).
questions.why: When age and weight fit two categories, the stricter rule applies. A child under age 2 needs a rear-facing seat, even if the child weighs over 30 pounds (Driver's Manual, page 12).
wrong: Because the child is under 2, the stricter rear-facing rule applies.
Booster seats are for older, heavier children; a child under 2 must be rear-facing.
An adult seat belt is for age 8 or older and 60 pounds or more.

questions.q: A vehicle owner's insurance lapses and the insurance company reports the cancellation to the DMV. The owner ignores the DMV warning notice. What happens?
options: The driver's license is suspended for 45 days
The registration of the vehicle is suspended
The owner is fined $75 on the spot
The vehicle is impounded
questions.ref: p.13 Connecticut Insurance Laws: failure to respond to your warning notice will result in suspension of the registration.
questions.why: If you ignore the DMV's warning notice about lapsed insurance, your vehicle's registration is suspended (Driver's Manual, page 13).
wrong: The manual says the registration is suspended, not the driver's license.
The 75 dollar fine is for seat belt violations; ignoring this notice leads to registration suspension.
The manual's rule is registration suspension, not impoundment.

questions.q: You notice a water bottle rolling around on the floor of your car. Why should you secure it before driving?
options: It could roll under the brake pedal and prevent you from stopping
It could cause a tire to lose pressure whenever the car goes over a bump
It will cause the car to pull to one side when you apply the brakes
It could damage the exhaust system and let gases leak into the passenger compartment
questions.ref: p.12 Loose Objects: make sure there are no objects on the floor that could roll under the brake pedal and prevent you from stopping the vehicle.
questions.why: Objects on the floor can roll under the brake pedal and keep you from stopping (Driver's Manual, page 12).
wrong: A loose bottle cannot affect tire pressure; the danger is rolling under the brake pedal.
Pulling to one side when braking points to a brake problem, not a loose object.
A bottle inside the car cannot damage the exhaust; the danger is the brake pedal.

questions.q: Safer drivers look at least 12 seconds ahead of their vehicles. About how far is that on the highway?
options: One city block
Half a mile
About a quarter of a mile (four city blocks)
Two city blocks
questions.ref: p.14 Look Ahead: in the city 12 seconds is about one block; on the highway it is about four city blocks (a quarter of a mile).
questions.why: On the highway, 12 seconds is about four city blocks, or a quarter of a mile (Driver's Manual, page 14).
wrong: One block is the 12 second distance in the city, not on the highway.
The highway distance is a quarter of a mile, not half a mile.
The highway distance is four city blocks, not two.

questions.q: You are on a multi-lane highway and need to move across three lanes to the left. What is the safest approach?
options: Wait until all lanes are clear, then cross all three at once
Change one lane at a time, checking for traffic each time
Sound your horn and cross quickly
Cross two lanes together and the last one separately
questions.ref: p.23 Changing Lanes: take one lane at a time; it is very difficult to determine that all lanes are free and safe to cross at once.
questions.why: Change one lane at a time and check traffic each time. It is very hard to tell that all the lanes are clear at once (Driver's Manual, page 23).
wrong: Waiting for all lanes to clear can tie up traffic and even cause a crash.
Honking and rushing is not safe; take one lane at a time.
Take each lane separately, not two at once.

questions.q: You are on an entrance ramp and there is no opening in the highway traffic yet. What should you do?
options: Speed up and force your way into the gap between the vehicles in the main lane
Drive to the end of the ramp and stop there until a large enough gap appears
Stop at the beginning of the ramp and wait until traffic on the highway clears
Slow down on the ramp so you have room to speed up before merging
questions.ref: p.20 Space to Enter: if you have to wait for space, slow down on the ramp so you have room to speed up; do not drive to the end of the ramp and stop.
questions.why: If you must wait for space, slow down on the ramp. That leaves room to speed up before you merge (Driver's Manual, page 20).
wrong: Do not force into a gap that is too small; it can quickly get even smaller.
Do not drive to the end of the ramp and stop; you will not have room to reach traffic speed.
Stopping on the ramp is not the advice; slow down so you have room to speed up.

questions.q: You are traveling at 55 mph and want to pass on a two-lane road. About how much clear distance do you need to pass safely, counting oncoming traffic?
options: About 400 feet
About 800 feet
Over 1,600 feet (about one-third of a mile)
About one-quarter mile
questions.ref: p.23 Rules of Passing: at 55 mph you travel over 800 feet in 10 seconds and so does an oncoming vehicle, so you need over 1600 feet (about one-third mile).
questions.why: At 55 miles per hour you travel over 800 feet in 10 seconds, and so does the oncoming car. So you need over 1,600 feet, about one-third of a mile (Driver's Manual, page 23).
wrong: 400 feet is far too short; you need over 1,600 feet.
800 feet only covers your own travel; the oncoming car also moves 800 feet.
The manual says about one-third of a mile, not one-quarter.

questions.q: You are driving through an intersection when you hear a siren behind you. You have already entered the intersection. What should you do?
options: Drive through the intersection, then pull over to the right and stop
Stop immediately where you are inside the intersection and wait for it to pass
Pull over to the left side of the road just beyond the intersection
Speed up and stay ahead of the emergency vehicle until you can pull over
questions.ref: p.37 Right-of-Way: if you are in an intersection, drive through the intersection before you pull over to the right and stop.
questions.why: If you are already in the intersection, drive through it first. Then pull over to the right and stop (Driver's Manual, page 37).
wrong: Do not stop in the intersection; drive through, then pull over to the right.
Pull over to the right, not the left.
You must yield to the emergency vehicle by pulling over to the right and stopping.

questions.q: A motorcycle approaching an intersection has its left turn signal flashing. You want to turn left across its path. What should you do?
options: Assume it is turning and go ahead
Wait until you see that it is actually beginning to turn
Honk your horn to warn the rider
Speed up to pass in front of it
questions.ref: p.18 Motorcycles: do not assume a motorcycle is turning; its signals may not self-cancel. Do not pull out in front of it until you see it actually beginning to turn.
questions.why: Motorcycle signals may not turn off by themselves. Wait until you see the motorcycle actually begin to turn before you pull out (Driver's Manual, page 18).
wrong: Do not assume it is turning; the signal may have been left on.
The manual's rule is to wait for the turn, not to honk.
Never rush to pull out in front of a motorcycle; wait until it begins to turn.

questions.q: You approach three horseback riders on a public road. According to the manual, how must they ride?
options: Two abreast near the center line, so drivers coming from both directions can see them
Single file along the left edge of the road, facing oncoming traffic as pedestrians do
Single file near the right curb or road edge, or on a usable right shoulder
In the middle of the lane, with a rider at the back signaling for the group
questions.ref: p.18 Horses: horseback riders must ride single file near the right curb or road edge, or on a usable right shoulder, lane or path.
questions.why: Horseback riders must ride single file near the right curb or road edge, or on a usable right shoulder, lane or path (Driver's Manual, page 18).
wrong: Riders must go single file near the right edge, not two abreast.
Riders keep to the right edge, not the left.
Riders keep near the right edge, not in the middle of the lane.

questions.q: You are driving on a four-lane divided highway with a grassy median. A school bus traveling toward you on the other roadway has its red lights flashing. What must you do?
options: Stop, because the bus has its red lights flashing, even though it is on the other roadway
Stop only if you can see children waiting at the side of the road
Slow to 10 mph and proceed past the bus once you have checked for children
You are not required to stop, because a median separates the roadways
questions.ref: p.37 Right-of-Way: you must stop for a school bus with red lights flashing, but you are not required to stop if the bus is traveling toward you and a median or other physical barrier separates the roadway.
questions.why: You must stop for a school bus with flashing red lights. But you do not have to stop if the bus is coming toward you and a median or other barrier separates the roadway (Driver's Manual, page 37).
wrong: The median exception means you do not have to stop here.
With a median between you, stopping is not required.
The manual has no 10 miles per hour rule; with a median you are not required to stop.

questions.q: You are driving along a street with a bicycle lane on your right and plan to turn right at the next corner. What should you do?
options: Stay out of the bike lane until you turn, and yield to bicyclists before crossing it
Move into the bike lane well before the corner so you are in position to turn right
Drive in the bike lane with your hazard lights on so bicyclists can see you
Turn without yielding if your turn signal is on, since bicyclists must yield to cars
questions.ref: p.17 Bicyclists: do not drive in a bicycle lane when approaching a turn; you may turn across a bike lane but must yield to bicyclists in the lane before you turn across it.
questions.why: Do not drive in a bike lane when getting ready to turn. You may turn across it, but you must yield to bicyclists in the lane first (Driver's Manual, page 17).
wrong: You may not drive in the bike lane when approaching a turn.
Hazard lights do not make it legal to drive in a bike lane.
Drivers must yield to bicyclists in the bike lane before turning across it.

questions.q: You normally drive 50 mph on this road when it is dry. The road is now covered with packed snow. About how fast should you drive?
options: 40 mph
25 mph
5 mph
45 mph
questions.ref: p.25 Slippery Roads: on packed snow you should cut your speed in half (on a wet road, reduce speed by about 10 mph).
questions.why: On packed snow, cut your speed in half. Half of 50 is 25 miles per hour (Driver's Manual, page 25).
wrong: Cutting 10 miles per hour is for a wet road; packed snow means half speed.
Slowing to a crawl is for ice; packed snow means half speed.
Packed snow means cutting speed in half, not by 5.

questions.q: After a road dispute, a hostile motorist begins following you. What should you do?
options: Drive home as quickly as possible and lock the doors once you are inside
Pull over and make eye contact with the driver to try to calm him down peacefully
Stop on the shoulder and wait until the driver gives up and leaves
Do not go home; drive to a police station or other well-lit public place
questions.ref: p.26 Eye Contact: do not make eye contact; if a motorist pursues you, do not go home but drive to a police station, convenience store, or other public, well-lit location.
questions.why: If a hostile driver follows you, do not go home. Drive to a police station, convenience store, or other public, well-lit place where you can get help (Driver's Manual, page 26).
wrong: The manual says do not go home when someone is following you.
Do not make eye contact; it can be seen as a challenge and lead to violence.
The manual says to drive to a public, well-lit place, not to stop and wait.

questions.q: A friend says that coffee and a cold shower will sober him up quickly before he drives. According to the manual:
options: Coffee works within about 30 minutes
Fresh air and exercise are enough
Nothing helps except time
A cold shower works if it lasts 15 minutes
questions.ref: p.33 Alcohol and You: there is no way to sober up quickly; coffee, fresh air, exercise, or cold showers will not help; time is the only thing.
questions.why: There is no way to sober up quickly. Only time will sober you up (Driver's Manual, page 33).
wrong: Coffee does not help; only time works.
Fresh air and exercise do not help; only time works.
