questions.ref: p.28 Fatigue: working the night shift increases your risk of falling asleep at the wheel by nearly 6 times (people with untreated sleep apnea are 7 times more likely).
questions.why: Working the night shift raises your risk of falling asleep at the wheel by nearly 6 times. (Driver's Manual, p. 28)
wrong: The study says nearly 6 times, which is much more than double.
Seven times is the number for untreated sleep apnea, not night-shift work.
The study says nearly 6 times, not 10.

questions.q: Besides night-shift and rotating-shift workers, the manual warns that people working more than how many hours a week need to be particularly careful about drowsy driving?
options: 50 hours
40 hours
60 hours
80 hours
questions.ref: p.28 Fatigue: rotating-shift workers and people working more than 60 hours a week need to be particularly careful.
questions.why: The manual says rotating-shift workers and people working more than 60 hours a week need to be extra careful about drowsy driving. (Driver's Manual, p. 28)
wrong: The manual's number is 60 hours a week, not 50.
The manual's number is 60 hours a week, not 40.
The manual's number is 60 hours a week, not 80.

questions.q: According to the manual, how much sleep do most adults need to stay properly alert during the day?
options: 7 to 9 hours
5 to 6 hours
6 to 7 hours
9 to 11 hours
questions.ref: p.28 Before a Trip: get adequate sleep; most adults need 7 to 9 hours to maintain proper alertness during the day.
questions.why: Most adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep to stay properly alert during the day. (Driver's Manual, p. 28)
wrong: That is less than the 7 to 9 hours the manual says most adults need.
The manual says 7 to 9 hours, so 6 is too little.
The manual says 7 to 9 hours, not 9 to 11.

questions.q: You are planning a 400-mile road trip. How often does the manual recommend scheduling breaks?
options: About every 50 miles or 1 hour
About every 150 miles or 3 hours
About every 100 miles or 2 hours
About every 200 miles or 4 hours
questions.ref: p.28 Before a Trip: schedule proper breaks, about every 100 miles or 2 hours during long trips.
questions.why: On long trips, schedule a break about every 100 miles or 2 hours. (Driver's Manual, p. 28)
wrong: The manual says about every 100 miles or 2 hours, not every hour.
That is too long; the manual says about every 100 miles or 2 hours.
That is far too long; the manual says about every 100 miles or 2 hours.

questions.q: According to the manual, during which hours should you try not to drive in order to avoid a fatigue-related crash?
options: 11 p.m. to 5 a.m.
10 p.m. to 2 a.m.
Midnight to 6 a.m.
Sunset until sunrise
questions.ref: p.28 Ways to Prevent a Fatigue-Related Crash: try not to drive late at night between the hours of midnight and 6 a.m. (11 p.m.-5 a.m. is the teen curfew, not this advice).
questions.why: To avoid a fatigue-related crash, try not to drive late at night between midnight and 6 a.m. (Driver's Manual, p. 28)
wrong: Those are the teen curfew hours, not the manual's fatigue advice.
The manual's window is midnight to 6 a.m.
The manual names midnight to 6 a.m., not the whole night.

questions.q: Which statement about caffeine matches the manual?
options: 2 cups of coffee can raise alertness for hours, but it wears off
One cup of coffee keeps a tired driver fully alert for an entire day
Caffeine should never be combined with taking a short nap
Caffeine is the best way to prevent fatigue on any long drive you take
questions.ref: p.28 Ways to Prevent a Fatigue-Related Crash: the equivalent of 2 cups of coffee can increase alertness for several hours; it wears off; do not rely on caffeine; try caffeine before a short nap; the best prevention is sleep.
questions.why: About 2 cups of coffee can raise alertness for several hours, but caffeine wears off. Do not rely on it to prevent fatigue. (Driver's Manual, p. 28)
wrong: Caffeine wears off, and the manual says not to rely on it.
The manual actually suggests caffeine before a short nap to get both benefits.
The manual says the best way to prevent fatigue is sleep, not caffeine.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the warning signs of fatigue listed in the manual?
options: Feeling restless, irritable or aggressive
Checking your mirrors every few seconds
Tailgating or missing signs or exits
Daydreaming or having wandering thoughts
questions.ref: p.28 Warning Signs of Fatigue: radio/window, trouble focusing, yawning, drifting/tailgating/missing exits, daydreaming, restless/irritable, impaired reaction time, decreased performance.

questions.q: You have a stiff neck and a bad cough, but you need to get to a store. What does the manual advise?

Take cough medicine and then drive
Drive, but only on local roads

Call a friend on a hands-free phone to talk it through

questions.q: When does the manual say a family should complete and sign the Teen-Parent Driver Agreement?
options: When the teen passes the road test, and review it at age 18
At the learner's permit; review again at licensing
When the teen finishes the 8-hour safe driving course
Only after the teen's first traffic ticket or violation
questions.ref: p.30 Teen-Parent Driver Agreement: complete and sign this Agreement when your teen obtains a learner's permit, and review it again when your teen obtains a license.
questions.why: Sign the agreement when the teen gets a learner's permit, and review it again when the teen gets a license. (Driver's Manual, p. 30)

The agreement is signed when the teen gets a learner's permit.

questions.q: Your cousin just passed driver training and got a license. According to the Teen-Parent Driver Agreement, what does this mean?

She no longer needs any supervising adult at all
She has overcome the brain's risk-taking stage
She is only a beginner, not necessarily a safe driver

wrong: The agreement says a new license holder is only a beginner.

questions.q: Under the Teen-Parent Driver Obligations, what is 'joyriding'?

Driving with no destination or reason
Driving faster than the posted speed limit
Driving after the 11 p.m. curfew

questions.q: Under the Teen-Parent Driver Agreement's driving plan, what must the teen and supervising adult agree on each time the teen drives?
options: Route, destination, return time, and passengers
Only the destination and the time you will return
Only which roads have the lowest speed limits
Gas money, insurance costs, and which car is used
questions.ref: p.31 Driving Plan: the teen gets permission every time and agrees on route, destination, time of return, and passengers.
questions.why: The teen gets permission every time and agrees on the route, destination, time of return, and passengers. (Driver's Manual, p. 31)

The DMV and the court, after a conviction is entered
Law enforcement, neighbors, school staff, or friends

questions.q: According to the manual, alcohol is involved in more than what share of traffic crashes in which someone is killed?

25 percent
60 percent

questions.q: A friend orders a large 'specialty' mixed drink at a restaurant. How does the manual treat a drink like this?
options: It can be the same as having several normal drinks
It counts as exactly one drink, like a 12 oz. beer
It counts as half a drink because of the mixer

questions.q: The manual compares drinking alcohol to getting a sunburn. What is the point of that comparison?
options: Alcohol wears off faster when you are out in the sun
By the time you feel it, it's already too late
A little alcohol has no effect, just like a little sun
Water prevents impairment the way sunscreen prevents a burn

wrong: The comparison is about feeling it too late, not about the sun.

questions.q: You are taking a prescription medicine and are invited to have a beer. What does the manual say about combining them?
options: One beer is safe if you wait an hour before driving
Never mix them; drugs can multiply alcohol's effects
Only over-the-counter drugs, not prescriptions, interact with alcohol

questions.q: According to the manual, who imposes Connecticut's penalties for driving under the influence of alcohol?

The state legislature and the local police

questions.q: A 16-year-old with a learner's permit, not a license, is convicted of speeding 20 mph over the limit. Does the DMV suspension table apply?

questions.q: According to the manual, what do speed limits take into account?

Proceed only after the officer blows a whistle
questions.ref: p.36 Right-of-Way: you must obey signals given by a law enforcement officer, even if they contradict the traffic signal.
questions.why: You must obey a law enforcement officer's signals, even when they go against the traffic signal. (Driver's Manual, p. 36)
wrong: The officer's signal comes before the traffic light.
You must obey the officer, not ignore the officer.
The manual says to obey the officer's signal, with no whistle needed.

questions.q: You are driving where a marked bicycle path crosses the road, and a cyclist and a jogger are about to cross on it. What must you do?
options: Proceed if you reach the crossing first, then let them cross
Yield to the jogger only; bicyclists must yield to cars
Yield to the cyclist only; joggers must use a crosswalk
Yield the right-of-way to both the cyclist and the jogger
questions.ref: p.36 Right-of-Way: drivers must yield the right-of-way to bicyclists and pedestrians where a bicycle path crosses the roadway.
questions.why: Drivers must yield the right-of-way to both bicyclists and pedestrians where a bicycle path crosses the road. (Driver's Manual, p. 36)
wrong: You must yield to them, no matter who gets there first.
The rule covers bicyclists too, not only pedestrians.
The rule covers pedestrians too, not only bicyclists.

questions.q: Traffic is backed up on the far side of an intersection, and your light is green. What does the manual say?
options: Wait until you can get through without stopping
Enter and stop partway so cross traffic can see you
Enter only if you sound your horn as a warning
Enter the intersection, since your light is green
questions.ref: p.37 Right-of-Way: drivers may not enter an intersection unless they can get through it without having to stop; wait until traffic ahead clears.
questions.why: You may not enter an intersection unless you can get through it without stopping. Wait until traffic ahead clears so you do not block it. (Driver's Manual, p. 37)
wrong: Stopping partway would block the intersection, which the manual says not to do.
A horn does not change the rule; wait until you can get all the way through.
A green light is not enough; you must be able to get through without stopping.

questions.q: You are passing a car traveling in the same direction when it starts slowing down. Who must yield?
options: Whoever is going faster has the right-of-way
The slowing car must yield to you
You, the overtaking driver, must yield to it
Neither driver; you should speed up to finish
questions.ref: p.37 Right-of-Way: drivers overtaking a vehicle traveling in the same direction must yield to that vehicle, even if it is slowing or coming to a stop.
questions.why: A driver passing a car going the same way must yield to that car, even if it is slowing or stopping. (Driver's Manual, p. 37)
wrong: The rule is about who is overtaking, not who is faster.
The overtaking driver must yield, not the car being passed.
The overtaking driver must yield, not speed up.

questions.q: You pulled over and stopped for an ambulance with its siren on. When may you start moving again?
options: As soon as it gets within about 100 feet of where you stopped
Once you can no longer hear its siren from inside your car
After it passes, unless police or a firefighter say otherwise
When the drivers stopped behind you begin moving again
questions.ref: p.37 Right-of-Way: you must remain stopped until the emergency vehicle has passed, unless otherwise directed by a State or local police officer or a firefighter.
questions.why: You must stay stopped until the emergency vehicle has passed, unless a police officer or firefighter tells you otherwise. (Driver's Manual, p. 37)
wrong: You must stay stopped until it has passed you.
The rule is to wait until it has passed, not until the siren fades.
The rule is to wait until it has passed, not to follow other drivers.

questions.q: Which of these signals from an emergency vehicle does the manual say requires you to yield the right-of-way?
options: A flashing amber light or the vehicle's hazard flashers
Flashing headlights or a flashing green light
A siren, but only when combined with headlights
A siren, an air horn, or a red or blue flashing light
questions.ref: p.37 Right-of-Way: yield to a police vehicle, fire engine, ambulance or other emergency vehicle using a siren, air horn or a red or blue flashing light.
questions.why: Yield to any emergency vehicle using a siren, an air horn, or a red or blue flashing light. (Driver's Manual, p. 37)
wrong: The manual's list is a siren, an air horn, or a red or blue flashing light.
The manual's list is a siren, an air horn, or a red or blue flashing light.
A siren alone is enough; it does not need headlights too.

questions.q: You are approaching an intersection. On the cross street, a school bus is stopped with its red lights flashing. What must you do?
options: Stop; the rule covers a bus at an intersection you approach
Slow down; you need not stop since the bus is on another road
Stop only if children are visible crossing in front of you
Keep going if the bus is on the far side of the intersection
questions.ref: p.37 Right-of-Way: you must stop for a school bus stopped with red lights flashing whether it is on your side, the opposite side, or at an intersection you are approaching.
questions.why: You must stop for a school bus with red lights flashing on your side, the opposite side, or at an intersection you are approaching. (Driver's Manual, p. 37)
wrong: The rule says you must stop for a bus at an intersection you are approaching.
You must stop whether or not you see children.
The rule covers a bus at an intersection you are approaching.

questions.q: You are pulling out of a driveway onto a busy street. Who must yield?
options: You must yield to vehicles already on the main road
The vehicle approaching from your right must yield to you
Whoever signals first has the right-of-way
Vehicles on the main road must slow down and let you in
questions.ref: p.37 Right-of-Way: drivers entering a road from a driveway, alley or roadside must yield to vehicles already on the main road.
questions.why: Drivers entering a road from a driveway, alley, or roadside must yield to vehicles already on the main road. (Driver's Manual, p. 37)
wrong: You are the one entering, so you must yield.
Signaling does not give you the right-of-way.
The main road traffic does not have to let you in; you must yield.

questions.q: You are in a roundabout and about to reach the street where you want to exit. What does the manual say to do?
options: Signal left and speed up so you can clear the roundabout
Turn on your hazard lights and exit without signaling
Stop inside the roundabout until the exit lane is fully clear
Signal right and yield to pedestrians in the exit crosswalk
questions.ref: p.37 Roundabouts: use your right turn signal when you are about to reach your exit, and yield to any pedestrians in the crosswalk on the exiting leg.
questions.why: Use your right turn signal as you near your exit, and yield to pedestrians in the crosswalk on the exit. (Driver's Manual, p. 37)
wrong: The manual says to use your right signal, not your left.
The manual says to signal right as you reach your exit.
The manual says not to stop inside the roundabout to let other traffic in.

questions.q: You are approaching a two-lane roundabout. How do you choose which lane to use?
options: Follow posted signs and lane-use controls for your movement
Always use the left lane, since it is closest to the center island
Always use the right lane, since traffic inside must yield to you
Use whichever lane is empty; lanes in a roundabout do not matter
questions.ref: p.37 Roundabouts: if there is more than one lane as you approach, follow the posted signs and lane-use controls to choose the proper lane for your intended movement.
questions.why: If there is more than one lane, follow the posted signs and lane-use controls to pick the right lane for where you are going. (Driver's Manual, p. 37)
wrong: The manual says to follow the signs, not always use the left lane.
Entering traffic must yield to traffic already circling.
The manual says to follow the signs for your movement.

questions.q: How is each road approaching a roundabout marked, according to the manual?
options: A stop sign and a white stop line across each lane
A yield sign, and possibly yield lines on the pavement
A flashing red signal and a stop sign on each side
A flashing yellow signal and a 'Roundabout Ahead' sign only
questions.ref: p.37 Roundabouts: each road approaching them is marked with a yield sign and may also have yield line markings on the pavement.
questions.why: Each road coming into a roundabout has a yield sign, and may also have yield lines on the pavement. (Driver's Manual, p. 37)
wrong: Roundabouts use yield signs, not stop signs.
Roundabouts use yield signs, not flashing red signals.
Roundabouts are marked with yield signs.

questions.q: You park a car with a manual transmission on a flat street. What does the manual say to do?
options: Leave it in neutral with the parking brake off
Leave it in gear; the parking brake is only for hills
Set the parking brake and leave it in neutral
Set the parking brake and leave the car in gear
questions.ref: p.37 Parking: always set your parking brake; leave the vehicle in gear if it has a manual transmission or in 'park' if automatic.
questions.why: Always set your parking brake. Leave a manual transmission in gear, or an automatic in park. (Driver's Manual, p. 37)
wrong: The manual says always set the parking brake and leave a manual in gear.
The manual says to always set the parking brake, not just on hills.
A manual transmission should be left in gear, not neutral.

questions.q: You are parking on a hill. How does the manual say to position your wheels?
options: Keep them pointed straight ahead so the car won't roll
Turn them sharply toward the side of the road or curb
Turn them sharply toward the middle of the road
Turn them slightly toward the travel lane
questions.ref: p.37 Parking: when you park on a hill, turn your wheels sharply towards the side of the road or curb, so the vehicle rolls away from traffic.
questions.why: On a hill, turn your wheels sharply toward the side of the road or curb. If the car rolls, it will roll away from traffic. (Driver's Manual, p. 37)
wrong: Straight wheels could let the car roll into traffic.
Turning toward the middle would send the car into traffic.
The manual says to turn sharply toward the curb, away from traffic.

questions.q: You parallel park at a curb, but your car ends up 18 inches away from it. Is this legal?
options: Yes; you may park up to two feet away from the curb
No; you may not park more than one foot from the curb
Yes, as long as you are at least 25 feet from a stop sign
No; your tires must be touching the curb when you park
questions.ref: p.37 No-Parking Zones: do not park more than one foot from the curb.
questions.why: You may not park more than one foot from the curb, so 18 inches is too far. (Driver's Manual, p. 37)
wrong: The limit is one foot, not two feet.
Being far from a stop sign does not fix being more than one foot from the curb.
The rule is no more than one foot away, not touching the curb.

questions.q: Which of these places is NOT one of the manual's no-parking zones?
options: Inside a tunnel or underpass, even if the lane is wide
A construction area where you would not block traffic
Across a lowered curb that gives access to the sidewalk
On the wrong side of the street, facing traffic
questions.ref: p.37 No-Parking Zones: do not park in a construction area IF your vehicle will block traffic; tunnels/underpasses, the wrong side of the street, and lowered curbs are listed.
questions.why: The manual only bans parking in a construction area if your car will block traffic. (Driver's Manual, p. 37)
wrong: Tunnels and underpasses are on the no-parking list.
A lowered curb for sidewalk access is on the no-parking list.
The wrong side of the street is on the no-parking list.

questions.q: It is late afternoon on a clear day, and you are driving east with the setting sun behind you. What does the manual advise?
options: No lights are needed until the sun has fully set
Use your high beams so drivers ahead notice you
Turn on only your parking lights so you do not dazzle anyone
Turn on your headlights so oncoming drivers can see you
questions.ref: p.38 Use Headlights: when driving away from a rising or setting sun, turn on your headlights; drivers coming towards you may have trouble seeing your vehicle.
questions.why: When you drive away from a rising or setting sun, turn on your headlights. Drivers coming toward you may have trouble seeing your car. (Driver's Manual, p. 38)
wrong: The manual says to turn on headlights when driving away from a setting sun.
The manual says headlights, and to dim high beams near oncoming cars.
Parking lights are for parked vehicles only.

questions.q: According to the manual, how far can you see with high beams compared with low beams?
options: About four times as far
About twice as far
About 50 percent farther
About three times as far
questions.ref: p.38 Lights: high beams let you see twice as far as low beams.
questions.why: High beams let you see twice as far as low beams. (Driver's Manual, p. 38)
wrong: The manual says twice as far, not four times.
The manual says twice as far, which is more than 50 percent.
The manual says twice as far, not three times.

questions.q: You are using your high beams on a dark road at night. When should you dim them for an oncoming vehicle?
options: When you come within about 100 feet of it
Only if the other driver flashes their lights at you
When you come within about one block of it
When you come within about two blocks of it
questions.ref: p.38 Lights: dim your high beams whenever you come within about a one-block distance of an oncoming vehicle.
questions.why: Dim your high beams when you come within about one block of an oncoming vehicle. (Driver's Manual, p. 38)
wrong: The manual's distance is about one block, which is much more than 100 feet.
You should dim within about one block, without waiting for a signal.
The manual's distance is about one block, not two.

questions.q: At night you are on an unfamiliar country road with no oncoming traffic, and people may be walking along the side of the road. Which lights should you use?
options: High beams, to help you see people along the road
Fog lights alone, since they light up the road edges
Parking lights plus low beams for a wider beam pattern
Low beams, so you do not blind people walking by the road
questions.ref: p.38 Lights: use high beams whenever there are no oncoming vehicles; it is important to use high beams on unfamiliar roads, in construction areas, or where there may be people along the side of the road.
questions.why: Use high beams when there are no oncoming vehicles. They are important on unfamiliar roads and where people may be along the road. (Driver's Manual, p. 38)
wrong: The manual says to use fog lights in fog, rain, or snow, not as your only lights here.
The manual says never to drive with parking lights; use high beams here.
The manual says high beams are important where people may be along the road.

questions.q: Why does the manual tell you to use low beams instead of high beams in fog or hard rain?
options: Low beams reach farther ahead in wet weather
High beams reflect back and cause glare
High beams are not bright enough to cut through fog
High beams make your taillights harder to see
questions.ref: p.38 Lights: use low beams in fog or when it is snowing or raining hard; light from high beams will reflect back, causing glare and making it more difficult to see ahead.
questions.why: In fog or hard rain, light from high beams reflects back. That causes glare and makes it harder to see ahead. (Driver's Manual, p. 38)
wrong: The reason is that high beams reflect back and cause glare.
The problem is glare from reflected light, not brightness.
The reason is glare that makes it hard for you to see ahead.

questions.q: An oncoming driver has high beams on. You flash your headlights a couple of times, but the driver still does not dim them. What should you do?
options: Keep your high beams on until the other driver dims
Look at the center line to judge the other car's position
Look toward the right side of the road to stay on course
Turn your headlights off so the other driver notices
questions.ref: p.38 Lights: if the driver fails to dim the lights, look toward the right side of the road; do not try to 'get back' by keeping your bright lights on.
questions.why: If the other driver does not dim, look toward the right side of the road. That keeps you from being blinded and lets you stay on course. (Driver's Manual, p. 38)
wrong: The manual says not to get back at them with your bright lights.
The manual says to look toward the right side of the road.
The manual says to look to the right, not turn off your lights.

questions.q: Your high beams let you see about 400 feet ahead at night. To be able to stop within that distance, about how fast should you drive?
options: About 65 mph
About 55 mph
About 40 mph
About 50 mph
questions.ref: p.38 Darkness: high beams let you see about 400 feet ahead; drive at a speed that allows you to stop within this distance, or about 50 mph.
questions.why: High beams let you see about 400 feet ahead. Drive at a speed that lets you stop in that distance, which is about 50 miles per hour. (Driver's Manual, p. 38)
wrong: The manual says about 50 miles per hour, not 65.
The manual says about 50 miles per hour, not 55.
The manual says about 50 miles per hour for 400 feet.

questions.q: In a very heavy rain, snowstorm, or thick fog, the manual says you may not be able to see much more than how far ahead?
options: 200 feet
100 feet
500 feet
400 feet
questions.ref: p.38 Rain, Fog, or Snow: in very heavy rain, snowstorm, or thick fog, you may not be able to see much more than 200 feet ahead.
questions.why: In very heavy rain, a snowstorm, or thick fog, you may not see much more than 200 feet ahead. (Driver's Manual, p. 38)
wrong: The manual says about 200 feet, not 100.
The manual says about 200 feet, not 500.
400 feet is how far high beams reach at night, not the bad weather figure.

questions.q: You are caught in a downpour so heavy that you cannot see well enough to drive. What should you do?
options: Pull off the road in a safe place and wait
Put on your hazard flashers and keep going in your lane
Slow down and follow the taillights of the car ahead
Switch to high beams so you can see farther ahead
questions.ref: p.38 Rain, Fog, or Snow: in a very heavy downpour, you may not be able to see well enough to drive; pull off the road in a safe place and wait until it clears.
questions.why: In a very heavy downpour, you may not see well enough to drive. Pull off the road in a safe place and wait until it clears. (Driver's Manual, p. 38)
wrong: The manual says to pull off and wait, not keep going.
The manual says to pull off and wait if you cannot see well enough to drive.
The manual says to use low beams in hard rain because high beams cause glare.

questions.q: You drive the same road every day. As you approach the crest of a hill where you cannot see over the top, what should you do?
options: Keep your speed, since you know what is on the other side
Speed up slightly to keep momentum up the hill
Move toward the center line for a better view ahead
Adjust your speed so you could stop if needed
questions.ref: p.38 Hills and Curves: you may not know what is on the other side of a hill even if you have driven the road many times; adjust your speed so you can stop if necessary.
questions.why: Even on a road you know well, you may not know what is over a hill. Adjust your speed so you can stop if you need to. (Driver's Manual, p. 38)
wrong: The manual says you may not know what is there, even on a familiar road.
The manual says to adjust your speed so you can stop.
The manual's advice is to adjust your speed so you can stop.

questions.q: A person on a bike ahead appears to be drifting into your lane, but there is no immediate danger. How should you use your horn?
options: Sound a sharp blast on the horn
Do not use the horn; flash your high beams
Give the horn a light tap
Hold the horn down until the rider moves
questions.ref: p.38 Horn: if there is no immediate danger, a light tap is all you need, such as when a person on foot or on a bike appears to be moving into your lane.
questions.why: If there is no immediate danger, a light tap on the horn is all you need, like when a bike rider drifts toward your lane. (Driver's Manual, p. 38)
wrong: A sharp blast is for real danger, and the manual says a light tap is enough here.
The manual says a light tap on the horn is the right choice here.
The manual says a light tap is all you need.

questions.q: Your car slides on ice, and you have lost control while moving toward a person standing by the road. What should you do with the horn?
options: Tap it three or four times in a steady rhythm
Sound a sharp blast to warn the person
Leave it alone and keep both hands on the brake
Give a light tap so you do not startle the person
questions.ref: p.38 Horn: sound a SHARP BLAST when you have lost control of your vehicle and are moving towards someone.
questions.why: Sound a sharp blast when you have lost control of your car and are moving toward someone. (Driver's Manual, p. 38)
wrong: The manual calls for a sharp blast in danger.
The manual says not to be afraid to sound a sharp blast in danger.
A light tap is only when there is no immediate danger.

questions.q: Which pair lists two situations in which the manual says you should NOT use your horn?
options: Greeting a friend, and a child about to run into the street
Greeting a friend, and approaching horses
Approaching horses, and a car in danger of hitting you
Telling a driver of an error, and a bike drifting into your lane
questions.ref: p.38 When Not to Use Your Horn: encouraging someone to drive faster, notifying other drivers of an error, greeting a friend, around blind pedestrians, when approaching horses.
questions.why: The manual says not to use your horn to greet a friend or when approaching horses. (Driver's Manual, p. 38)
wrong: A child about to run into the street calls for a sharp blast.
A car in danger of hitting you calls for a sharp blast.
A bike drifting into your lane calls for a light tap.

questions.q: According to the manual, at least how far ahead of time should you try to signal before you make your move?
options: Two seconds
One second
Three seconds
Five seconds
questions.ref: p.39 Turn Signals: try and signal at least three seconds before you make your move.
questions.why: Try to signal at least three seconds before you make your move. (Driver's Manual, p. 39)
wrong: The manual says at least three seconds, not two.
The manual says at least three seconds, not one.
The manual's rule is at least three seconds.

questions.q: You plan to turn right at the next street. A car is waiting to pull out of a driveway between you and that street. When should you signal?
options: Only after you have started your turn into the street
At least five seconds before you reach the driveway
Right away, so the waiting driver knows your plan early
After you have passed the waiting car
questions.ref: p.39 Turn Signals: if another vehicle is about to enter the street between you and where you plan to turn, wait until you have passed it to signal; otherwise the driver may think you plan to turn where they are.
questions.why: If a car is about to enter between you and your turn, wait until you pass it to signal. Otherwise that driver may think you are turning where they are and pull out. (Driver's Manual, p. 39)
wrong: The manual says to signal once you pass the car, before your turn.
Signaling that early could make the waiting driver think you are turning there.
Signaling right away could make the waiting driver pull into your path.

questions.q: You just made a small lane change, and your turn signal is still blinking. Why does the manual say to turn it off?
options: Leaving it on is a reason to fail a road test
It causes the brake lights to flash as well
Others might think you plan to turn again
The signal could drain the car's battery
questions.ref: p.39 Turn Signals: after small turns, the signals may not turn off by themselves; turn it off, or others might think you plan to turn again.
questions.why: After small turns, the signal may not turn off by itself. If you leave it on, others might think you plan to turn again. (Driver's Manual, p. 39)
wrong: The manual's reason is that others might think you will turn again.
The manual's reason is that others might think you will turn again.
The manual's reason is that others might think you will turn again.

questions.q: Around a curve, you see stopped traffic ahead that the driver behind you cannot yet see. What does the manual suggest you do?
options: Hold your left arm straight out the window
Give the horn a sharp blast as you slow down
Tap your brake pedal quickly three or four times
Turn on your right turn signal to show you are stopping
questions.ref: p.39 Signal When You Slow Down: tap your brake pedal quickly three or four times to warn those behind you, such as when avoiding something in the road a driver behind cannot see, including stopped or slowing traffic.
questions.why: Tap your brake pedal quickly three or four times to warn drivers behind you. This helps when there is stopped traffic they cannot see. (Driver's Manual, p. 39)
wrong: An arm held straight out is the hand signal for a left turn.
The manual says to tap the brake pedal, not sound the horn.
A right turn signal means you are turning right, not stopping.

questions.q: Your turn signals are not working, and you need to turn right. Which hand signal shown in the manual should you give?
options: Left arm held straight out the window
Left arm bent up at the elbow, hand pointing up
Left arm waved in a circle out the window
Left arm bent down at the elbow, hand pointing down
questions.ref: p.39 Hand Signals illustration: Right Turn is shown as the left arm bent upward; Left Turn is the arm straight out; Slow or Stop is the arm bent downward.
questions.why: The hand signal for a right turn is the left arm bent up at the elbow, with the hand pointing up. (Driver's Manual, p. 39)
wrong: An arm held straight out means a left turn.
The manual does not show waving the arm in a circle.
An arm bent down means slow or stop.

questions.q: A driver ahead holds their left arm out the window, bent down at the elbow with the hand pointing toward the ground. What is the driver signaling?
options: A left turn
A right turn
Slowing or stopping
Pulling out to pass
questions.ref: p.39 Hand Signals illustration: arm bent downward = Slow or Stop; arm straight out = Left Turn; arm bent up = Right Turn.
questions.why: A left arm bent down at the elbow, with the hand pointing down, is the hand signal to slow or stop. (Driver's Manual, p. 39)
wrong: A left turn is shown with the arm held straight out.
A right turn is shown with the arm bent up.
The manual has no hand signal for passing; arm bent down means slow or stop.

questions.q: Your car breaks down on a highway, and you cannot get it off the roadway. Where should you try to stop?
options: In the left lane, closest to the median
Just past the top of a hill, out of the main flow
Just around a curve, where the road is widest
Where other drivers have a clear view of it
questions.ref: p.39 Use Emergency Signals: if you cannot get your vehicle off the roadway, try to stop where other drivers have a clear view (do not stop just over a hill or just around a curve).
questions.why: If you cannot get off the road, try to stop where other drivers have a clear view of your car. (Driver's Manual, p. 39)
wrong: The manual's rule is to stop where other drivers can clearly see you.
The manual says not to stop just over a hill.
The manual says not to stop just around a curve.

questions.q: Your disabled car is stuck on the side of a highway. Where should you place emergency flares?
options: In front of the vehicle
Next to the driver's door
Behind the vehicle
On the roof of the car
questions.ref: p.39 Use Emergency Signals: place emergency flares behind the vehicle; this allows other drivers to change lanes if necessary.
questions.why: Place emergency flares behind your vehicle. This gives other drivers time to change lanes if needed. (Driver's Manual, p. 39)
wrong: The manual says flares go behind the vehicle, where traffic is coming from.
The manual says flares go behind the vehicle.
The manual says flares go behind the vehicle.

questions.q: Your car has broken down, and you have no flares or other warning devices. What does the manual tell you to do?
options: Stand off the road, safe from traffic, and wave cars around
Stand in the lane behind your car and wave cars around it
Walk along the travel lane toward the nearest exit
Sit in the car with your seat belt on and wait
questions.ref: p.39 Use Emergency Signals: if you do not have flares or other warning devices, stand by the side of the road where you are safe from traffic and wave traffic around your vehicle; never stand in the roadway.
questions.why: Without flares, stand by the side of the road where you are safe from traffic, and wave traffic around your car. (Driver's Manual, p. 39)
wrong: The manual says never stand in the roadway.
The manual says never stand in the roadway.
The manual says to stand safely by the side of the road and wave traffic around.

questions.q: You get a flat tire on the left side of your car on a busy road, and changing it would put you in a traffic lane. What does the manual say?
options: Change it if someone stands behind you to warn traffic
Change it quickly with your hazard flashers on
Do not change it if you would be in a traffic lane
Change it if you place flares in front of the car first
questions.ref: p.39 Use Emergency Signals: never stand in the roadway; do not try to change a tire if it means you have to be in a traffic lane.
questions.why: Never stand in the roadway. Do not try to change a tire if it means you have to be in a traffic lane. (Driver's Manual, p. 39)
wrong: A helper does not change the rule; do not change it in a traffic lane.
Flashers do not change the rule; do not change it in a traffic lane.
Flares go behind the car, and you still should not stand in a traffic lane.

questions.q: Besides using your flashers, how does the manual say you can signal that your stopped car has an emergency?
options: Lift the hood or tie a white cloth to the antenna or mirror
Open the trunk and tie a red cloth to the rear bumper
Tie an orange cloth to the steering wheel and open windows
Leave the high beams on and lock all of the doors
questions.ref: p.39 Use Emergency Signals: lift the hood or tie a white cloth to the antenna, side mirror or door handle to signal an emergency.
questions.why: Lift the hood, or tie a white cloth to the antenna, side mirror, or door handle, to signal an emergency. (Driver's Manual, p. 39)
wrong: The manual says a white cloth, not red, and to lift the hood.
The manual says a white cloth on the antenna, mirror, or door handle.
The manual says to lift the hood or tie on a white cloth.

questions.q: Your brakes fail. Pumping the pedal does not work, and the parking brake does not stop you either. What should you do next?
options: Shift to lower gears and find a safe place to stop
Shift into reverse to slow the car down
Keep pumping the brake pedal until it starts working
Turn the ignition to the lock position to stop the car
questions.ref: p.39 Brake Failure: pump the pedal; if that does not work, use the parking brake; if that does not work, start shifting to lower gears and look for a safe place to slow to a stop.
questions.why: If pumping the brakes and the parking brake both fail, shift to lower gears and look for a safe place to stop. (Driver's Manual, p. 39)
wrong: The manual says to shift to lower gears, not into reverse.
Pumping already failed, so the next step is shifting to lower gears.
The manual says never turn the key to lock while moving, or the steering locks.

questions.q: A tire suddenly blows out at highway speed. Which action is WRONG according to the manual?
options: Hold the steering wheel tightly and keep straight
Pull off the road in a safe place
Take your foot off the gas and brake lightly
Brake hard right away and stop in your lane
questions.ref: p.39 Tire Blowout: hold the wheel tightly, keep straight, slow down gradually (foot off gas, brake lightly), and do not stop on the road if at all possible.
questions.why: After a blowout, slow down gradually and do not stop on the road if at all possible. Braking hard and stopping in your lane goes against that. (Driver's Manual, p. 39)
wrong: Holding the wheel tightly and going straight is what the manual tells you to do.
Pulling off the road in a safe place is what the manual tells you to do.
Easing off the gas and braking lightly is how the manual says to slow down.

questions.q: The engine suddenly dies while you are driving. What does the manual say about your brakes?
options: They work normally, with no extra effort needed
They stop working until you restart the engine
Only the parking brake will still work
They still work, but you may need to push hard
questions.ref: p.40 Power Failure: pull off the roadway; the brakes will still work, but you may have to push very hard on the brake pedal.
questions.why: If the engine dies, the brakes will still work. But you may have to push very hard on the pedal. (Driver's Manual, p. 40)
wrong: The manual warns you may have to push very hard.
The manual says the brakes will still work.
The manual says the regular brakes still work.

questions.q: Your headlights suddenly go out at night. You slow down, pull off the road, and try the switch a few times, but they stay off. What should you do?
options: Follow another car's taillights to get home
Drive slowly to a service station with your flashers on
Turn on your flashers and do not keep driving
Keep driving using only your parking lights
questions.ref: p.40 Headlight Failure: slow down and pull off; try the switch a few times; if that does not work, put on the emergency flashers, turn on signals or fog lights; do not operate your vehicle.
questions.why: If the headlights still will not work, turn on your emergency flashers, and do not keep driving. (Driver's Manual, p. 40)
wrong: The manual says do not operate your vehicle.
The manual says do not operate your vehicle.
The manual says never drive with only parking lights on.

questions.q: Your engine stalls while the car is still rolling. A passenger tells you to turn the key all the way to 'lock.' What does the manual warn?
options: The brakes will lock, and the car will go into a skid
The car will shift into park and stop suddenly
The steering will lock, and you will lose control
The airbags will turn off until you restart
questions.ref: p.40 Steering Wheel Locks: never turn the ignition to the 'lock' position while the vehicle is in motion, or the steering will lock and you will lose control.
questions.why: Never turn the key to lock while the car is moving. The steering will lock, and you will lose control. (Driver's Manual, p. 40)
wrong: The manual warns about the steering locking, not the brakes.
The manual warns about the steering locking.
The manual warns about the steering locking, not the airbags.

questions.q: The manual says drivers have three options for avoiding a collision. Which is NOT one of them?
options: Sound the horn and hold your course
Stop the vehicle as quickly as you can
Turn the vehicle away from the danger
Speed up to get clear of the danger
questions.ref: p.40 Avoiding Collisions: in avoiding a collision, drivers have three options: stop, turn or speed up.
questions.why: The manual says your three options to avoid a collision are to stop, turn, or speed up. Holding your course is not one of them. (Driver's Manual, p. 40)
wrong: Stopping is one of the three options.
Turning is one of the three options.
Speeding up is one of the three options.

questions.q: Your car does NOT have ABS. While braking hard, the wheels lock and you feel the car start to skid. What should you do?
options: Hold the pedal down and steer hard
Press the brake pedal even harder
Shift into neutral and coast
Quickly let up on the brake pedal
questions.ref: p.40 Stopping Quickly (without ABS): apply the brakes as hard as you can without locking them; if they lock up and you feel a skid, quickly let up on the brake pedal, then push down again once the skid stops.
questions.why: Without ABS, if the brakes lock and you start to skid, quickly let up on the brake pedal. Push down again once the skid stops. (Driver's Manual, p. 40)
wrong: Holding the pedal down is the advice for cars with ABS, not without.
Pressing harder would keep the wheels locked.
The manual says to let up on the brake, not shift to neutral.

questions.q: Your car has no ABS, and you must turn quickly to avoid a crash. What procedure does the manual describe?
options: Step on the brake, then let up and turn the wheel
Speed up and turn so the car does not skid
Turn the wheel first, then brake hard in the turn
Keep the brake pressed hard while you turn the wheel
questions.ref: p.40 Turning Quickly, Without ABS: step on the brake pedal, then let up and turn the steering wheel; braking slows the vehicle, puts more weight on the front tires, and allows a quicker turn.
questions.why: Without ABS, step on the brake, then let up and turn the wheel. Braking puts more weight on the front tires for a quicker turn. (Driver's Manual, p. 40)
wrong: The manual says to brake first, then let up and turn.
The manual says to brake first, then let up before turning.
Without ABS, braking hard while turning can make the car skid ahead.

questions.q: An oncoming car crosses the center line into your lane, and you cannot stop in time. The road edge to your right is open. What does the manual say is generally better?
options: Braking hard and staying in your own lane
Holding your course and sounding your horn loudly
Running off the road instead of a head-on crash
Steering left into the oncoming lane
questions.ref: p.40 Turning Quickly: it is generally better to run off the road than to crash head-on into another vehicle.
questions.why: The manual says it is generally better to run off the road than to crash head-on into another vehicle. (Driver's Manual, p. 40)
wrong: You cannot stop in time, so staying in your lane means a head-on crash.
The manual says to act, and running off the road beats a head-on crash.
Steering into the oncoming lane could cause another crash.

questions.q: Another vehicle is about to hit you from the side, and there is open room ahead of you. What does the manual suggest?
options: Shift to neutral and brace yourself against the seat
Speed up to get clear, then slow down once it passes
Brake hard so that the other vehicle passes in front of you
Steer toward the other vehicle to take a glancing blow
questions.ref: p.40 Speeding Up: it may be best to speed up when another vehicle is about to hit you from the side or from behind and there is room to the front; be sure to slow down once the danger has passed.
questions.why: If a car is about to hit you from the side and there is room ahead, speeding up may be best. Slow down once the danger passes. (Driver's Manual, p. 40)
wrong: The manual says to try to avoid the crash, and speeding up can do that here.
With room ahead, the manual suggests speeding up, not braking.
The manual suggests speeding up to get out of danger.

questions.q: You are steering out of a skid, and the car begins to straighten out. What should you do next?
options: Press the brake firmly now that it is straight
Hold the wheel where it is until the car stops
Turn the steering wheel back the other way
Let go of the wheel so it centers on its own
questions.ref: p.40 Dealing with Skids: as soon as the vehicle begins to straighten out, turn the steering wheel back the other way, or the vehicle may swing around and start a new skid.
questions.why: As soon as the car begins to straighten out, turn the steering wheel back the other way. If you do not, you could start a new skid. (Driver's Manual, p. 40)
wrong: The manual says to stay off the brake in a skid.
If you do not turn back, the car may swing around the other way.
The manual says to keep steering and correcting.

questions.q: You hear that a house fire is burning a few streets away, and your friend wants to drive by to see it. What does the manual say?
options: You may go if you leave your hazard flashers on
Do not go; you could block rescue vehicles
You may go slowly as long as you stay in your car
You may go if you park at least 500 feet from the fire
questions.ref: p.41 Traffic Crashes: never drive to the scene of an accident, fire, or other disaster just to look; you may block the way for police, firefighters, ambulances, tow trucks, and other rescue vehicles.
questions.why: Never drive to a fire or crash just to look. You may block police, firefighters, ambulances, and other rescue vehicles. (Driver's Manual, p. 41)
wrong: The manual says never drive there just to look.
The manual says never drive there just to look.
The manual says never drive there just to look.

questions.q: While parking, you dent an empty parked car, and you cannot find the owner. What must you do?
options: Leave a note in plain sight with the date, time, and contact info
Leave a note that gives only your name and license plate number
Wait 30 minutes, and then leave if the owner does not return
Leave, since no one was hurt and the owner is not around
questions.ref: p.41 Report the Accident: if the accident involves a parked vehicle, try to find the owner; if you cannot, leave a note where it can be seen with the date and time and information on how the owner can reach you.
questions.why: Try to find the owner. If you cannot, leave a note where it can be seen with the date, time, and how the owner can reach you. (Driver's Manual, p. 41)
wrong: The note must include the date and time and how to reach you.
The manual says to leave a note if you cannot find the owner.
You must try to find the owner or leave a note.

questions.q: You are in a crash in which the other driver is injured. The other driver says you can just swap phone numbers and go home. What does the manual say?
options: You may leave once you have exchanged information
You may leave if the other driver signs a statement
You may leave if the injury is only minor
Leaving before police talk to you is a crime
questions.ref: p.41 Traffic Crashes: it is a crime to leave a crash site in which your vehicle was involved if there is an injury or death before police have talked to you and gotten all the information they need.
questions.why: It is a crime to leave a crash with an injury or death before police have talked to you and gotten what they need. (Driver's Manual, p. 41)
wrong: Exchanging information is not enough when someone is injured.
A signed statement does not change the rule.
Any injury means you must wait for police.

questions.q: You have a minor crash. No one is hurt, but both bumpers are dented. Must you report it to police?
options: No, because no one was injured or killed
Only if the damage is more than $1,000
Yes, because there is property damage
Only if the other driver has no insurance
questions.ref: p.41 Report the Accident: you must report the accident to police if there is an injury, a death or property damage.
questions.why: You must report a crash to police if there is an injury, a death, or property damage. Dented bumpers are property damage. (Driver's Manual, p. 41)
wrong: Property damage alone means you must report it.
The manual sets no dollar amount; any property damage counts.
Insurance does not matter; property damage must be reported.

questions.q: You see in your mirror that the car behind you is about to hit you from the rear. What should you do?
options: Press back into your seat, head against the head restraint
Lean forward over the wheel to brace for the impact
Turn sharply to the left to get out of the way of the impact
Take your foot off the brake to soften the impact
questions.ref: p.41 Hit From the Rear: press yourself against the back of your seat and put your head against the head restraint; be ready to apply your brakes so you will not be pushed into another vehicle.
questions.why: Press yourself against the back of your seat with your head against the head restraint. Be ready to brake so you are not pushed into another car. (Driver's Manual, p. 41)
wrong: Your body is thrown backward, so press back into your seat.
The manual says to brace in your seat and be ready to brake.
The manual says to be ready to brake so you are not pushed into another car.

questions.q: Your car is about to be hit from the side. According to the manual, which way will your body be thrown?
options: Backward, into the back of your seat
Forward, toward the steering wheel
Away from the side that is hit
Toward the side that is hit
questions.ref: p.41 Hit From the Side: if your vehicle is hit from the side, your body will be thrown towards the side that is hit; front airbags will not help, and lap and shoulder belts help keep you behind the wheel.
questions.why: If you are hit from the side, your body is thrown toward the side that is hit. (Driver's Manual, p. 41)
wrong: You are thrown backward when hit from the rear.
The manual says toward the side that is hit.
The manual says toward the side that is hit, not away from it.

questions.q: A collision from the front is about to happen. What does the manual say you should try to do?
options: Hold the wheel straight so the airbag lines up with you
Take your hands off the wheel before the airbag opens
Speed up so the crash is over more quickly
Turn so you take a glancing blow, not a head-on hit
questions.ref: p.41 Hit From the Front: try to have a 'glancing blow' rather than being struck head-on; if a collision is about to happen, you should try to turn the vehicle.
questions.why: Try to turn the car so you take a glancing blow instead of being hit head-on. You might even miss it. (Driver's Manual, p. 41)
wrong: The manual says to turn the car for a glancing blow.
You need your hands on the wheel to turn away.
The manual says to turn for a glancing blow, not speed up.

questions.q: An injured person at a crash scene is bleeding badly from the arm. What does the manual tell you to do?
options: Press directly on the wound with your hand or a cloth
Move the person so the arm hangs lower than the heart
Wait for the ambulance, since bleeding needs a doctor's care
Give the person water to replace the lost fluid
questions.ref: p.41 If someone is injured: if there is bleeding, apply pressure directly on the wound with your hand or with a cloth; even severe bleeding can almost always be stopped or slowed this way.
questions.why: Apply pressure directly on the wound with your hand or a cloth. Even severe bleeding can almost always be stopped or slowed this way. (Driver's Manual, p. 41)
wrong: The manual says do not move the injured unless they are in danger.
The manual says to press on the wound right away.
The manual says not to give injured people anything to drink.

questions.q: An injured crash victim who is awake asks you for a drink of water. What does the manual say?
options: Give nothing to drink, not even water
Give water only after checking the person's breathing
Give small sips of water to prevent shock
Give water only if the person is not bleeding
questions.ref: p.41 If someone is injured: do not give injured persons anything to drink, not even water.
questions.why: Do not give injured people anything to drink, not even water. (Driver's Manual, p. 41)
wrong: The manual says nothing to drink, even after checking breathing.
The manual says nothing to drink; keep them warm to help prevent shock.
The manual says nothing to drink, bleeding or not.

questions.q: To help keep an injured crash victim from going into shock, what does the manual advise?
options: Lay the person on the cool pavement to calm them
Walk the person around to keep the blood flowing
Cover the person with a blanket or coat
Give the person a warm drink, such as tea
questions.ref: p.41 If someone is injured: to help prevent an injured person from going into shock, cover them with a blanket or coat to keep them warm.
questions.why: To help prevent shock, cover the injured person with a blanket or coat to keep them warm. (Driver's Manual, p. 41)
wrong: The manual says to keep the person warm.
The manual says do not move the injured unless they are in danger.
The manual says do not give injured people anything to drink.

questions.q: After a crash, you exchange information with the other driver. Which item is NOT on the manual's list?
options: Insurance company and policy number
Social Security number
Make, model, and year of the vehicle
Driver's license number
questions.ref: p.41 Report the Accident: exchange name, address, driver's license number, vehicle information (plate, make, model, year), and insurance company and policy number.
questions.why: You exchange name, address, license number, vehicle details, and insurance information. A Social Security number is not on the list. (Driver's Manual, p. 41)
wrong: Insurance company and policy number are on the list.
Make, model, and year are on the list.
Driver's license number is on the list.

questions.q: You are on a multi-lane road and a solid white line separates your lane from the lane beside you, which goes the same direction. What does it mean?
options: It marks the right edge of the roadway
Stay in your lane unless a special situation requires a change
You may change lanes whenever it is safe to do so, even to pass
Traffic in the next lane goes the opposite way
questions.ref: p.43 Lane Lines: solid white lines between lanes of traffic indicate you should stay in your lane unless a special situation requires you to change lanes.
questions.why: A solid white line between lanes going the same way means stay in your lane unless a special situation requires a change. (Driver's Manual, p. 43)
wrong: Edge lines mark the side of the road; this line is between two lanes.
That describes a dashed white line, not a solid one.
Lane lines are white and separate traffic going the same direction.

questions.q: A dashed line separates your lane from the lane to your left. How can you tell whether traffic in that lane is going your direction?
options: A dashed line always means the same direction
A dashed line always means traffic is coming toward you
White means the same direction; yellow means opposite
Yellow means the same direction; white means opposite
questions.ref: p.43 Lane Lines and Center Lines: lane lines are white lines that separate lanes traveling in the same direction; center lines are yellow lines that separate traffic moving in opposite directions.
questions.why: White lines separate lanes going the same direction. Yellow lines separate traffic going in opposite directions. (Driver's Manual, p. 43)
wrong: A dashed yellow line separates traffic going opposite ways, so the color matters.
A dashed white line separates lanes going the same direction.
That has it backwards; yellow means traffic goes the opposite way.

questions.q: A solid white line runs along the far right side of the road, outside the right-hand travel lane. What does it show?
options: A lane you may cross to pass on the right
The right edge of the roadway
The start of a no-passing zone
A lane reserved for bicycles only
questions.ref: p.43 Edge Lines: edge lines are solid lines along the side of the road that show you where the edge of the road is located; solid white lines are used on the right of the roadway edge.
questions.why: Edge lines show where the edge of the road is. Solid white edge lines are used on the right side. (Driver's Manual, p. 43)
wrong: An edge line shows the edge of the road, not a passing lane.
A no-passing zone is marked with a pennant sign and center line markings.
The manual says a bicycle lane is marked by signs; this line marks the road's edge.

questions.q: According to the manual, where are yield lines used?
options: Where drivers must yield, such as a mid-block crosswalk
Wherever a stop sign controls an intersection
At every railroad crossing, right in front of the tracks
Along the edge of lanes reserved for buses
questions.ref: p.43 Center Lines: Yield Lines are used at locations where drivers are required to yield, such as a mid-block crosswalk.
questions.why: Yield lines are used where drivers are required to yield, such as at a mid-block crosswalk. (Driver's Manual, p. 43)
wrong: At a stop sign, you stop before the stop line.
The manual describes yield lines at places like mid-block crosswalks.
Bus lanes are marked by signs and white diamonds.

questions.q: You are on a two-lane road with solid double yellow center lines, and you want to turn left into a driveway. What does the manual say?
options: You may cross only to make a U-turn
You must go to the next intersection to turn
You may cross only if the driveway is marked
You may cross them to make the left turn
questions.ref: p.44 Solid Double Yellow Lines: solid yellow lines may be crossed to make a left turn to or from an alley, private road, driveway, or street.
questions.why: Solid double yellow lines may be crossed to make a left turn to or from an alley, private road, driveway, or street. (Driver's Manual, p. 44)
wrong: The manual says you may cross them to turn left into a driveway.
The manual says you may cross them to turn left into a driveway.
The manual allows it for any driveway, with no marking needed.

questions.q: You are stopping for a stop sign at an intersection that has a painted stop line. Where must you stop?
options: Before your vehicle reaches the stop line
Just past the stop line, where you can see
At the far edge of the crosswalk
With your front bumper on top of the stop line
questions.ref: p.44 Crosswalks and Stop Lines: when required to stop because of a sign or signal, you must stop before your vehicle reaches the stop line.
questions.why: When a sign or signal requires you to stop, you must stop before your vehicle reaches the stop line. (Driver's Manual, p. 44)
wrong: You must stop before the line, not past it.
You must stop before the stop line.
You must stop before you reach the line.

questions.q: A lane is marked with signs that say 'Transit' or 'Bus.' Who may use it?
options: Buses and vehicles with two or more people
Buses only
Any vehicle during non-rush hours
Buses and bicycles
questions.ref: p.44 Reserved Lanes: 'Transit' or 'bus' means the lane is for bus use only.
questions.why: A lane marked Transit or Bus is for bus use only. (Driver's Manual, p. 44)
wrong: Lanes for cars with more than one person are HOV lanes, not bus lanes.
The manual says a bus lane is for bus use only.
Bicycles have their own lanes marked Bicycle.

questions.q: Lanes that carry traffic one way at certain times and the opposite way at other times are usually marked by:
options: A solid yellow line beside a dashed yellow line
Double solid white lines
Single dashed white lines
Double-dashed yellow lines
questions.ref: p.44 Reversible Lanes: these lanes are usually marked by double-dashed yellow lines.
questions.why: Reversible lanes are usually marked by double-dashed yellow lines. (Driver's Manual, p. 44)
wrong: A dashed yellow line beside a solid yellow line is a passing rule marking.
A double solid white line means no lane changes.
A dashed white line means you may change lanes when safe.

questions.q: On a road with reversible lanes, a flashing yellow 'X' appears over your lane. What does it mean?
options: Use of the lane is changing; leave it when safe
You may not drive in the lane at all
You may use the lane to go straight
The lane may be used only for turning
questions.ref: p.44 Reversible Lanes: a flashing yellow 'X' means the lane is only for turning; a steady yellow 'X' means use of the lane is changing; a red 'X' means you cannot use it.
questions.why: Over a reversible lane, a flashing yellow X means the lane is only for turning. (Driver's Manual, p. 44)
wrong: A steady yellow X means the lane use is changing.
A red X means you may not use the lane.
A green arrow means you can use the lane.

questions.q: In a standard vertical traffic light with three lights, which color is at the bottom?
options: Green
It varies by town
Yellow
Red
questions.ref: p.45 Traffic Signals: traffic lights are usually green, yellow, and red (bottom to top) when together.
questions.why: Traffic lights are usually green, yellow, and red from bottom to top, so green is at the bottom. (Driver's Manual, p. 45)
wrong: The manual gives a standard order: green, yellow, red from the bottom up.
Yellow is in the middle.
Red is at the top.

questions.q: You are stopped at a red light, and it turns green. A car from the cross street is still in the intersection. What must you do?
options: Tap your horn and then proceed
Go, since the other driver ran a red light
Go, since the green light gives you the right-of-way to proceed
Let crossing traffic clear the intersection first
questions.ref: p.45 Green traffic lights: if you are stopped and then the light turns green, you must allow crossing traffic to clear the intersection before you go ahead.
questions.why: If you are stopped and the light turns green, you must let crossing traffic clear the intersection before you go. (Driver's Manual, p. 45)
wrong: The manual says to wait for crossing traffic to clear, not honk.
You must still let the crossing car clear first.
A green light still requires you to let crossing traffic clear.

questions.q: You want to turn right, and the signal for your lane shows a red arrow pointing right. Under the manual's rule, when may you turn?
options: After a full stop, if no traffic or pedestrians are coming
When the oncoming traffic gets a red light
When the red arrow goes out and a green signal comes on
Right away, since right turns on red are allowed
questions.ref: p.45 Arrows: a red arrow means you must stop and you cannot go in the direction of the arrow; you may proceed when the red arrow goes out and a green arrow or light goes on.
questions.why: A red arrow means stop, and you cannot go in the direction of the arrow. You may go when the red arrow goes out and a green signal comes on. (Driver's Manual, p. 45)
wrong: That is the rule for turning right on a red light, not a red arrow.
You wait for the red arrow to go out, not for other traffic.
A red arrow means you cannot go that way at all.

questions.q: You are turning left on a green arrow. What does the manual say about other traffic while the arrow is green?
options: You must still yield to oncoming traffic
There should be no oncoming or crossing traffic
Oncoming traffic also has a green light at the same time
Crossing traffic may turn right on red into you
questions.ref: p.45 Arrows: a green arrow means you can safely turn in the direction of the arrow; there should be no on-coming or crossing traffic while the arrow is green.
questions.why: A green arrow means you can safely turn. There should be no oncoming or crossing traffic while it is green. (Driver's Manual, p. 45)
wrong: That is the rule for a steady green light, not a green arrow.
There should be no oncoming traffic while the arrow is green.
There should be no crossing traffic while the arrow is green.

questions.q: A pedestrian signal over the road has one round yellow light centered beneath two round red lights placed side by side. What is it called?
options: A rectangular rapid flashing beacon
A lane-use control signal
A HAWK signal
A railroad crossing signal
questions.ref: p.45 HAWK Signals: the HAWK is composed of a circular yellow signal centered under two horizontally-aligned circular red signals; it is activated by a push button.
questions.why: A HAWK signal has one round yellow light centered under two round red lights side by side. (Driver's Manual, p. 45)
wrong: A rapid flashing beacon goes under a pedestrian crossing sign; this is a HAWK.
Lane-use signals use green arrows and X shapes over lanes.
That light pattern is the HAWK pedestrian signal.

questions.q: You approach a HAWK pedestrian signal, and all of its lights are dark. What should you do?
options: Proceed through the crossing
Slow down and prepare to stop
Treat it as a broken signal and stop
Stop, then go if the crosswalk is clear
questions.ref: p.45 HAWK: Dark means the signal has not been activated; vehicles proceed through the pedestrian crossing.
questions.why: A dark HAWK signal has not been activated. Vehicles proceed through the crossing. (Driver's Manual, p. 45)
wrong: Dark means no one has pushed the button, so you may proceed.
Dark is normal for a HAWK signal and means you may go.
You do not need to stop when the signal is dark.

questions.q: A HAWK signal starts flashing yellow. What does this mean?
options: The signal is about to turn off
A pedestrian has activated the signal
Pedestrians are in the crosswalk now
Drivers must stop and then may proceed
questions.ref: p.45 HAWK: Flashing Yellow means a pedestrian has activated the HAWK signal.
questions.why: A flashing yellow HAWK signal means a pedestrian has activated it. (Driver's Manual, p. 45)
wrong: A flashing red light means the signal is about to turn off.
Solid red means pedestrians are in the crosswalk.
Flashing red means stop, then go when pedestrians have cleared.

questions.q: A HAWK signal is showing solid red, with both red lights steady. What does this mean?
options: The signal has not been activated, so you may proceed
A pedestrian has just pushed the button to activate it
Pedestrians are in the crosswalk, and you must stop
The signal is about to go dark, so you may go if clear
questions.ref: p.45 HAWK: Solid Red - pedestrians in crosswalk; motorists must stop. (Dark = not activated; Flashing Yellow = activated; Flashing Red = about to deactivate, may proceed once pedestrians clear.)
questions.why: Solid red on a HAWK signal means pedestrians are in the crosswalk, and drivers must stop. (Driver's Manual, p. 45)
wrong: A dark signal means it has not been activated.
Flashing yellow means a pedestrian has just activated it.
Flashing red means the signal is about to turn off.

questions.q: You see a five-sided sign shaped like a house. What does this shape mark?
options: A school zone or school crossing
A railroad crossing ahead
A yield point at an intersection ahead
The start of a no-passing zone
questions.ref: p.46 Shapes: pentagon (five-sided) marks school zones and warns about school crossings; circle = railroad; pennant = no passing; triangle = yield.
questions.why: A five-sided pentagon sign marks school zones and warns about school crossings. (Driver's Manual, p. 46)
wrong: A round sign warns of a railroad crossing.
A downward triangle means yield.
A three-sided pennant marks a no-passing zone.

questions.q: You come to a complete stop at an eight-sided sign. What must you do before pulling forward?
options: Nothing more, since stopping first gives you the right-of-way
Yield to vehicles or pedestrians coming from either direction
Yield only to pedestrians who are already in the crosswalk
Yield only to vehicles approaching from your right side
questions.ref: p.46 Octagon: you must come to a complete stop at the sign, stop line, pedestrian crosswalk or curb, then yield the right-of-way to any vehicle or pedestrian approaching from either direction.
questions.why: At a stop sign, come to a complete stop. Then yield to any vehicle or pedestrian coming from either direction. (Driver's Manual, p. 46)
wrong: Stopping does not give you the right-of-way; you must still yield.
You must yield to vehicles too, not only pedestrians.
You must yield to traffic from either direction.

questions.q: You approach a downward-pointing red-and-white triangle sign, and no traffic is coming on the road you are entering. Must you come to a full stop?
options: Yes, you must always come to a full stop at this sign
No, slow down, yield, and stop only if necessary
No, and you may keep your speed if it is clear
Yes, but only between sunset and sunrise
questions.ref: p.46 Triangle: Yield - slow down to a speed reasonable for the conditions and yield the right-of-way; stop if necessary. p.47 Yield sign: downward pointing triangle, red and white with red letters.
questions.why: At a yield sign, slow down to a reasonable speed and yield the right-of-way. Stop only if necessary. (Driver's Manual, p. 46)
wrong: A full stop is required at a stop sign, not a yield sign.
You must still slow down at a yield sign.
The yield rule is the same at all hours.

questions.q: According to the manual, horizontal (wider than tall) rectangular signs generally:
options: Tell you the law you must obey
Mark a school zone or school crossing
Give directions or information
Warn of a railroad crossing
questions.ref: p.46 Rectangle/square: vertical signs generally give instructions or tell you the law; horizontal signs may give directions or information.
questions.why: Horizontal rectangular signs may give directions or information. Vertical ones generally tell you the law. (Driver's Manual, p. 46)
wrong: Vertical rectangles generally tell you the law.
A five-sided pentagon marks school zones.
A round sign warns of a railroad crossing.

questions.q: Which statement about black-and-white signs is correct?
options: Some are warning signs, and others point to services
Some are guide signs, and others mark parks
Some mark work zones, and others mark detours
Some are regulatory, and others are route markers
questions.ref: p.47 Colors: some black and white signs are regulatory signs and must be obeyed; other black and white signs are used as route markers.
questions.why: Some black and white signs are regulatory and must be obeyed. Others are route markers. (Driver's Manual, p. 47)
wrong: Yellow is for warnings and blue is for services.
Green is for guide signs and brown is for parks.
Orange is for work zone warnings.

questions.q: Which group lists only signs that the manual says are red regulatory signs?
options: STOP, DO NOT ENTER, DETOUR, and MERGE
STOP, YIELD, ONE WAY, and SPEED LIMIT
STOP, YIELD, DO NOT ENTER, and WRONG WAY
YIELD, WRONG WAY, SIGNAL AHEAD, and NO U-TURN
questions.ref: p.47 Colors: all red signs are regulatory signs and must be obeyed; they include STOP, YIELD, DO NOT ENTER or WRONG WAY.
questions.why: All red signs are regulatory and must be obeyed. They include STOP, YIELD, DO NOT ENTER, and WRONG WAY. (Driver's Manual, p. 47)
wrong: DETOUR is an orange work sign, and MERGE is a yellow warning sign.
ONE WAY and SPEED LIMIT are not on the manual's list of red signs.
SIGNAL AHEAD is a yellow warning sign.

questions.q: A white sign shows a black arrow with a red circle around it and a red slash across it. What does this kind of sign mean?
options: The action shown is recommended but optional
The action shown by the symbol is prohibited
A warning that the road ahead turns that way
The action shown is allowed only at certain times
questions.ref: p.47 Regulatory Signs: some regulatory signs have a red circle with a red slash over a symbol; these signs prohibit certain actions, i.e., 'no left turn,' 'no right turn,' 'no U-turn.'
questions.why: A red circle with a red slash over a symbol means the action shown is prohibited, like no left turn or no U-turn. (Driver's Manual, p. 47)
wrong: The red circle and slash means the action is not allowed.
Warnings about the road are on yellow signs; this one forbids the action.
The red circle and slash means the action is not allowed.

questions.q: At which location would you NOT expect to see a Do Not Enter sign, according to the manual?
options: At an exit ramp, where you would be going the wrong way
At a highway entrance ramp you are allowed to use
At one-way streets, facing traffic going the wrong way
At a crossover on a divided roadway
questions.ref: p.47 Do Not Enter: seen at roadway openings you should not enter, such as exit ramps where you would be going in the wrong direction, crossovers on divided roadways, and on one-way streets.
questions.why: Do Not Enter signs mark openings you should not enter, like exit ramps, crossovers on divided roads, and one-way streets. An entrance ramp you may use is not one of them. (Driver's Manual, p. 47)
wrong: Exit ramps where you would go the wrong way are on the manual's list.
One-way streets are on the manual's list.
Crossovers on divided roads are on the manual's list.

questions.q: The manual makes special mention of NO U-TURN signs at what kind of location?
options: Entrances to public parking garages and parking lots
Mid-block crosswalks near schools and playgrounds
Openings in a divided highway leading to the other side
Railroad crossings that have both gates and flashing lights
questions.ref: p.48 No U-Turn: special mention should be made of 'NO U-TURN' signs posted on divided highways or expressways where there is an opening that leads to the other side.
questions.why: The manual makes special mention of NO U-TURN signs on divided highways, where an opening leads to the other side. (Driver's Manual, p. 48)
wrong: The manual points to openings in divided highways, not parking lots.
The manual points to openings in divided highways, not crosswalks.
The manual points to openings in divided highways, not railroad crossings.

questions.q: A white vertical rectangular sign for your lane shows a black arrow pointing straight up and a second arrow curving off to the left. What does it tell you?
options: Keep to the left of the traffic island just ahead
You may go straight or turn left from this lane
The road curves to the left ahead, so slow down
Only left turns are allowed from this lane ahead
questions.ref: p.48 Lane Use Control: this sign indicates permitted movement from a lane (the pictured sign shows a straight arrow and a left-turn arrow).
questions.why: A lane use control sign shows the moves allowed from that lane. Here, you may go straight or turn left. (Driver's Manual, p. 48)
wrong: A Keep Right sign is the one about traffic islands.
Curve warnings are yellow diamond signs, not white lane signs.
The straight arrow means going straight is also allowed.

questions.q: Ahead of you is a traffic island in the middle of the road with a Keep Right sign. What must you do?
options: Stop before the island and yield
Drive on the side shown by the arrow
Drive on whichever side has less traffic
Move right only if traffic is coming
questions.ref: p.48 Keep Right: this sign tells you where to drive when you approach traffic islands, medians or other obstructions; you must drive to the side indicated by the arrow.
questions.why: A Keep Right sign tells you where to drive around traffic islands or medians. You must drive on the side shown by the arrow. (Driver's Manual, p. 48)
wrong: The sign does not mean stop; it tells you which side to drive on.
You must drive on the side the arrow shows.
You must always drive on the side the arrow shows.

questions.q: According to the manual, what are passing areas and no-passing signs based on?
options: How far you can see ahead
The posted speed limit
